Katalog Berita (Halaman 26/58)

#6402. A South African dig shows early humans were already showing signs of advanced, complex thinking 60,000 years ago

60,000-year-old red ochre from a South African cave revealed hidden antelope proteins, proving early humans intentionally mixed animal parts into their ancient recipes.

It is a 60,000-year-old cold case that scientists finally solved using modern technology. By hunting for ancient proteins hidden in a patch of red dirt, researchers discovered that early humans deliberately mixed crushed clay with the remains of a massive African antelope.

This proves that modern science can now unlock the exact recipes used by humans in the Stone Age.

Between 2011 and 2013, archaeologists at Klipdrift Shelter in South Africa dug through a thin red ochre surface that may have been over 3 feet (1 meter) long. The shelter sits in the coastal cliffs of De Hoop Nature Reserve.

Bits of it were bagged and archived at the University of the Witwatersrand‘s satellite lab in Cape Town.

Years later Zahra Haghighi of the University of Bergen in Norway pulled five of those bags for protein analysis. Two held collagen from a common eland, a large antelope native to southern Africa.

The layer is about 60,000 years old. Haghighi’s team reads the result as eland material mixed with ochre powder on purpose, or as an ochre-treated eland hide left at the site. Two positive samples are not enough to pick between them.

Klipdrift Shelter is about 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Cape Town. It is one of three sites of the Klipdrift Complex, with Klipdrift Cave and Klipdrift Cave Lower.

Bergen’s SFF Centre for Early Sapiens Behaviour (SapienCE) lists the complex among the sites its team has exclusive access to. Crews excavated there in 2011, 2012, 2013 and 2018.

Single-grain luminescence dates the shelter’s 23 Middle Stone Age units to between about 52,000 years ago at the top and 72,000 at the bottom. Out came stone tools, marine shells, animal bones, hearths, engraved ostrich eggshell and 597 pieces of ochre.

Layer PBE, one of the dig’s numbered sediment layers, where the red surface lay, is part of the Howiesons Poort, a stone tool phase of southern Africa.

Patches of ochre powder of various sizes turned up all through those layers. This one was exceptional, possibly 16 inches (40 centimeters) wide, with surviving pieces 5 to 7 millimeters thick.

Its precise extent was not documented during the dig, and the surface was taken out entirely in 2011 to 2013. The size estimate therefore comes from site notes and from photographs, some of them by Magnus Haaland and Ole Unhammer.

Haghighi, first author of the paper, chose five archived samples from layers PBD, PBE, PCA and PBA-PBB, weighing 30 to 150 milligrams each.

None had been collected with protein work in mind. The export permits came from Heritage Western Cape and the South African Heritage Resources Agency.

Her co-authors include Takumi Tsutaya of Kyushu University in Japan and Enrico Cappellini of the University of Copenhagen. Sediment does not give up proteins the way bone does, so the group devised a method it calls AB (acid and base) digestion.

Two samples of about 130 milligrams sat in a guanidine buffer at 99°C (210°F) for 10 minutes. Then came hydrochloric acid overnight at 4°C (39°F), and then sodium hydroxide. Enzymes then chopped up whatever protein had come loose.

That screen turned up mammal collagen. A second extraction with strong acid and no enzyme followed on all five samples.

The peptides were read on an Exploris 480 Orbitrap mass spectrometer. The search used 711 mammal collagen sequences plus those of 44 African bovid species.

Collagen was confidently identified in two of the five, one sample from PBE and one from PBD, which sits right above it.

The COL1A1 chain, one of the two protein chains that make up type I collagen, matched several African bovids, the cattle-and-antelope family. Fragments of the COL1A2 chain matched one species alone, the common eland, Taurotragus oryx.

Sixty-nine peptides were identified, adding up to 171 amino acids or 16.5 percent of COL1A2. A proline at position 693, a serine at 720 and a threonine at 878 occur in eland only. The 720 and 878 sites were picked up in both layers, in at least three spectra apiece.

The giant eland, the other member of the genus, now lives in central Africa and has no published collagen sequence. The authors assumed the two species kept their present ranges 60,000 years ago.

Nearly every asparagine and glutamine, two of the amino acids in the peptides, had deamidated, a chemical change that builds up over long spans of time.

The paper suggests iron in the ochre may have helped the collagen last. The oldest ancient DNA recovered in Africa is about 18,000 years old. Older material calls for protein work, as with the ancient proteins pulled from Homo naledi fossils in South Africa.

Stray eland bone in the sediment would also leave collagen. So 15 samples went under optical microscopes, and some under a Zeiss Supra 55VP scanning electron microscope at the University of Bergen’s ELMILAB.

Only four of the 15 had anything resembling bone, one or two fragments apiece, none over about 0.1 inch (3 millimeters). Three of those four were from PBD, and PBE had none at all.

A thin section of the PBE surface mixed rounded ochre particles of around 1 micrometer with fragments of 2 to 5 millimeters.

That range, plus the quantity of ochre needed, supports the authors’ view that people formed the feature. They described the eland collagen as “most probably due to human action.”

Earlier work on the shelter’s animal bones had already identified eland among the remains.

The paper offers two scenarios. Either eland protein went into an ochre mixture that became part of the surface, or an ochre-coated eland hide was left in the shelter. In the second case the hide decayed and its ochre stayed in place.

Elsewhere in South Africa, two abalone shells at Blombos Cave, along the same coast, held an ochre-rich compound around 100,000 years old. At Sibudu, milk proteins on a stone flake pointed to a paint of ochre and milk about 49,000 years old.

Ochre has been linked to hafting glue, hide work, medicine and sunscreen. Sunscreen comes up in research on how Homo sapiens coped with intense UV light.

In an October 21 release, Kyushu University said evidence of organic components mixed with ochre had been “extremely rare, especially in Africa.”

All of this hangs on two of five small samples from a single feature at a single site. Which eland tissue the collagen came from is not known. The authors wrote that working it out would need a database built to tell tissues apart.

Eland are revered in San mythology, the paper notes, yet the authors called this one case “not sufficient to support the ritual significance of eland” in the Middle Stone Age.

They want the work repeated at other sites from that period. In Senegal, Middle Stone Age tools stayed in use 20,000 years longer than once thought.

The mass spectrometry data are in the PRIDE archive under PXD069507. The red surface in layer PBE no longer exists at Klipdrift. What is left of it is a handful of small bags of sediment in Cape Town, and two of them held the eland.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

#6401. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6399. Extreme heatwaves may cross a threshold that makes them even hotter

A feedback loop involving dry soil and high pressure may intensify extreme heatwaves, helping explain why some shatter temperature records.

As the planet warms, the most extreme heatwaves might be expected to warm at roughly the same rate as other hot spells.

The Pacific Northwest heatwave of 2021 beat the old record by 8.3°F (4.6°C). In parts of Europe, the hottest summer days have been warming faster than ordinary hot ones.

A new study finds a reason. Past a certain temperature, drying soil, high pressure, and the heat itself start reinforcing one another.

Where it operates, the loop supplies about a tenth of the extra heat at the peak of the most extreme heatwaves.

Heatwaves caused more than 70,000 excess deaths in Europe in 2003 and 60,000 in 2022, the authors wrote.

Yinglin Tian of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research led the work with colleagues at IIASA, Columbia University, and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

The team trained a computer program on 45 years of weather records.

“The two-way relationship between rising temperatures and drying soils has been understood for a while and is already factored into what we expect from a typical extreme heat event,” Tian said.

“But when we look at these mega heatwaves that have been significantly outstripping previous temperature records, what we’re seeing is that once you reach a certain temperature, all three factors – drying soils, high pressure and extreme heat – begin to interact and drive each other further in a way that we haven’t understood before.”

One driver of a summer heatwave is a large, slow-moving zone of high pressure, the kind behind a heat dome. Air sinks and warms inside it, and clear skies let more sunlight reach the ground.

The other is the ground itself. Wet soil cools the air above it as water evaporates, the way sweat cools skin.

As a heatwave drags on, the soil dries out, the cooling fades, and the surface heats faster.

The records, from the Copernicus climate archive, covered every summer from 1979 to 2023. The program learned to predict the daily high, averaged over three days, from two inputs.

One was the strength of the high pressure several miles overhead, and the other the moisture in the top layer of soil.

A second technique then split each prediction into three parts. Two were the shares from high pressure alone and from soil alone.

The third captures the additional heat associated with high pressure and dry soil acting together.

In Central Europe, the loop stayed small until the daily high climbed nearly 7°F (3.8°C) above the region’s average summer high.

Past that line, every extra degree of heat brought another tenth of a degree from the interaction.

At the peak of the 2022 Central European heatwave, the loop accounted for 13% of the extra heat. High pressure supplied 55% and dry soil 32%.

The two familiar drivers still produced most of the heat, and the loop was the extra on top. Across all the hot spots the team found, the loop’s share averaged 10%.

The hot spots covered about 15% of land in the mid-latitudes, the band that holds most of Europe and the northern United States.

The loop was strongest where summers are normally humid. Soil there starts a heatwave wet, so it can lose far more water.

In these normally humid regions, soil moisture fell rapidly during roughly the first 12 days of a heatwave.

In Central Europe, the chance that a summer day cleared the threshold was 6% between 1979 and 1983. In 2018–2022, it was 23%.

The area where the loop operates grew by about 25% between the first half of the record and the second.

The loop also explained about a third of the year-to-year change in the gap between the hottest Central European days and an ordinary warm one.

High pressure and dry soil each explained less.

The pattern may help explain why Europe’s heat waves keep pushing the continent beyond its records, and why future heatwaves may do so by wider margins.

“If we’re right and this interaction is making the most extreme heat events even hotter, it means we could be in store for more severe future heatwave risks than what is currently expected,” said Kai Kornhuber, a co-author at IIASA and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

The team ran the same test on 12 global climate models from the CMIP project, plus 40 runs of a single model. More than 90% of the models failed to reproduce the switch.

Above the threshold, the loop came out about 69% weaker in the models than in the weather records.

Soil moisture appears to help explain the mismatch.

At the start of a Central European heatwave, the models’ soil held about a third less water than the records showed.

It then dried at a little over half the real rate, 1.4% a day compared with 2.4%.

Soil that begins a heatwave already dry has little left to lose. The sharp drying that switches the loop on is muted, so the models miss much of the extra heat.

The loop is one route to extreme heatwaves, not the only one. Western North America, eastern Australia, and parts of central Africa have all warmed sharply at the top end without a strong loop.

The authors pointed to other possible causes there, including air pollution, vegetation, and terrain.

A pattern isn’t proof of cause, so the team ran independent checks.

A separately derived soil-moisture threshold matched the temperature threshold, and in a model experiment with soil moisture held fixed, the loop weakened sharply. That last test used a single model.

The main analysis also compared the three factors on the same day.

A follow-up over Central Europe found the loop still held with a three-day gap between cause and effect. The team cautioned that this check covered only that region.

The authors called for global experiments that track the three factors over time, and for climate models that represent the feedback properly.

Until then, they said, projections of the most extreme heat in the hot spots may be too low.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

#6397. Nurses could play a bigger role in preparing for the next outbreak

Nurses already do One Health work, from vaccination drives to antibiotic advice about pets, yet rarely sit on the bodies that set the agenda.

Picture a nurse, and most people imagine someone caring for a patient in a hospital. But in Chad, joint teams have vaccinated children and livestock on the same trip.

In some North American clinics, nurses work beside vets. In antibiotic programs, they consider patients’ contact with animals.

Treating human, animal and environmental health as one system is an approach called One Health.

A new commentary says nurses already do a large share of that work under other labels. They are still mostly missing from the bodies that set its priorities.

Paulo Ferrinho of the Instituto de Higiene e Medicina Tropical (IHMT) in Lisbon led the paper. His co-authors are Rosa Ferrinho of Universidade Aberta, Anabela Coelho of the University of Évora and two colleagues.

The paper is an argument built from chosen studies, policy papers and examples, not a systematic review, and it carries no new data.

In an interview with Earth.com, Ferrinho said the problem starts with labels.

“A central finding is that nurses are already doing much One Health-related work, but it is often described under other headings – primary care, environmental health, antimicrobial stewardship, disaster response, community education, or planetary health – so its contribution remains invisible,” he said.

The phrase One Health has been in use since 2003, the authors wrote, and an agreed definition came only in 2022. It takes in plants and whole ecosystems as well as people and animals.

Nursing was not late to the idea. A 2008 report by the American Veterinary Medical Association listed nurses alongside doctors and vets, and the American Nurses Association endorsed the concept in 2010.

Yet the World Health Organization left it out of its 2021 guidelines for the profession, the authors wrote. So did the core definitions of nursing that the International Council of Nurses adopted in 2025.

Nursing groups tend to talk about environmental or planetary health instead.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him in Florence Nightingale’s work, Ferrinho said the fit itself did.

“Her work was concerned not only with the care of individual patients, but also with the environmental conditions that shape health,” he said.

The authors distinguish three situations that usually get lumped together.

Nurses can be left out of One Health structures altogether. They can be counted in only as part of “the human health sector,” with doctors and public health specialists doing the deciding.

Or they can do the work on the ground with no say over priorities, money or results.

Each needs a different fix, the authors wrote. The gap is widest where nurses are the front line.

In many lower-income countries, they provide primary care where doctors are scarce, yet the committees above them often remain doctor-led.

The everyday list is long. Nurses monitor heat illness, warn communities about contaminated water, hand out bed nets against malaria, and provide disaster relief after wildfires and floods, the authors wrote.

Nurses are also the largest health workforce there is.

The paper asks for One Health to be taught in nursing degrees as a subject in its own right. That would cover animal-borne diseases, environmental health, antibiotic resistance, climate-related illness and systems thinking.

Nursing students would learn it alongside future doctors, vets and environmental scientists.

The paper also asks for seats. “Nurses should have seats – and an effective voice – in national and international One Health advisory bodies, with a role in setting priorities, allocating resources, and evaluating programmes,” Ferrinho told Earth.com. “This cannot be tokenistic.”

Nurses should be recognized as strategic leaders and connectors across the three fields, not only as service providers, he said.

He was just as clear about the cost. New duties, he added, have to come with training, authority, resources, pay and protected time, rather than being added to an already stretched workforce.

Some countries have started. Ferrinho pointed to national plans in Bangladesh, Kenya, Italy and the United States, as well as the Chad campaigns and clinics that combine nursing with veterinary care.

Nursing bodies in Australia and Portugal have backed the approach, he said. Progress remains uneven.

The commentary does not report how many nurses serve on One Health advisory bodies or how much of their work fits the approach.

It uses selected examples to illustrate the three forms of exclusion, without measuring how common each is.

Whether including nurses in these decisions improves a country’s preparedness for a heatwave or disease outbreak remains an open question.

Answering it will require tracking whether greater nursing involvement improves preparedness and response.

The full study was published in the journal CABI One Health.

#6395. Could comets have sparked life on Earth? Scientists tested the odds

New simulations suggest comets struggled to deliver life’s ingredients to early Earth because of destructive impacts and scarce exposed land.

Comets are loaded with the carbon and nitrogen molecules that chemists can turn into the building blocks of a living cell.

For more than a century, that has made comets a possible source of the ingredients that helped life begin on Earth. The trouble is the arrival.

A comet hits Earth at around 17 miles (28 kilometers) per second. The heat of that impact destroys most of the fragile molecules on board.

In new computer simulations that replayed Earth’s first 500 million years 100,000 times, the usual outcome was that not one comet delivered a useful dose.

Richard Anslow of the Institute of Astronomy at the University of Cambridge led the work, with colleagues at Cambridge and the University of Edinburgh. The result is a model rather than a measurement.

“It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely,” Anslow said.

The authors trace the idea to a 1908 paper, and it has lasted because comets really do carry the right molecules.

Anslow’s team focused on one of them, hydrogen cyanide. In the lab, a strong enough solution of it can be turned into sugars, fats and the building blocks of DNA and RNA.

Comets carry hydrogen cyanide at about a tenth of a percent of their water ice.

It’s the only such raw ingredient, or feedstock molecule, found in comets at a level that would matter, and it holds up to heat better than most of them.

If comets struggled to deliver hydrogen cyanide intact, delivering more fragile molecules would be even harder.

Comets are porous and weak, and a planet’s atmosphere breaks them apart.

Anything smaller than about 330 feet (100 meters) across explodes high in the air, spreading whatever it carried over a wide area.

A shallow angle means more air to cross, and even some comets more than half a mile (1 kilometer) wide never reach the ground.

Losing the shallow ones matters, because a shallow, slow impact is exactly the kind that lets hydrogen cyanide survive the heat of the crash.

Fewer than 7% of comets arrive at an angle shallower than 15 degrees, and only the largest of those get through the atmosphere.

The team ran Earth’s comet bombardment 100,000 times, each with a different random mix of comet sizes, speeds and angles.

A hit counted as a success only if it landed on exposed land and left hydrogen cyanide at the concentration the lab experiments need.

Every uncertain assumption was chosen to favor the comets.

Across those runs, the median number of successful impacts was zero. In 54% of the runs, not one comet qualified, out of more than 100,000 comets striking the planet in each run.

When a run did produce a success, it came early, most often around 4.4 billion years ago.

That is more than 100 million years before the last common ancestor of all living things, which other researchers place at about 4.2 billion years ago.

In an interview with Earth.com, Anslow was asked what surprised him most when the simulations ran.

“It was a surprise how strongly our simulations – building on recent advances in the modeling of cometary impacts – disfavored this long-standing hypothesis in origins of life research, finding in most cases no comets delivering sufficient feedstock molecules for the origins of life,” he said.

By the team’s count, all the hydrogen cyanide that comets delivered intact over the whole period, spread through the oceans, would be more than 10,000 times too dilute to matter.

So the only version of the idea that works is a local one: a single comet landing on dry land and leaving a concentrated pool.

A comet strike shatters and melts the ground, groundwater floods into the new crater, and rain and runoff dilute the cyanide within days to weeks.

The chemical reactions needed to start life would have to occur within that window. By the authors’ rough calculation, the expected wait for such an event is longer than the age of the Universe.

“We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way,” Anslow said. “But it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke.”

The team ran the same model for Mars and Venus, and the picture changed. Mars is smaller, so comets arrive more slowly, and its thin air lets almost every comet reach the ground.

In the model, Mars took about one-fifth as many comet hits as Earth. Even so, the simulations gave it 744 successful deliveries on average, against 87 for Earth and 24 for Venus, before land was taken into account.

“This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars,” Anslow said.

“Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative, is that it didn’t happen on either planet.”

Asked where Earth’s first building blocks came from if not from comets, Anslow said he wouldn’t speculate. He pointed instead to research he finds promising.

Molecules might have been made and concentrated on Earth’s own surface, or made after large asteroid impacts, or delivered by carbon-rich asteroids such as Ryugu and Bennu.

Several of the model’s inputs are still open. The formula for how much hydrogen cyanide survives an impact leaves out a comet’s internal strength and porosity, and the authors wrote that this probably makes their estimates too generous.

Early Mars was modeled with today’s atmosphere. If its atmosphere was once thicker, fewer comets might have reached the ground intact.

The team expects the same physics to hold for exoplanets, the planets around other stars. Bigger planets pull comets in faster, and most rocky planets found so far are bigger than Earth.

“Exoplanets significantly larger than the Earth are expected to be much poorer candidates for the successful cometary delivery of these key feedstock molecules,” Anslow told Earth.com.

Astronomers could use that to shorten the list of targets when NASA’s proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory begins its search for Earth-like planets.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#6394. A Caltech robot just became the first to build a structure in space without any help from astronauts

A Caltech robot launched on March 30, 2026 assembled one bay of a truss in orbit with no astronauts, in what Caltech calls a first.

Early on March 30, 2026, a SpaceX rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base. On board was a Caltech robot packed into a box about 35 cubic feet (1 cubic meter) in size.

On the ground, Jaden Suh, then a Caltech postdoctoral scholar on the team, watched the launch with tears in his eyes.

Months later, that box built a structure in orbit without help from astronauts, a first according to Caltech. Its robotic arm picked up struts and joints from nearby dispensers. It then assembled a new section of a truss in orbit.

The demonstration, called ASTRA, was meant to build an entire reflector antenna. The team ran short of time and built only the initial section. The mission ends in December, according to Caltech.

ASTRA, short for Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly, flew as one of 10 payloads on Vigoride 7. That orbital vehicle was built by Momentus Inc. Vigoride 7 itself rode to low Earth orbit on SpaceX’s Transporter-16 mission.

Inside the payload were two truss sections, or bays, that had been built on the ground, plus an armlike manipulator. Motorized dispensers held the rest of the parts needed to finish the structure.

The team leader is Sergio Pellegrino, a professor of aerospace and civil engineering at Caltech. He is also a senior research scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory. He called it “the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space.”

The payload was completed, tested and handed over to Momentus in less than 12 months. Pellegrino said that schedule was an enormous undertaking for a small team.

Once ASTRA reached orbit, the team sent commands to its computer through the Vigoride vehicle. First, the restraints that held the parts in place during launch were released.

Next, the robot pushed the two prebuilt bays out of the builder. Then it assembled the third bay on an assembly plate.

Three team members sent the commands. They were Charles Sommer, a former Caltech systems engineer, Alan Truong, a Caltech research engineer, and graduate student Tara Venkatadri.

After each step they checked the result against photos downloaded from orbit. The payload carries 11 cameras.

Contact with the payload was limited to about seven or eight windows a day, each lasting roughly 15 minutes. Operations were repeated to get around unforeseen problems, of which Caltech said there were many.

To fix them, the engineers kept a twin of the payload, a flight spare, in Pellegrino’s Caltech lab. They tested possible fixes on the spare and then sent the working version up to orbit. When an issue is confirmed in space, Sommer said, the team tries “to mimic the problem on the ground.”

ASTRA was meant to build a reflector antenna about 4.6 feet (1.4 meters) across from composite fiber tubes, aluminum joints and Kapton, a thin, heat-resistant plastic film. DARPA calls the robot a relatively simple gantry, able to move along three straight axes.

On a normal cycle the arm builds one bay on an assembly plate, attaches the reflective film and pushes the bay out into space. Springs keep the two film nets under tension. Then it starts on the next bay, until all 11 are done.

Igor Bargatin’s group at the University of Pennsylvania co-invented the perforated film with the Caltech team. Per Caltech, it needs less built-in tension than the knitted metal mesh normally used in foldable reflectors, so engineers can design lighter structures.

Andrew Detor, the DARPA program manager for the project, compared the approach to building with Tinkertoys or K’Nex construction toys in the agency’s statement.

ASTRA belongs to DARPA‘s Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design program, known as NOM4D. DARPA started it in 2022.

Until now there have been two ways to put a large structure in space. One is to fold it for launch and unfurl it in orbit. The other is to piece it together by hand from sections sent up over several launches.

Caltech describes building the structure in orbit as a third option. Detor said NOM4D is aiming at structures “hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale.”

NOM4D was not first planned around a flight test. After good results from teams in phase 2, Detor changed the last phase to a space demo. He said the program went from the idea of an on-orbit demo to launching a working prototype in 15 months.

ASTRA is one of two projects that reached phase 3. The other comes from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Later this year it will test a new resin for composite structures on the International Space Station.

The team considers it unlikely that ASTRA will finish the full truss before December. Two bays were built on Earth and one in orbit, so eight of the 11 remain unbuilt.

Caltech said the engineers learned enough to show that the assembly approach is viable. They also learned that the design needs to be simplified and refined.

Suh is now an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin. He said orbit differs from the ground in many ways, and that is the reason for proof-of-concept flights.

Even complete, the ASTRA antenna would span only 4.6 feet (1.4 meters). DARPA’s target is hundreds of meters or more, and Detor said nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today.

Caltech video on the ASTRA assembly demonstration for DARPA’s NOM4D program. Credit: Caltech.

Pellegrino said the method fits structures too large to be built on the ground and unfolded. Large reflectors could serve as mirrors for space telescopes, like the big optics planned for NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory, or as wide radio antennas.

Pellegrino also co-directs Caltech’s Space Solar Power Project, which aims to collect solar power in orbit and send it to Earth without wires. He said the same approach could help build very large solar arrays for that work.

Detor listed large space depots, habitats, solar arrays and radio antennas as things a future space economy will need. Robots also appear in plans for building on the Moon, such as NASA’s plan to use 3D printing and robots for a lunar base. Any such economy would share orbit with the millions of pieces of debris that already circle the planet.

Suh joined ASTRA at the start, as a postdoctoral scholar at Caltech. He said many of his original ideas are in the system, and that “sending your stuff to space is what I’ve been dreaming of my entire life.” Part of that system is now a truss bay in orbit, photographed by the payload that built it.

The information was obtained from Caltech and DARPA.

#6393. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

In this excerpt from "This is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth," author and physicist Christophe Galfard explores the way 19th century scientists were starting to use thermodynamics to understand just how old Earth is.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 1950s, American geochemist Clair Patterson presented findings that showed Earth is around 4.55 billion years old. His evidence was based on lead isotopic analysis that he used to calculate the age of the Canyon Diablo meteorite, which was discovered in Arizona in 1891. That result is now widely accepted as the age of our planet, but the buildup to this discovery was a long time coming.

Earth's true age was a subject of much debate among scientists in the 19th century. And rather than geologists taking the helm, it was physicists who realized that this giant ball of rock we live on must be far older than the thousands of years that had been assumed in prior centuries. Their main reasoning was heat.

In this excerpt from "This Is Life: A Journey from Inside Your Body to Beyond Earth" (University of Chicago Press/Picador, 2026), author and physicist Christophe Galfard looks at the progression among scientists who were coming to realize that thermodynamics was an essential piece of this long-standing puzzle.

Some two and a half centuries ago, the foremost experts on scientific matters knew a thing or two about heat. They knew, for instance, how heat could be transferred from one place to another. A new science was about to emerge out of this knowledge, a science called thermodynamics, which means "movements of heat" in Greek.

Thermodynamics isn't a force. It is more like a guidebook, a set of rules that apply to large

numbers of particles when they come together. It gives us, humans, a way to understand how particles behave when there is a lot of them without needing to refer to each one of them individually. It shows us how properties that don't exist on their own arise when many particles are together. It deals with these things we call emergent phenomena, such as heat and pressure, and which [Philip] Anderson's "More Is Different" tried to make sense of.

Understanding the dynamics of heat meant a lot to nineteenth-century scientists — so much so that many saw in it the roots of a philosophy so universal and powerful that they thought it should guide us through all our lives. Some even went as far as believing that heat was the source of eternal life. A prominent scientist became so convinced that this was the case that he locked himself up in his house and overheated it, thus shielding himself from all mortal diseases (ageing and death included). The experience was a true torture for the occasional guests who came to visit him, not to mention his wife, who had to endure it day and night.

The scientist held fast to his belief, though, piling on layer after layer of clothing to keep himself ever warmer. Unfortunately, the bulk made it difficult to move, and he eventually missed a step on his own staircase and died from the fall.

As a scientific discipline, thermodynamics was born with a book written in 1824 by a 27-year-old French physicist named Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot, who, as he explained how heat could produce work, told everyone how the steam engine worked.

Lord Kelvin giving a lecture at Glasgow University in 1899.

With Carnot's vision, the way hot objects cool down began to be understood, raising hopes that the resolution of one particular problem might be imminent: the determination of the Earth's age. Were we to somehow guess how hot our planet was at birth, thermodynamics could then be used to tell us how much time had gone by for it to have cooled to its present temperature. Many scientists tried it, keen to be the first one to nail the true age of our world.

Considering our planet in all its complexity to be far too difficult, simplifications were in order, and British physicist William Thomson shot first by picturing our world as a ball. A very simple, rock-solid ball made of pretty much the same stuff throughout, from surface to core. No ocean, no mountain, just a smooth ball the size of the Earth. He then calculated how long it would take it to cool down from being red hot to its present temperature, and declared that the Earth was something between 40 and 400 million years old.

Refining his calculations, he then announced that the world was 100 million years old, before settling for 40 million again.

Thomson's result does not correspond to the true age of the Earth, but it was a start. It was the result of a model, an attempt at figuring out something about our world using still-to-be-refined laws, and mathematical sense. What was more problematic was that no one dared question his results. Even as it shifted from one paper to another, the age of the Earth given by Thomson was always greeted as the right one. A reason for this is that at the end of the nineteenth century Thomson had become Lord Kelvin.

The same Kelvin after whom the Kelvin unit of absolute temperature is named. A scientific superstar who had the power to undo, in a snap of fingers, the career of anyone who disagreed with him.

Lord Kelvin was a physicist, not a geologist, so geologists could have questioned his work, but they didn't. In fact, they weren't bothered. Many of them back then believed that being a geologist was all about intuition and proper English, a language they deemed far more efficient than mathematical gibberish.

That being said, and however wrong the results, Kelvin's calculations were beautiful, giving whoever wanted to think about the problem of the age of the Earth a way forward, which is exactly what one of his former students, Northern Irishman John Perry, did. He thought that Kelvin had overlooked something. As a man of science talking to his former mentor (and job provider), Perry explained his vision to Kelvin but was ignored.

John Perry, a student of Kelvin's, who realized Earth was billions of years old — and that its mantle was a liquid, not a solid.

Still, he published his thoughts in Nature. But again, the article was ignored. Not just by Kelvin, but by the scientific community at large, including geologists.

It would have saved us all quite a bit of time had this not been the case, because Perry not only found a much more correct way to picture the Earth and estimate its age than Kelvin had, but he also found the source of the power that makes our planet's continents drift.

In his model, Perry didn't picture the Earth to be uniformly the same from surface to core as Kelvin had. Instead, he modelled the Earth's interior as being divided into three regions: a metallic core at its centre, a solid crust at its surface, and a mantle that lay in between the two. Rather unexpectedly, Perry didn't envision the mantle as everyone else would have; he believed that it didn't behave like the solid rock it was, but as a liquid.

No wonder his former master didn't take him seriously. However, he pictured the mantle behaving like a liquid only when considered over long periods of time. Sandwiched between a hot core and a colder crust that very much looked like a lid, he believed the mantle had no choice but to behave just like water does in a heated pan, with the hottest parts at the bottom rising and cooling before diving back down and rising up again, in repeated loops, albeit in extremely slow motion. This type of movement is called convection, and it happens in solids, too.

If he was right, there would be two immediate consequences. The first one was that the time it would take for our planet's surface to cool down from red hot to its current temperature could now be far longer than Kelvin had estimated. The lid and the convection patterns prevented our planet from quickly radiating away all its energy into space, so we were now inhabiting an Earth that could be as old as 2 or 3 billion years. Maybe even more. Such timescales were unheard of in the scientific community. Back then, no one knew that the universe itself was 13.8 billion years old. They knew next to nothing.

The second consequence of Perry's model was that the mantle's circular movements underneath the crust could drag the crust itself via friction. The solid surface of our world would then move, and split into pieces that would drift, and collide, and plunge underneath — or slide above — one another. Where they collided, mountain ranges would rise, like the Alps, the Himalayas, the Rockies . . . Where they split apart, rifts would appear, probably in the middle of oceans, along ridges . . . just like [Marie] Tharp had found.

Nowadays, these broken pieces of our planet's surface have all been mapped. They are our world's plates and their movements through time are called plate tectonics. Today, most of us have heard about plate tectonics. Back then, however, no one had, and if very few people remember Perry today, it is because another scientific breakthrough made the estimation of the age of the Earth much easier and precise, showing us that our world isn't 2 or 3 billion years old, as Perry suggested, but precisely 4.567 billion, give or take a few million.

#6390. A 5th-century boat burial held a carved alder chair, and its owner carried a leprosy branch new to northern Europe

DNA from a 5th-century boat burial at Fallward, Germany, points to a man of about 50 with Danube roots and a leprosy branch new to northern Europe.

Between 1995 and 1998, the archaeology service of Germany’s Cuxhaven district excavated a boat burial at Fallward, near the North Sea coast. In grave 265, a man of about 50 lay in an oak boat more than 13 feet (4 meters) long, with a carved chair outside it.

His skeleton then went into storage. Nearly three decades later, a genetics lab in Kiel sampled his heel bone and a molar. It found leprosy bacteria, plus DNA that points to the Danube region.

The strain sits on a branch first known from an Egyptian mummy and had not been found in central or northern Europe before. His exact homeland is still not pinned down, the researchers say.

Fallward was a village on a terp, an earth mound raised on a beach ridge to keep homes above storm floods. There were no dikes yet. The study lists it among eight mound villages between the Elbe and the Weser founded in the 1st century BCE.

The village was probably abandoned by the end of the 5th century CE. Its cemetery was used from the late 3rd century onward and held about 200 cremations and 60 burials of bodies. Some pits went 6.5 feet (2 meters) down into old marsh clay.

The wet clay kept wood, furs, cloth and plant mats from rotting. Several graves were lifted as whole blocks and frozen. A German Research Foundation project at the Lower Saxony Institute for Historical Coastal Research (NIhK) in Wilhelmshaven is now opening them in the lab.

The man died in the second quarter of the 5th century. Wooden panels closed his boat like a roof. Inside, he lay on a reed mat, and fish bones turned up in the boat with him.

The chair outside the boat was cut out of one alder trunk, with notched patterns, and was probably painted when new. The NIhK calls it the Throne from the Marsch.

A maple footstool lay by his feet, with a runic inscription and a hunting scene on its underside. Rolf Kiepe of the NIhK photographed both pieces.

Diggers also found a game board, a bronze basin, a clay pot and a little box in the shape of a water bird. A late Roman military belt lay in the grave too.

Many of these things show wear and old repairs. The authors think they belonged to him or his family and were not made for the grave.

Hauke Jöns of the NIhK said the belt had already suggested that the man “had had connections across great distances.” The wood came from local trees, but the decoration shows the influence of late Roman art.

In Kiel, the Ancient DNA Working Group of the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology (IKMB) got 12 bone samples from 11 people buried at Fallward. It read the DNA on a high-throughput sequencing machine. Seven males and one female could be identified.

Three people had enough DNA to compare with other ancient groups. The adult man in grave 14 and a 3-year-old girl in grave 250 matched northwestern Europe, closest to Anglo-Saxons in England. Their relatives may have joined the North Sea crossings of the migrations of the first millennium AD.

The man in grave 265 grouped elsewhere. His DNA fell among Roman-era people from the Danube frontier in present-day Croatia, Slovenia, Hungary and Serbia.

A mapping program called mobest placed the most likely location of genetic similarity more than 870 miles (1,400 kilometers) southeast of Fallward, near the old Roman border.

His Y chromosome, passed from father to son, belongs to a lineage called haplogroup G, which today is most common in the Caucasus.

A scan for germs found Mycobacterium leprae, the bacterium that causes leprosy, in both the tooth and the heel bone. There was more bacterial DNA than human DNA. The team read over 99 percent of the bacterial genome at least four times.

Lead author Daniel Myburgh, a doctoral researcher at the IKMB, and his colleagues built a family tree of 44 ancient and 185 modern leprosy genomes.

The Fallward strain landed near the root of branch 4. Only one genome on that branch is older, from a mummy at Abusir in Egypt dated to the 4th to 2nd centuries BCE.

Myburgh said the man “is the first individual from this group to have been identified in Europe.” Earlier work on medieval graves tracked other strains, such as one from central or western Asia in a pilgrim’s skeleton found by Winchester researchers.

According to the World Health Organization, leprosy mainly harms the skin and the nerves. The Fallward man’s bones show no leprosy damage.

Either he had no symptoms or the infection had only reached soft tissue. Almut Nebel, a professor at the IKMB, said, “He may have travelled long distances whilst carrying the disease.”

The authors give more than one possible life story. He may have been a foederatus, a hired soldier who served in the Roman army.

Ben Krause-Kyora, who leads the study at the IKMB, said the man could have been a mercenary who later “settled between the Elbe and the Weser,” or a long-distance trader.

The paper adds that the belt does not necessarily mean army service. Such belts were also traded, inherited or taken as war booty. Roman soldiers carried habits and symbols across provinces, as a study on what held Roman soldiers together found.

His bones suggest a third option. His upper arm muscles were very well developed. Together with the boat, the reed mat and the fish bones, that could point to a boatman or a fisherman.

Most of the human DNA was in bad shape. The three usable genomes covered only 32,000 to 67,000 of the roughly 1.24 million genetic markers that ancient DNA labs usually check. The man’s sample also showed less ancient damage than the girl’s.

Other statistical ancestry models could not set him apart from the two local people. The authors write that his origin needs caution and that three people do not speak for all of Fallward.

Two children in graves 224 and 282 read as boys in the DNA, though they were buried with brooches and beads. Their data were too weak to be sure.

The raw sequences sit in the European Nucleotide Archive. The ROOTS Cluster of Excellence paid for the work, Kiel University said on November 3, 2026.

Many Fallward grave goods ended up in museum cases while the bones stayed in storage. A sample from one heel now links the man with the alder chair to the Danube frontier and to a leprosy branch whose earliest known member comes from Egypt.

The full study was published in the journal iScience.

#6388. Four volunteers spent 378 days inside a windowless NASA Mars habitat

Four NASA CHAPEA volunteers left a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston on Oct. 31, 2026, after 378 days.

Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery walked out of NASA’s Mars habitat in Houston on Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026. They had gone in on Oct. 19, 2025, and stayed 378 days with no windows and no live calls home.

Ellis, the crew’s medical officer, later told NASA that on most days she did not feel isolated. She said she relied on her three teammates every day to get through the mission.

The year inside was CHAPEA Mission 2, NASA’s second yearlong simulation of life on the surface of Mars. NASA posted the crew’s reflections on Nov. 9. The health data are still to be interpreted in two weeks of post-mission evaluations.

The habitat is called Mars Dune Alpha. It was 3D-printed, covers roughly 1,700 square feet (158 square meters) and sits inside a building at Johnson Space Center.

On entry day in October 2025, the crew rode to the habitat in the Space Exploration Vehicle, a prototype pressurized rover, according to NASA’s Human Research Program.

Suzanne Bell, the mission’s co-principal investigator, spoke to them at the door. Two alternate crew members posed with them for photos before the start.

CHAPEA is short for Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog. The first mission used the same habitat and ended on July 6, 2024.

Before the second crew went in, the plans for a second yearlong rehearsal in the printed habitat put crew autonomy at the center.

NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway spoke about the time they were away. While they were inside, he flew a 237-day mission on the International Space Station and came back. The Artemis II crew also traveled around the Moon in that period and set a distance record for humans.

Hathaway said the year required “immense physiological and psychological strength, teamwork, and human grit.”

Messages between the habitat and mission control took up to 22 minutes each way. The crew spoke with their families only by email, with a Mars-like delay, NASA said in a one-year update on Oct. 19.

On May 7 the crew reached day 200. That week they were in a two-week loss of signal, a planned blackout like the one when Mars passes behind the Sun, according to a NASA update from May. They worked with no contact with mission control and used preplanned procedures.

The crew also had to handle simulated equipment failures and limited supplies. Michael Stenger, chief scientist of the Human Research Program, said the mission was starting to show NASA what year-long missions need, including medical and psychological care across communication delays.

Elder was the commander, Ellis the medical officer, Montgomery the science officer and Spicer the flight engineer. As part of their personal item allowance, the four brought musical instruments into the habitat.

Elder is a former U.S. Air Force experimental test pilot. According to NASA, he found the Marswalks and robotic work very similar to working as part of a flight.

For a Marswalk, the crew put on suits, went through an airlock and walked on red sand outside the habitat. That area is still inside the building. From inside, crew members also ran a drone and a rover to survey the ground and find or collect rock samples.

Elder said that getting suits ready, doing airlock procedures and making long traverses took time and stamina. He said food, exercise and rest were needed to keep up that pace.

Montgomery helped identify the rocks brought back from the walks. One NASA photo shows Ellis and Elder doing a maintenance task outside during a simulated walk. Another shows photos the crew placed around a boot print in the sand.

Spicer worked in satellite communications and spacecraft development before the mission. At the exit, he was thanked for keeping the habitat’s systems running and was called the crew’s resident data scientist.

He compared the year to living on a submarine or a boat. The crew counted supplies from dish soap to respirator filters, and they rationed food and water.

Spicer said he was surprised by how little he missed the news and social media, even though the crew could get news. He told his crewmates they made the year “not a chore, but a joy.”

Montgomery had worked in hardware engineering, robotics, tech startups and independent films. He set up the habitat’s 3D printing capabilities and ran a seed germination test with simulated Martian soil and a control.

He also grew vegetables in a hydroponic system. NASA has run other work on growing lettuce, peppers and tomatoes in microgravity, because packaged food can lose flavor and vitamins.

Ellis is a U.S. Space Force officer and has worked at the National Reconnaissance Office. Inside the habitat she helped organize biological sample collections and prepare supplies for the health studies.

She said it was hard to explain to other people what life inside was like. “It would be difficult to convince someone who has never lived in isolation that most days, I don’t feel isolated,” she said.

Ellis thanked the exercise, behavioral health, nutrition and medical specialists on the ground. She said the main lesson for her was that a Mars crew will need a closely integrated ground team.

Isolation has also been studied at Concordia Station in Antarctica, where researchers linked living in close quarters to more conflict and mistrust.

The crew started two weeks of tests and debriefs with NASA scientists after the exit. Scientists will compare the data with what the crew reported. Mission 2’s results are still to come, and each crew has only four people.

Grace Douglas, the principal investigator, said the results will help NASA weigh health risks against crew time, communication capacity and food and water systems. She also said many of the resource problems in space are like problems on Earth.

Sara Whiting, the project scientist, said the data will feed into plans for NASA’s Moon Base near the lunar South Pole. “This is really the now moment for this kind of data,” she said.

NASA’s live broadcast of the CHAPEA Mission 2 crew leaving the Mars Dune Alpha habitat on Oct. 31, 2026. Credit: NASA Johnson.

On Oct. 31, the four stepped outside for the first time in 378 days, where family, friends and colleagues met them. Ellis had said that on most days inside, she did not feel isolated.

#6386. Sea otters are adorable and iconic, but few people understand how important they are to ocean ecosystems

Otters eat urchins, and urchins eat kelp. On Southern California reefs, a study suggests, competition among grazers and seaweeds weakened that chain.

Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp, so otters are famous for bringing kelp forests back. Off Vancouver Island, it happened so fast that a reef was almost always one or the other: covered in urchins or covered in kelp.

Around San Nicolas Island, off Southern California, otters, urchins, and kelp lived together for years.

A study of both coasts suggests that on the southern reefs, competition among other species weakened the otters’ effect on kelp.

The fur trade wiped out sea otters across most of the places where they once lived. Otters were brought back to Vancouver Island from 1969 to 1972 and to San Nicolas Island from 1987 to 1990.

Researchers surveyed the same marked sites year after year, eight off Vancouver Island and six around San Nicolas. The records run through 2017.

A team led by Ryan Langendorf of the Department of Environmental Studies at the University of Colorado Boulder built a statistical model from those records. The study was published in March 2025.

The model’s numbers are estimates of how strongly species affected one another, not direct measurements.

Ecologists call the sea otter a keystone species. That means it has an unusually large effect on the other species around it.

“We always thought keystone species control their ecosystem the same way, regardless of where they are or what else is in the ecosystem,” Langendorf said.

“A more modern view is that they are still very important, but they can have different effects in different places.”

Otters reduce urchins, and urchins reduce kelp. Two negative effects in a row make a positive one for kelp.

Competition can add a third negative step, and three in a row make a negative one.

At San Nicolas, one of the strongest chains of that kind involved turban snails. Otters eat the snails, and the snails compete with red urchins. With fewer snails, red urchins can do better, and red urchins eat giant kelp.

The model estimated that these extra chains often made little difference. In some years at some San Nicolas sites, though, they reduced the otters’ effect on giant kelp by 15% to 20%.

Off Vancouver Island, the extra chains made almost no difference.

Fish aren’t in the model, because the team lacked the data. Records of what the otters ate are missing too.

Around San Nicolas, grazing animals didn’t eat giant kelp down to nothing, even before otters were brought back. The authors wrote that their models don’t adequately explain why.

Future analyses could include otter diets, the authors wrote. That may help explain how much the mix of urchin species shaped the otters’ effect.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Antonacci, N., Labombarda, M., Ricci, C., Buscemi, S., Casadei, R., & Minni, F. (2013). A bizarre foreign body in the appendix: A case report. World Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery, 5(6), 195–198. https://doi.org/10.4240/wjgs.v5.i6.195
