#6383. Scientists built a wearable device meant to let a friend in another city smell your coffee

An electronic nose names a food from its fumes, a message crosses the internet, and a wearable puffs out the matching scent, so far only in a lab.

Sending a friend a picture of your coffee takes a second. The smell stays in the kitchen, however, because phones carry pictures and sound but nothing for the nose. A new wearable device now gets around that.

A sensor sniffs the coffee and software recognizes it. Then a short message tells a device on your friend’s wrist to release a coffee smell that it already holds.

What crosses the internet is a label rather than the smell itself, and that is both the trick and the limit. The system is a laboratory prototype.

It knows five smells so far: beer, cake, coffee, orange, and red wine. It reproduces each one from a scented liquid loaded into the device ahead of time.

Engineers at Ohio State University built the system and named it Scentronic. Chunyu Yang, a doctoral student in the University’s Department of Materials Science and Engineering, is the first author.

Jinghua Li’s group ran the work with colleagues at Zhejiang Laboratory in China.

In an interview with Earth.com, Yang described what the device is for. “Scentronic has the potential to allow people to share smells with others over long distances, much like we currently share images, sounds, and videos,” he said.

“For example, someone could share the aroma of their coffee with a friend in another city.”

The sniffing end is a ring of six gas sensors around a spot where the food sits. Each sensor is a heated chip of tin dioxide.

Vapors from food, such as the alcohol in beer and wine, change how easily electricity flows through the sensor. Engineers call a sensor array like this an electronic nose.

No single sensor can tell coffee from cake. The six together produce a pattern, so the team trained a pattern-matching program on it.

They recorded each of the five foods 50 times, for 200 seconds at a stretch. That made 250 recordings, one brand of each: the cake was a bag of King’s Hawaiian sweet rolls.

On recordings the program had not seen before, the best version named all five foods correctly.

Coffee gave the faintest signal, and the authors wrote that many of the compounds behind its aroma may not be the kind that these sensors detect well.

Once the program decides on coffee, that word is all that travels. It goes to a program on a cloud server and on to the wearable, a trip that took about 65 thousandths of a second in the team’s tests.

Recognizing the food takes longer, from several seconds to a few tens of seconds.

The wearable is built around a thin disk that vibrates about 110,000 times a second. A cotton pad feeds it scented liquid from a small chamber, and the vibration pushes that liquid through tiny holes as a fine mist.

Switching the vibration on and off sets how much mist comes out.

A wristband version of the device holds two smells. A necklace holds five, lined up, as the authors wrote, “like pearls on a string.” Run flat out, a cartridge empties in under five minutes, and at the lowest setting it lasts more than 35 minutes.

After an hour of continuous use, the warmest spot on the device measured 96.4°F (35.8°C), below body temperature.

Sixteen volunteers from the University kept their noses 8 inches (20 centimeters) from a device while a smell of orange rose through ten strength levels, and said when they noticed it.

The middle level was where the most volunteers first noticed it, and the spread formed a bell shape, which told the team which settings people can actually smell.

Fourteen volunteers then took tests built like a standard smell exam. After learning the five food scents from labeled tubes, they identified single scents from the device about 73 percent of the time.

They named both parts of a two-scent mixture about 71 percent of the time. The hardest test was ranking five strengths of an alcohol scent from weakest to strongest, and they got about 59 percent of those right.

The volunteers were smelling scents released in the same room. Earth.com asked Yang what surprised him when volunteers first received a smell sent from a distance.

“These were separate experimental evaluations, and we did not specifically investigate volunteers’ reactions to receiving odors transmitted remotely,” he said.

Medicine is the use the authors focus on. Head injuries, infections, and diseases of the brain can dull, distort, or erase the sense of smell, and smell problems became a common aftereffect of COVID-19.

Today’s clinic tests use scratch-and-sniff cards or scented pens at a few fixed strengths.

An adjustable device, the authors wrote, could let a clinician raise an odor step by step, over the internet, until a patient notices it. That would find the threshold without an office visit.

A patient who needs a strong puff to notice anything has a weakened sense of smell, the kind of loss seen after COVID-19.

One who notices a faint puff that others miss may be oversensitive, which happens during migraines and pregnancy. The National Institutes of Health describes these smell disorders.

The team also built a cup with five scent cartridges in its lid and five small pumps in its wall, each pump holding a flavoring liquid.

When the electronic nose smelled beer, coffee, or the two together, the cup released the matching aroma and dripped the matching flavor into the water inside.

In a second demonstration, a person wearing a Meta Quest 3 headset reached for a virtual beer or coffee on a virtual shelf. The real cup then dispensed that drink’s flavor and smell.

The authors wrote that today’s virtual reality headsets focus on sight and sound, while smell and taste shape how real an experience feels.

The authors also wrote that making food seem to taste better could matter for patients with nutritional problems, for astronauts facing unappealing food supplements, and for soldiers eating field rations.

Five smells is a small vocabulary, and the authors wrote as much. The device reproduces a category, coffee rather than this particular coffee, from a liquid chosen in advance, and it doesn’t match the chemistry of the original.

Yang told Earth.com that the number of odors was limited mainly by the time it took to collect training recordings. Adding more, he said, depends on how sensitive and selective the sensors are and on how complex the mixtures get.

The human tests were simple, with few control conditions, and the authors wrote that this could introduce bias. Each food came from a single brand, so whether the program would recognize a different coffee is untested.

Next steps the team listed include working with smell researchers under controlled conditions and recording brain signals while the device delivers a scent.

“Scentronic is currently a laboratory prototype,” Yang said, and “we expect it will take several years, potentially longer, before such devices become commercially available.”

Until then, every smell the device has sent was sent and received inside a lab.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6382. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

E. Kendall. ‘The bright sun was extiguish’d’: metabolic health and vitamin D status in a Little Ice Age population (18-19th c.) in North East England. Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. 2026. Doi: 10.3389/fearc.2026.1909791

#6381. Paying down debt can leave a country more exposed when the next hurricane hits

After Hurricane Melissa, Jamaica borrowed about 18% of its economy to recover, and researchers say lenders reward debt cuts but not seawalls.

Paying down debt is supposed to make a country safer. Lenders reward it with better credit ratings and lower borrowing costs. Jamaica spent more than a decade doing exactly that, but one hurricane undid much of the progress in a matter of weeks.

The reason, four researchers argue, is that the rules rewarding a country for paying off loans offer nothing comparable for building seawalls and drains.

Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica as a Category 5 storm in October 2025. It caused an estimated $12.2 billion in damage, losses, and costs.

This represents about 57 percent of the country’s entire economic output for 2024. Insurance covered about 2 percent of that, and Jamaica borrowed roughly $3.6 billion to recover.

Aayushi Mishra, a doctoral candidate at Northeastern University, traced what happened next. Her co-authors are Advait Arun of the Center for Public Enterprise and Northeastern’s Evan Kodra and Auroop Ganguly.

The paper is a policy analysis built on Jamaica’s public finance and disaster-loss figures, not a new data study. It argues for changes at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the development banks, and the rating agencies.

In an interview with Earth.com, Mishra said the people running those institutions are not the villains of the story. “No one here is acting in bad faith: every institution is doing exactly what its own rules ask of it,” she said.

“The problem is that those rules, once taken together, leave resilience underfunded.”

In 2013, Jamaica owed about 144 percent of its yearly economic output in debt. By 2023 it had cut that to about 72 percent, and it was on track for 60 percent by the 2027 to 2028 budget year.

The country did this through years of tight budgets and strict spending rules that it adopted on its own, not as a condition set by the IMF.

Lenders noticed. In September 2025, the rating agency S&P Global upgraded Jamaica’s credit rating. A few weeks later, Melissa made landfall.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Mishra pointed to the speed of the reversal. “Honestly, how little time it took for Jamaica’s hard-won progress to get diluted by just one storm, albeit a massive one,” she said.

The team projects Jamaica’s debt will now peak at about 68.5 percent of its economy, roughly 8.5 points above the path it was on. New borrowing makes up most of that increase, and the storm’s damage to output accounts for the rest, shrinking the economy against which analysts measure the debt.

Jamaica had done the things disaster experts recommend. It held a catastrophe bond through the World Bank, which pays investors’ money to the country if a storm crosses set thresholds for wind speed, track, and pressure.

It also bought insurance from a regional pool, the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF), that pays on the same measurements rather than on assessed damage.

Both paid quickly. The bond paid its full $150 million, and with the insurance and other aid the total reached about $242 million, within 3 to 14 days of landfall. Jamaica waited about three months for its IMF money to be approved.

But $242 million against $12.2 billion in losses is 2 percent. Speed was never the problem; scale was.

The year before, Hurricane Beryl had caused about $1 billion in damage, and the bond paid nothing because the storm’s measured strength fell short of its trigger. The insurance pool covered $26.6 million of Beryl’s damage, under 3 percent.

The instruments worked exactly as specified, the team wrote. Insurers have a name for the gap between what a storm measures and what it costs: basis risk. For a whole country, that gap was about 98 cents of every dollar lost.

The country is paying for the rest of the recovery with roughly $3.6 billion in new loans, about 18 percent of Jamaica’s pre-storm output in a single year. That is above the level the IMF treats as a warning sign for emerging economies.

The loans come from the IMF, the World Bank, and three regional development banks, mostly on terms that have not been made public.

So the team modeled a range, from low-cost development lending to near-market rates. The team put total repayments, including interest, at $4.9 billion to $5.7 billion.

What matters to Jamaica’s budget is the yearly cash payment. At peak repayment, the team estimates, servicing the new debt alone would approach or exceed Jamaica’s entire annual budget for public investment.

Jamaica’s investment budget was already small. In the 2024 to 2025 budget year, Jamaica spent about $3.15 billion servicing debt and about $510 million on public capital projects.

That second budget is the one that pays for coastal defenses and drainage. “So for every $1 the country spent on things like public infrastructure, it paid $6 in debt service,” Mishra told Earth.com.

How much would it have taken to avoid the borrowing? Using cost-benefit ratios from disaster research, the team estimates that spending $360 million to $900 million a year on protection before the storm could have offset the new debt entirely.

The IMF’s own 2025 review of Jamaica’s economy found the country could afford only $40 million to $80 million a year on climate adaptation without straining its debt path. That is 4 to 22 times less than the estimated need.

The gap narrows if private investors cover most of the cost, as the researchers assume they would.

The government’s share would then be about $120 million to $300 million a year, still 1.5 to 7.5 times what the IMF considered sustainable.

The team wrote that these figures can’t say which investments would have worked best, or how long they would have taken to build.

Researchers have modeled this pattern before and call it a climate-debt doom loop.

A disaster hits an underprepared country, and the country borrows to recover. The repayments then crowd out spending on protection, so the country is just as exposed when the next disaster arrives.

The authors wrote that no one had documented the loop unfolding in real time inside a single country before.

Rating agencies grade countries on budget surpluses, how fast debt falls, and how strictly budget rules are followed. Some have begun adding climate risk to side reports, but the authors wrote that it stays peripheral to the core decision. Nothing in that system changes when a country builds a seawall.

The IMF’s health check on a country’s debt added climate risk guidance for some programs in 2024. The authors wrote that it is still not part of the core method.

Jamaica’s 2025 review asked how much adaptation the country could afford without hurting its debt path. It didn’t ask the reverse: what happens to the debt when adaptation falls short and a catastrophe follows.

The paper’s four proposals aim at the lenders, not at Jamaica. Resilience spending should count in the IMF’s debt analysis as something that lowers the odds of a catastrophic loss.

An IMF trust fund created in 2022 for low-cost, long-term climate lending should be scaled up for the most indebted small island states.

Storm insurance triggers should use rainfall and surge as well as wind, and development banks should back the pools so they can pay more.

The fourth is a clause in loan contracts. Mishra said countries can add these now, while their finances are strong, as Barbados has.

“Simply put, these clauses let debt payments pause for up to two years after a disaster, so the country doesn’t have to take on new debt to cover them,” she said. Seventy-three countries and the major development banks have committed to them.

Ganguly, Mishra’s doctoral advisor, said much of the underlying data in this field is kept behind institutional walls or never disclosed.

“We would like to see funders and multilateral institutions to treat disclosure of these terms as standard practice (and not a courtesy), since the public and researchers alike are left to trust conclusions that they can’t necessarily check independently,” he said.

Nearly a year after Melissa, many of the terms of Jamaica’s recovery loans have still not been disclosed, Mishra said. Until they are, the cost of one storm to Jamaica is a range, not a number.

The next test is whether pause clauses get written into loans before the next hurricane arrives, rather than after.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6378. One of the dodo’s closest relatives was seen in Samoa for the first time in five years, but no one got a photo

Five sightings of Samoa's critically endangered manumea, a rare relative of the dodo, offer hope for a bird threatened by hunting and habitat loss.

The manumea, or tooth-billed pigeon, is Samoa’s national bird and one of only three surviving relatives of the extinct dodo. Its scientific name is Didunculus strigirostris, and the genus name means “little dodo” in Latin.

During a survey from October 17 to November 13, 2025, the Samoa Conservation Society recorded five manumea sightings in Upolu’s Uafato rainforest.

No photograph was taken, the society said. The bird’s call is also easily confused with that of the more common Pacific imperial pigeon.

Like the dodo, the manumea is a pigeon. It is stout and short-toed, about 12 inches (31 centimeters) long.

Its head and neck are a glossy blackish green, and its back and wing coverts are chestnut brown.

The bird is named for several notches along the cutting edge of its lower bill. Its bill is adapted to saw through the tough seeds of Dysoxylum trees, relatives of mahogany, according to the EDGE of Existence program.

It flies clumsily and slowly along a low path, which helps set it apart from other Samoan pigeons. The only nest ever recorded sat about 82 feet (25 meters) up in a banyan tree.

The bird prefers the large, hard-coated fruits of Dysoxylum. Hunters interviewed for the conservation effort said it also feeds on several other fruiting trees, and it may forage on the ground.

The species has been listed as Critically Endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) since 2014. It had been listed as Endangered from 2000 to 2014.

Samoa’s Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Conservation Society published a recovery plan for the species in March 2020. At that time, the last definite, confirmed sighting dated from August 4, 2017, in the Uafato forest.

A juvenile photographed on Savai’i in December 2013 was the first certain record of the species this century. It also showed that the manumea was still breeding.

The species is known from ten localities on Savai’i, and remote areas of forest on that island have never been surveyed.

Earlier fieldwork suggested that one definite sighting was possible every three to five years, even with medium to intensive search effort.

The 2025 observers saw only adult birds, and the society has said it is unclear whether the sightings involved one bird or several.

The manumea’s advertising call is nearly identical to one of the calls of the Pacific imperial pigeon, or lupe. Even local hunters and experts struggle to tell the two apart.

A 2020 study in Pacific Conservation Biology tested whether hunters’ traditional knowledge could help. Recordings at nine forest sites on Upolu and Savai’i yielded 104 clear call sequences.

Two top hunters each identified the species behind 80 sequences. They agreed on 54 of them, or 67 percent.

Sound analysis found that the manumea’s coo calls are lower in pitch and more regularly spaced than those of the lupe. The regular rhythm may help observers recognize the bird in the field.

The study also described the manumea as actively hiding in the dense canopy when it hears people moving through the forest.

Surveys in the late 1980s put the population at 4,800 to 7,200 birds across Samoa.

A later estimate of about 500 birds, from 2005 and 2006, is now considered far too high. It relied on calls that are easily confused with the lupe’s.

Surveys in 2012 and 2013 estimated fewer than 50 birds on each of Samoa’s two main islands, Upolu and Savai’i.

The recovery plan names three main threats: habitat loss and degradation, hunting and invasive predators. In recent decades, it appears that manumea have been killed mainly by mistake or as bycatch during lupe hunts.

Black rats and feral cats may also harm the species, though there is no direct evidence of it yet. Cyclones Ofa in 1990 and Val in 1991 reduced forest canopy cover by an estimated 27 percent, and the population appears never to have recovered.

Samoa has banned hunting all endemic pigeons, doves and fruit bats since at least 2004, but the rule has never been enforced nationally.

The ten-year plan sets out eight objectives and 26 activities, with an estimated budget of about $1.8 million. Its goal is to improve the species’ status from Critically Endangered to Endangered by 2029.

Early priorities included a conservation working group, a two-year fundraising campaign and a dedicated manumea coordinator.

A 2019 to 2020 national campaign strategy called the manumea “highly threatened and at risk of extinction in our lifetimes.”

Surveys of remote forest areas are still needed to find any undiscovered groups of the bird.

The information was obtained from the Samoa Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment and the Samoa Conservation Society.

#6377. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

#6376. Today’s the First Day You Can Officially Download Grand Theft Auto VI—If You Pre-Order Now

The anticipation is (almost) finally over.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

I’m not sure I’ve waited for anything longer than I have for GTA VI. But that applies to virtually everyone. The anticipation itself has become a meme of sorts: “I can’t believe we got [X] before GTA VI,” etc. You know the deal.

Anyway, we’re a week out, and it almost feels surreal. On the other hand, it’s possibly the only time it’s ever felt real, at least for gamers—today is the first day the game can be officially delivered and downloaded.

The game has been available to pre-order for Xbox Series X, PlayStation 5, and PC for a while now, but today is the first day you can physically download it. Bad news for old-school physical-media junkies like me: the disc version is no longer available. But there are plenty of codes to spare, and like always, Amazon makes it easy. The other benefit of pre-ordering: you get the Vintage Vice City Pack, which includes retro-themed vehicles, properties, clothes, and weapon finishes

We’re still a week away from full access, but having the game in hand and downloaded feels like a massive milestone in this decade-long journey. Technically, it’s been more than a decade—GTA V was originally launched in September 2013.

It’s been a slow rollout, to say the least. The game was announced officially in 2022 after years of speculation. It was in development hell for years, and after several pushed-back release dates, we’re finally seeing it come to fruition.

If you’re inexplicably one of the people who haven’t pre-ordered it yet, now is essentially the best time to do so. You’ll have a full week to download the game so you can play it as soon as the clock strikes midnight on 11/19. And if you couldn’t already tell, that’s exactly what I’m doing.

#6375. Malaria mosquito bites aren’t one quick jab but five separate moves under the skin

Under the skin, a malaria mosquito bite runs in five steps, and the researchers who filmed it say the first two are the ones to stop.

A mosquito bite feels like a single stab. Beneath the surface, however, it’s a sequence. A malaria mosquito pierces the skin in a fraction of a second.

Then she spends about 20 seconds pushing a flexible needle in and out, searching for a blood vessel. Only then does she start to drink.

Researchers who filmed and recorded that process on a living human arm counted five separate steps, and the mosquito’s legs and mouthparts move in time with each one.

The experiments were done in Christopher Potter’s lab in the Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine.

Joanna Konopka, who is at the Johns Hopkins Malaria Research Institute, and Danny Poinapen, who also works at Western University’s Robarts Research Institute in Canada, led the work.

Every bite happened on the right forearm of one volunteer, and the mosquitoes were lab-raised Anopheles coluzzii, a malaria carrier from sub-Saharan Africa.

In an interview with Earth.com, Konopka was asked whether any of the five steps could be interrupted to stop a bite or an infection. Her answer named the first two.

“The first two stages of the bite (skin piercing and blood vessel searching) are most important for disease transmission, because this is when the pathogen is most likely to be introduced via mosquito saliva,” she said.

The volunteer wore a small, clear acrylic box strapped to her forearm with sports wristbands. It left a window of skin about an inch (2.5 centimeters) square.

One female mosquito at a time was released onto that patch while a high-speed camera recorded at up to 250 frames per second. A tracking program followed the legs, the mouthparts, and the two feelers beside them, which are called palps.

What happens below the surface can’t be filmed, so the team recorded it electrically instead. Each mosquito was glued at the back to a gold wire finer than a human hair while the volunteer held an electrode.

The moment the needle broke the skin, the circuit closed, and every movement underneath showed up as a change in voltage.

“We were fascinated by the coordinated and synchronized movements that female mosquitoes exhibit above and below our skin when they are biting us,” Poinapen told Earth.com.

“And some of these movements occur as fast as an eye blink yet they are finely coordinated!”

Five stages stood out in the voltage traces: piercing the skin, searching for a vessel, drinking blood, pulling the mouthparts back, and withdrawing them.

A full bite took about 160 seconds on average. Roughly 128 of those seconds went to drinking and about 21 to the search for a vessel.

Above the skin, the body kept pace. As the mosquito pushes the needle deeper, her front legs bend and lift off the skin.

When she pulls back, the legs straighten and press down, and the bend begins a fraction of a second before the mouthpart moves.

A mosquito repeated that push and pull about three times before settling into a steadier search. Her palps changed with each stage too. During the hunt for a vessel they swung side to side above the skin, 10 to 25 times a second.

The moment blood began to flow, the palps stopped swinging and started a faint up-and-down vibration. The team suspects that vibration matches the pumps in the mosquito’s head that draw blood in.

The team ran the same recordings on Aedes aegypti, the mosquito that spreads yellow fever and dengue.

The two groups split about 150 million years ago, and the traces showed it. The malaria mosquito stabbed its needle in abruptly, while Aedes worked it in gradually, with a steady rhythm.

Once inside, Anopheles found a vessel about 17 seconds sooner, with shorter and more targeted probing. Even so, both finished a meal in about the same time, roughly 160 seconds for Anopheles and 165 for Aedes.

The volunteer reported that every Anopheles bite was noticeable whereas the Aedes bites were painless. Whether that holds for anyone else is still an open question, and Earth.com asked the researchers whether the abrupt stab is why malaria mosquito bites seem to hurt more.

“This is not an established phenomenon – different people can have different experiences and reactions to the bites of these two mosquitoes,” Konopka and Poinapen said.

They added that the different piercing patterns might relate to when each mosquito is active. Malaria mosquitoes bite mainly at dusk and at night, while yellow fever mosquitoes bite mostly in the daytime.

Mosquitoes taste and smell with their legs and mouthparts as well as their antennae. To test how much the bite depends on that, the team bred Anopheles that lacked one of two genes.

Whole families of taste and smell receptors need those genes in order to work.

One gene, called IR76b, is active in nerve cells of the legs, the mouth tip, and the needle itself, the three parts that touch the skin. The other, orco, is active in the mouth tip but not in the legs or the needle.

Mosquitoes missing both copies of IR76b mostly didn’t bite at all. More than half made no attempt in 20 minutes on the volunteer’s arm. Of the 14 tested, six probed and only four managed a partial meal.

Mosquitoes missing orco still bit, some of them a little later than normal, and 98 percent of their probes ended in a blood meal.

Mutants that did bite kept the same timing through all five steps. The one difference was in the drinking itself, which ran in a more regular, repetitive pattern than in normal mosquitoes.

“We found that some malaria mosquitoes with impaired sense of taste and smell had difficulty initiating and completing bites,” the two researchers wrote.

“This indicates that mosquitoes heavily rely on their ability to flavor us during the biting process.”

All of this rests on one volunteer’s arm and on lab strains of each species. So the team can’t yet say how much a bite changes on a different person’s skin, or with wild mosquitoes.

The mosquitoes with no working IR76b never fed while wired up, so there are no recordings of their bites. A third family of taste receptors couldn’t be switched off at all, because no shared gene controls it.

The biggest gap is under the skin. One possibility the researchers raise is that the needle itself senses chemical cues on the way to a blood vessel, and that mosquitoes without IR76b can no longer aim it.

Following the needle’s movements inside the skin, and finding those cues, is the work the team says is needed next. The same setup, they wrote, could also test how repellents, skin microbes, and different hosts change a bite.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

#6373. Childhood health problems may share hidden environmental links

A study following children into adolescence links early environmental exposures to overlapping patterns in physical and mental health.

The environment children grow up in can shape their health in more ways than we might realize.

From the air they breathe to the food they eat, everyday exposures may be connected to several health problems that continue into adolescence.

In a study of 586 European children, some exposures were linked to several problems at once.

A mother’s smoking during pregnancy was tied to a higher body mass index in her child and to more aggressive, impulsive behavior. Both links were still there in the teen years.

The findings suggest that a single early exposure may be tied to several parts of a child’s health.

Studying several health outcomes together can help reveal these overlapping links.

Augusto Anguita-Ruiz of the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal) and the University of Barcelona led the work with colleagues at Inserm, France’s national institute for health and medical research.

From pregnancy into the teen years, the researchers observed families and changed nothing about how they lived.

Xavier Basagaña, an ISGlobal researcher, is a senior co-author of the study.

“The study does not establish that these exposures cause the observed health outcomes,” said Basagaña.

All of the children came from six long-running birth studies in the United Kingdom, France, Spain, Lithuania, Norway and Greece. The six studies belong to a European project called HELIX.

For each mother and child, the team had 69 measures from pregnancy and 129 from childhood. Scientists have a name for that full mix of what a person eats, breathes and lives around: the exposome.

Blood and urine samples provided measures of tobacco exposure, metals, pesticides and other chemical pollutants.

Other exposure measures came from home and school addresses, which the team used to estimate outdoor air pollution, traffic and nearby natural spaces.

Questionnaires covered diet, sleep, physical activity and pets.

The team compared those measures with 11 health outcomes in four areas: weight and blood pressure, mental health, breathing, and allergies. Each child was examined twice, at an average age of about 8 and again at about 15.

Researchers behind a recent US atlas compared 619 exposures with 305 health traits, but their survey data captured each person at a single point in time.

Six pregnancy exposures and 42 childhood exposures were linked to more than one health outcome. The researchers call these four health areas domains.

Valérie Siroux is an Inserm researcher and senior co-author.

“Although no exposure was associated with all four domains, around one in three of the selected exposures was linked to more than one, suggesting that certain exposures can have broad and multisystemic effects on health,” said Siroux.

Smoking during pregnancy was one of those exposures. It was also tied to more ADHD symptoms in the teen years.

Among childhood exposures, fine particles in indoor air, known as PM2.5, were linked to worse results for weight and blood pressure and for mental health.

Higher copper levels in a child’s blood were linked to worse results in the same two areas.

Secondhand smoke and benzene in indoor air were each linked to higher BMI or blood pressure at both exams.

Why would one exposure be tied to such different problems? The authors suggested that the four health areas share biological pathways, most notably inflammation throughout the body. The team didn’t measure inflammation here.

Of those 42 childhood exposures, 16 were linked to outcomes across more than one health area, and 12 of those involved diet.

Diet also appeared when the team analyzed weight and blood pressure alone. There, following a diet closer to the Mediterranean pattern and eating more fruit were each linked to lower BMI and blood pressure.

In the team’s models, childhood exposures explained up to about 15% of the variation in mental health and in weight and blood pressure.

Pregnancy exposures explained up to about 7% of the variation in mental health and about 1.5% in weight and blood pressure.

So the measured exposures left most of the differences among children unexplained. Allergy outcomes were scarcely related to the exposures.

Some results were the reverse of what the team expected.

Higher blood levels of certain long-lasting chemicals, including PCBs and the PFAS chemical PFOA, were linked to lower BMI and blood pressure in children.

The authors didn’t read that as protection. These chemicals are stored in body fat, so a child’s body fat and growth are expected to affect how much of each chemical appears in blood.

Body size may be shaping the blood reading rather than the chemical shaping body size, the authors wrote, and they urged caution with those results.

The team also repeated every analysis six times, each time leaving out the children from one of the six birth studies.

Most links appeared again, in the same direction, in more than four of the six runs.

A few links didn’t meet that standard. One tied how much meat a mother ate during pregnancy to asthma and wheezing in her child. Another tied fast food in childhood to worse mental health.

Such links may reflect conditions in one region or one group of families rather than a general pattern, the authors wrote.

Among the 1,301 mother-child pairs in HELIX, the 586 in this study were those with data from every stage. About 87% of the children were white, and 53% of their mothers held a university degree.

The authors described the group as highly selective, so the links may not apply to other populations. The group was also too small to analyze boys and girls separately.

Some chemicals with highly variable levels were measured in only one or a few urine samples, which could make a link look stronger or weaker than it is.

The bacteria, viruses and fungi a child encounters weren’t measured. The authors suggested that could be why breathing and allergy problems were less clearly tied to the exposures.

Every association is posted in a free interactive online atlas that anyone can search or download.

“Further studies in larger and more diverse populations will be needed to better understand these relationships and determine whether modifying some of these exposures can alter health trajectories during childhood and adolescence,” Basagaña said.

Future research could also add outcomes this study lacked, such as thinking skills and metabolic health, and examine children at other ages.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6371. Diabetes and Alzheimer’s share a link that scientists are still trying to explain

A review of 40 studies examines the link between type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s, offering new estimates of risk and unanswered questions.

How many people with type 2 diabetes go on to develop Alzheimer’s each year? Five in every 1,000, according to a new estimate.

The estimate comes from a review of 40 studies. In it, people with type 2 diabetes were about 53% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s than people without it.

Diabetes has been tied to dementia for years. Trouble is, most earlier reviews threw several kinds of diabetes or dementia into one pot.

This one was limited to type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s disease, and a link between the two was still found. Yearly case counts, rarely reported before, were worked out as well.

Emmanuel Adewuyi is a researcher at the Curtin School of Population Health at Curtin University in Australia.

Adewuyi worked on the review with lead author Thi Thu Huong Nguyen and colleagues in Australia, the UK, and Nigeria.

The 53% figure describes the relative increase in risk. The rate of new cases over time is called incidence.

“Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer’s disease among people living with type 2 diabetes,” Adewuyi said.

Every study in the review was observational. People’s health was recorded, and no treatment was assigned.

Research like that can show that two conditions go together. It can’t show that one causes the other.

Dementia affects more than 57 million people worldwide. Alzheimer’s disease accounts for about 60% to 70% of those cases.

Type 2 is by far the most common form of diabetes, accounting for more than 90% of cases.

Both conditions become more common with age. Many of the same heart and metabolic risk factors are shared by the two.

Type 2 diabetes has a stronger link to vascular dementia than to Alzheimer’s. Vascular dementia follows damage to blood vessels in the brain.

Mixing the two, the authors wrote, blurs how much of the risk belongs to Alzheimer’s. Adewuyi’s team therefore kept only studies in which both type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer’s were clearly identified.

Studies that mixed type 2 with type 1 or pregnancy-related diabetes were dropped. Studies that could not separate Alzheimer’s from other dementias were dropped as well.

The researchers searched four medical databases for studies published through April 2026. They found 9,431 articles, but only 40 met their criteria.

Those 40 studies were published between 1997 and 2026 and covered 12 countries. South Korea contributed 10 studies, the United States eight, and the United Kingdom seven.

In 38 studies, researchers followed participants over time, with average follow-up periods ranging from two to 15 years. In most studies, the average participant age was between 55 and 75.

The combined study samples totaled more than 27 million people, though some people may have appeared in more than one study. For example, all seven UK studies used data from the same source, the UK Biobank.

In 26 of the studies, people with type 2 diabetes were compared with people without it. New Alzheimer’s cases were counted in each group.

The results had already been adjusted for other factors, most often age and sex, the authors wrote.

When the 26 were pooled, Alzheimer’s risk was 53% higher for people with type 2 diabetes. With any single study taken out, the increase stayed between 50% and 57%, the authors wrote.

Across subgroups such as region, age, and study date, the increase ranged from 40% to 66%.

Separate results for men and women were given in only a handful of studies. Similar increases were seen there: 76% for men and 73% for women.

The authors wrote that the sex-specific figures should be treated with caution.

The International Diabetes Federation’s Diabetes Atlas has its own, lower estimate. In the atlas, the increase for Alzheimer’s was put at 34%.

The authors wrote that the two estimates are compatible with each other. Different sets of studies in the two reviews may explain the gap, they wrote.

Across 23 of the 40 studies, covering about 9 million people, the pooled rate among people with type 2 diabetes was about 4.7 new Alzheimer’s cases per 1,000 people a year.

From study to study, it swung from under 1 case per 1,000 people a year to almost 14. Much depended on how a study went looking for Alzheimer’s.

Where hospital or national health records were combed, about 4 cases per 1,000 people a year were found.

Where participants were diagnosed using clinical criteria or memory tests, the figure was about 10. Health records probably miss milder cases, the authors wrote.

The yearly rate per 1,000 people varied by region. It was about 7.5 in North America and 5.8 in East Asia and the Pacific. In Europe and Central Asia, it was 1.2.

Health, access to care, and diagnosis may all differ by region, the authors wrote. Those explanations still need to be tested.

Only a few studies split their results by sex. In that small set, the yearly rate was 3.6 per 1,000 women and 2.8 per 1,000 men.

The authors used a standard scale to assess the evidence behind both main estimates. They rated its certainty as very low.

None of the 40 studies tested a treatment, and their results varied widely.

The team rated 38 studies as having a low risk of bias and two as having a moderate risk. But those ratings did not account for how often participants visited a doctor.

People with type 2 diabetes may have more medical appointments. That could give doctors more chances to notice and diagnose Alzheimer’s.

Earlier research by Adewuyi and colleagues found that the two diseases share some genetic influences. However, it found limited evidence that genes linked to type 2 diabetes directly increase Alzheimer’s risk.

Insulin resistance, high blood sugar, and inflammation could also help explain the connection, the authors said. But the 53% higher risk shows a pattern across groups of people, not proof that diabetes directly causes Alzheimer’s.

In 11 of the 40 studies, researchers relied on participants to report whether they had diabetes. Most studies also took place in high-income countries.

The review could not determine whether better diabetes management changes a person’s risk of Alzheimer’s.

Studies inconsistently reported how long participants had lived with diabetes, how well their blood sugar was controlled, and which medications they used.

Metformin, pioglitazone, and acarbose have each been tied to lower dementia risk in earlier research. So have other diabetes drugs, GLP-1 drugs among them, in people with type 2 diabetes. Cause is as hard to pin down there as here.

Adewuyi’s team described the new figures as a benchmark for future studies testing whether diabetes treatment changes Alzheimer’s risk.

In the meantime, the team sees a case for watching memory and thinking as part of long-term diabetes care.

The authors said that future studies would be better if researchers combined individual patient data from multiple studies instead of relying on published summaries.

This would help them account for other risk factors more accurately.

The full study was published in the journal Alzheimer’s Research & Therapy.

#6370. Tropical cyclones may follow a hidden winter pattern months before they form

A February weather pattern may offer clues to East Asia’s summer typhoon activity, providing information beyond El Niño.

Predicting how many tropical cyclones will reach East Asia months ahead is difficult. But a weather pattern that develops in late winter may offer an early clue.

New research suggests that this pattern could help researchers anticipate summer tropical cyclone activity beyond what El Niño alone can explain.

The study was led by Zeming Wu from Zhejiang University and examined more than 40 years of observations.

This year, many blamed the strong El Niño for the storms.

El Niño is a periodic warming of surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific that can influence where tropical cyclones form and how they travel.

But the researchers argue it may not be entirely El Niño’s fault this time.

The team focused on the Pacific–North American pattern, or PNA, a large-scale pattern of atmospheric pressure variations over the North Pacific and North America.

It operates in phases. Its “positive phase” brings warmer temperatures across the western United States and Canada and cooler temperatures across the central and southeastern United States. The negative phase is the reverse.

The researchers found that the February PNA pattern was linked to tropical cyclone activity over East Asia the following summer.

The relationship remained after accounting for the influence of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a recurring climate pattern that includes El Niño and La Niña.

“Our findings suggest that late-winter atmospheric variability may provide valuable information about East Asian summer tropical cyclone activity beyond the influence of ENSO,” Wu said.

“This highlights the potential importance of atmospheric circulation outside the tropics as an additional source of seasonal predictability.”

The positive phase of PNA in late winter is linked to fewer tropical cyclones forming over the western North Pacific and fewer storms reaching East Asia several months later.

But how does a February pattern stay connected to summer storms?

The original atmospheric anomalies may have weakened or vanished. Ocean temperatures kept the events linked.

“Through interactions between the atmosphere and ocean, sea surface temperature anomalies can preserve and transmit climate signals across seasons,” said co-author Chundi Hu from the same university.

The team found two complementary pathways, both mediated by the ocean and linking late-winter PNA variability to summer tropical cyclone activity.

“The ocean appears to act as a bridge between winter atmospheric variability and summer tropical cyclone activity,” Wu said.

“More importantly, our results suggest that this connection involves not only the familiar ENSO-related pathway but also another pathway associated with atmospheric variability beyond preceding-winter ENSO.”

The first pathway involves ENSO. A positive PNA pattern in late winter is associated with warming in the tropical North Atlantic and a relatively rapid weakening of El Niño in the tropical Pacific.

According to the researchers, these temperature changes match shifts in large-scale atmospheric circulation.

Those shifts favored the development and persistence of an anomalous anticyclone over the western North Pacific into summer.

The second pathway works beyond the linear influence of preceding-winter ENSO. Hu pointed to a mechanism called seasonal footprinting.

This pattern lets anomalies in atmospheric circulation leave a lasting and developing imprint on ocean temperatures.

In this case, the anomalies were wind changes over the subtropical North Pacific and were associated with cooling in the central tropical Pacific.

“Despite their different origins, both pathways converge on a similar atmospheric response: an anomalous anticyclone, or unusual system of high pressure, over the western North Pacific,” Wu said.

“This circulation pattern suppresses conditions favorable for tropical cyclone formation and modifies the winds that steer storms, reducing the number of tropical cyclones reaching East Asia during summer.”

Next, the researchers plan targeted climate model experiments to investigate these pathways further.

“Ultimately, our goal is to better understand the sources of tropical cyclone predictability and contribute to more reliable seasonal risk assessments for East Asian coastal communities,” Hu said.

Seasonal forecasts give coastal communities time to plan for storm risks. The findings suggest that February’s PNA pattern could provide useful information alongside ENSO.

Further testing will help establish whether this winter signal improves forecasts of summer tropical cyclone activity.

The PNA pattern is large scale. It distributes air and heat across the North Pacific and North America. Its late-winter phase may offer a clue months before the storms arrive.

For coastal communities in East Asia, better forecasts could mean better preparation and more reliable seasonal risk assessments. That could help people get ready before the storms hit.

The study is published in the journal Ocean-Land-Atmosphere Research.

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041
