#6368. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6366. Instagram posts may reveal subtle clues about loneliness

Instagram habits may reveal loneliness in college students but cannot reliably show their support networks, according to a new study.

Instagram users carefully choose what they share, but their posts may still reveal signs of loneliness.

A new study of U.S. college students found that posting habits, captions, and photos offered clues about how lonely students felt.

Those same accounts revealed far less about how many friends or relatives students could turn to for support.

The work was led by Sherry (Yueyi) Jiang with psychology professor Piotr Winkielman at the University of California San Diego. Jiang completed a doctorate in experimental psychology there in 2025.

All of the students attended that one university, and most of them were women. The results describe patterns across a group. They are not presented by the authors as a way to screen any single person.

Loneliness is difficult for other people to see. The authors also described it as a serious risk factor for early death. The effects are comparable in size to those of smoking and obesity, they wrote.

Each student completed questionnaires, then downloaded a full archive of their Instagram account and uploaded it to a secure server.

In total, 541 students took part, and 415 of them were kept in the analysis. A total of 93 students were excluded by the team because posts, likes, or comments were missing from their archives.

A further 33 students were removed since their questionnaires had been left unfinished.

Only part of an account can be seen on a public profile. About 62% of the students had private accounts.

Posts, likes, and comments that remain invisible to strangers on the app could therefore be studied by the researchers.

The archives contained 9,353 captions and 353,407 comments, together with the photos and the time of every post.

Faces in the photos were detected by one program, and the expression and head tilt of each face were estimated.

The tone of captions and comments was scored by other programs. Words were also sorted by these programs into themes, such as family or the past.

The share of each student’s posts made late at night, defined as 11 p.m. to 5 a.m., was also calculated.

Computer models were subsequently trained by the team to identify the lonelier students from those Instagram measures alone.

Data from 80% of the students were used to build the models, which were tested on the remaining 20%.

From the questionnaires, five scores were obtained for every student, and four of these reflected how lonely the student felt.

The fifth score addressed a separate matter. It reflected how many relatives and friends a student contacted regularly and could ask for help.

The main loneliness questionnaire included 20 statements, among them “I feel isolated from others.”

Model performance was judged on a scale where 0.5 equals a coin flip and 1 is perfect. A value of 0.77 was reached by the best model for this main questionnaire.

For each of two more specific loneliness scores, the models achieved 0.74, while a single-question score was predicted at 0.68. The first three results were described by the authors as moderate, and the last one as modest.

Weaker performance was recorded for the fifth score, which concerned support.

The best model reached 0.61, with an uncertainty range of 0.42 to 0.79. Because that range included 0.5, the result did not clearly establish performance better than chance.

Two kinds of loneliness have been separated by researchers since the 1970s.

Emotional loneliness is the distress of having no one close. Social loneliness is dissatisfaction with a person’s wider social circle.

On Instagram, students with higher social loneliness scores tended to be less active with other people.

These students liked fewer posts. They also commented less often and posted less on weekends.

A different pattern was seen in students with higher emotional loneliness scores. More of their posts went up late at night.

Their captions were more negative in tone, and sad or angry facial expressions were more common in their photos.

The emotionally lonely students also posted more often, not less. Frequent posting, the authors suggested, might be an effort to find emotional connection when close ties are missing.

Word choice was examined as well. Students who wrote “we” more often tended to score lower on emotional loneliness. Those who wrote “I” more often tended to score higher on social loneliness.

“Loneliness isn’t a one-size-fits-all experience, and neither are the solutions,” Winkielman said.

Two ideas were proposed by the authors for future testing. Social loneliness might be eased by more chances to engage with others.

For emotional loneliness, help with low mood and disrupted daily routines was suggested instead.

Lonely people are often depressed or anxious as well, and the same was true of these students.

The team therefore checked each Instagram sign again. This time, each student’s depression and anxiety scores were taken into account.

Only one sign was still linked to loneliness: fewer faces per post. Students whose photos contained fewer faces were more likely to score high on two of the loneliness measures.

According to the authors, fewer moments shared with other people may be reflected in photos that contain fewer faces. The same link between loneliness and the number of faces had been reported in an earlier study of Instagram users.

Past-focused words in captions were tied to two of the loneliness measures. Profile photos with the head tilted upward were tied to three.

That tilt is probably no accident, Jiang’s team wrote, given how carefully people pick their photo angles. But once depression and anxiety scores entered the analysis, neither sign was still tied to loneliness.

Nobody in the study was followed over time. Each of the 415 students filled out the questionnaires once and handed over an archive.

So the order is unknown: the Instagram habits may have come first, or the loneliness, or both.

The group itself was narrow. About 85% of the students were 21 or younger and about 79% were women.

Asian students (43.9%) and White students (38.8%) made up the two largest groups.

Age and culture change how loneliness is felt, the authors wrote, and they change posting habits on social media too.

Patterns found among San Diego undergraduates need to be tested in other populations.

There is also the question of misuse, which the authors raised themselves.

Flag the wrong person, and the result may be stigma or outreach that was never wanted. Miss the right person, and support does not arrive.

For that reason, the team limited its suggestion to consent-based research and to support services that people opt into.

Covert screening built only on these signs was advised against.

Two kinds of follow-up were proposed. One would measure the same people’s loneliness repeatedly while their Instagram activity is collected.

The other would briefly change how lonely people feel in an experiment, then record what they do online afterward. Cause is easier to isolate that way, according to the authors.

The full study was published in the journal npj Mental Health Research.

#6365. Breast cancer leaves signs in blood that may hint at its return

A new blood test showed promise for spotting breast cancer and predicting relapse, but larger studies remain essential.

Mammograms can sometimes miss breast cancer in women with dense breasts. A new blood test called EPINUC showed promise in detecting breast cancer regardless of breast density.

The test also found signs linked to cancer returning within five years.

Larger studies are needed to confirm whether it can help detect cancer early and predict its return.

The test was developed in the lab of Efrat Shema at the Weizmann Institute of Science.

For the new study, her team worked with Guy Ron, a physicist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Ron’s group belongs to the university’s Racah Institute of Physics.

The cancer status of every woman was already known when her blood sample was analyzed. The test has not yet been applied to women undergoing routine screening.

Inside a cell, DNA is wound around protein spools. Each spool, with its loop of DNA, is called a nucleosome.

Small chemical tags are added to the spool proteins. These tags help set which genes the cell uses, and biologists call them epigenetic tags.

Dying cells, whether healthy or cancerous, release nucleosomes into the bloodstream. The tags stay on.

Tumor DNA is the target of several blood tests for cancer. In Shema’s method, the tagged spools are instead examined individually under a microscope.

Each type of tag is marked with a fluorescent label of a different color. Tags that occur together on a single spool can therefore be identified.

The test needs less than 1 milliliter of plasma, the liquid part of blood – about one-fifth of a teaspoon.

Colorectal cancer was detected by an earlier version of the test.

Two further tags and three proteins related to breast tissue were added for the present study. A total of 29 measurements is now obtained from each sample.

The relevant tags were first sought in tumor tissue. Twelve women who had not yet received any treatment provided the samples.

The operations were performed at Kaplan Medical Center in Israel. Noa Furth, a researcher in Shema’s lab, is one of the study’s lead authors.

“Once a tumor is removed, there’s only a short window of opportunity before its epigenetic tags begin to deteriorate,” said Furth.

“So as each surgery began, the doctors would alert me. I would rush the tissue sample from the hospital to our lab on ice, and we’d start analyzing it that very day.”

The team measured the tags in more than 1.1 million individual cells.

Eleven of the 12 tumors were luminal. Hormone receptors are present on the cells of luminal tumors, which generally respond well to hormone-blocking drugs.

Each luminal tumor also contained a minor population of unusual cells. These cells resembled a different form of breast cancer, known as basal-like. A worse outlook is associated with that form.

Hormone signaling was reduced in the basal-like cells.

The same pattern of tags was observed in these cells across patients. In laboratory cultures of breast cancer cells, greater movement was recorded for cells of this kind.

The researchers then investigated whether genetic differences could explain the aggressive cells.

New colonies were established in the laboratory, each from a single cell.

“The differences appear to be mainly epigenetic,” Shema said.

“When we grew breast cancer models in the lab starting with nonaggressive cells, an aggressive population always emerged eventually.”

The test was then applied to stored blood from 77 women with luminal breast cancer. All had been treated at Mayo Clinic in Florida. Blood from 30 healthy women was also tested.

A computer model was trained to distinguish cancer samples from healthy samples. Its performance score was 0.95, where 0.5 indicates chance-level performance and 1 indicates perfect separation.

An identical score was obtained for the 42 patients with tumors in the smallest size class. Such tumors measure about 0.8 inches (2 centimeters) or less.

No change in performance was seen across density scores, which are assigned by radiologists from mammograms. This was also true of women with extremely dense breasts.

Samples from two Israeli hospitals and a second Mayo batch were subsequently included. The combined set comprised 137 patients and 51 healthy women.

Three-quarters of these samples were used to train a new model, and the remainder served as a test.

In the test group, 92% of the 13 healthy women were correctly identified as cancer-free.

Cancer was detected in 85% of the 34 patients and missed in 15%.

The test did about as well in 22 women with triple-negative breast cancer, which lacks hormone receptors.

Luminal breast cancer usually responds to treatment, but in many women it comes back. Differences among the cells within a tumor are suspected to be one reason tumors return.

All 77 Mayo patients gave blood before surgery. The women were then followed for at least five years. Cancer returned in 33 of them within five years, while 44 remained disease-free.

Two tags characteristic of the basal-like cells were elevated in the blood of women who later relapsed.

A model built on the blood measurements separated the two groups. It scored 0.81 on the same scale. Models based on age, tumor stage, grade, and other standard measures scored lower.

A score of 0.92 was recorded in a second, smaller set of 30 patients.

These differences in blood markers were also present in women with early-stage or low-grade tumors. Such tumors are rated as lower risk by standard measures.

The team also looked at Oncotype DX scores. Oncotype DX is a gene test performed on tumor tissue to estimate the risk of relapse.

Its scores did not differ between 40 women who stayed disease-free and nine who relapsed.

All samples had been collected earlier and were analyzed once the outcomes were known. The group to which each sample belonged was not concealed from the analysts.

The groups were small as well. Cancer returned in only 10 of the 30 patients in the second set.

Blood from healthy women was collected at the Weizmann Institute. Blood from patients was supplied by hospitals in the United States and Israel.

Nearly all of the tumors examined were luminal. Triple-negative tumors are usually treated with drugs before surgery, and few untreated ones were available.

The authors wrote that the tumor findings may not extend to other types of breast cancer.

Signals from tumor cells, damaged healthy tissue, and the immune system are combined in blood. A tag found in blood therefore cannot be attributed to the basal-like cells alone.

Both tumor tissue and blood were available from ten women. For most tags, higher levels in the tumor were accompanied by higher levels in the blood.

The blood-test method is covered by a patent application on which Shema is a named inventor. The exclusive license is held by a company called Epivision Genetics. Four of the study’s authors are affiliated with that company.

Larger studies of the blood test are still required, the authors wrote. In such studies, blood would be collected first and each woman’s outcome learned afterward.

A separate question concerns the basal-like cells. It remains to be tested whether tumor cells can be kept from switching states by epigenetic drugs.

“We’re now looking for treatments that could deprive cancer cells of their epigenetic flexibility – and perhaps even coax cells that have already turned aggressive into adopting less aggressive traits,” Shema said.

No such treatment was tested in this study.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9

#6362. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6360. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

The missing 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

More than a billion years of geological history is missing from the walls of the Grand Canyon, and now, scientists may know why.

In the canyon's sides, ancient metamorphic and igneous rocks that formed 1.7 billion years ago sit directly under younger sedimentary rocks laid down 500 million years ago. The 1.2 billion-year chunk of history in between wasn't preserved — leaving a geological gap known as the Great Unconformity.

This missing period was a very important time in Earth's history, because it was just before and during the Cambrian explosion, which saw a huge diversification of life on Earth. The Great Unconformity is not only at the Grand Canyon; there are big gaps in the rock layers of that time across North America, the Baltic region of Europe and in northern China. Researchers have long debated why this unconformity exists.

The unconformity is sharply evident in the transition between Cambrian Tapeats Sandstone and Proterozoic Brahma Schist in the Grand Canyon.

Now, a new model of the movement of Earth's middle layer, the mantle, has revealed an explanation: The slow, heat-driven circulation of the mantle pushed these three regions upward during the time when the Great Unconformity was formed, according to new research published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

This uplift would have helped facilitate erosion, meaning sediments formed at that time sloughed off the continents and landed in the ocean. Importantly, the model also shows that in the past 540 million years, these same areas started sinking instead of rising, creating areas for sediments to get caught and then keep piling up in neat layers on the continents — marking the point where the Great Unconformity ends. This matches what geologists can see in North America, the Baltics and northern China.

"We looked at, where are the best places that the mantle would help create a Great Unconformity?" study co-author Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, told Live Science. "And these three places turned out to be three places where it's known to be quite extensive."

Erosion during Neoproterozoic times, followed by sedimentation during early Phanerozoic times, formed the Great Unconformity. Bottom: Dynamic uplift was followed by subsidence for Laurentia ('LAU'), Baltica ('BAL') and North China ('NCH').

The cause of the Great Unconformity is hotly debated, with some arguing that a global deep freeze known as Snowball Earth could have shoveled sediment off the continents in this period. Glaciation probably played a major role in erosion, Flament said, but the new study suggests that the key driver was deep within the planet. Without the mantle pushing the continents upward, glaciers and other erosive forces would have had no slope to push sediments down, he said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Earth is in a constant state of recycling crust through plate tectonics, said Shanan Peters, a geologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. Oceanic crust sinks back into the mantle through the process of subduction ‪—‬ when one tectonic plate dives beneath another. The chemicals it carries down with it get released back into the atmosphere via volcanic eruptions, linking the mantle with the atmosphere.

And tectonics aren't steady. As continents break up and join back together over eons, different materials get pushed into the crust. For example, the ancient Paleo-Tethys ocean, which lapped off the shores of the supercontinent Pangaea until it closed about 200 million years ago, was rich in carbon-bearing sediments that eroded from the continents, Peters said. When the ocean floor was subducted back into the mantle, this carbon was pushed into the depths of the planet.

It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved.

Today, in contrast, most of Earth's subduction is around the Pacific Rim, and much of the Pacific seafloor is remote from continents, so the seafloor is relatively starved of carbon. What's getting pushed into the mantle now is therefore a different chemical composition than what existed 200 million years ago.

In that sense, referring to the Great Unconformity as "missing information" isn't accurate, Peters told Live Science. Instead, the absence of a rock record in those places at that time reveals something about the processes going on back then — and hints at how geology might have been affecting the atmosphere, and thus life's evolution.

The geological processes occurring during the time of the Great Unconformity may have set the stage for the Cambrian explosion, Peters said. For example, the crystalline rocks exposed on the surface at that time may have released elements like potassium, iron, manganese and carbon into the seas at an increased rate, prompting marine life to invent biomineralization — shells — in response and possibly shifting the composition of Earth's atmosphere to be more oxygen-rich, Peters said.

Flament agreed that the geological changes had significant knock-on effects for life. "It contributes to the environment in which complex life evolved," Flament said.

What's particularly interesting about the Great Unconformity is how it reveals not just a period of erosion but also a switch back to the deposition of sediments. The new paper provides an explanation for both, Peters said, and changes in the mantle are just the planetary-scale process to explain this big-picture phenomenon.

"This seems to me to be the only reasonable way to go back and forth between this state over time," he said.

There are still questions about what else the continents were doing in this time period. Peters leads an effort called Macrostrat that is pulling together observations of rock layers around the world, and Flament said he hopes that database will help ground-truth the new models' findings.

"So far in Africa and Russia, we don’t have as comprehensive a database," he said. "Once that is done, we can go and check whether the idea works."

Editor's Note: This story was updated at 10:30 p.m. E.D.T. to note that James Price, not Tia Ghose, edited this story.

Dhungana, S., & Flament, N. (2026). The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity. Nature, 659(8139), 106–112. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The gold bear would have been worn on a headdress.

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan have discovered a unique gold bear figurine in a 2,200-year-old burial mound that looters had hit but failed to empty completely.

The sculpted bear stands on its hind limbs and holds a pot-like container between its front paws. The artifact would have been worn as part of a headdress, and holes at its base indicate that it could have been sewn onto the garment, according to a translated statement from the Kazakhstan government.

The 2,200-year-old gold bear is a unique find in Kazakhstan.

The gold bear was unearthed at an Early Iron Age burial mound at the Karagaily burial ground in the southern city of Almaty, along with a surprisingly high number of human bones for a single burial mound.

Although other gold-crafted animals have been found in the region, the newly unearthed bear is the first of its kind.

"The sculpted bear figurine is unique to Kazakhstan. No similar finds have been discovered previously," Lyazzat Sagyndykova, director of the Almaty Museums Association, which conducted the excavation, said in the statement. "This discovery allows us to trace cultural parallels across the whole of Eurasia, from the Black Sea region to Altai."

Archaeologists in Kazakhstan excavated a 2,200-year-old burial mound.

The figurine dates to the Saka period, named for a nomadic horseback-riding people from Iran who lived on the Eurasian Steppe and Tarim Basin of what is now western China. Archaeologists have found comparable gold objects at other excavations in Kazakhstan, according to the statement. For example, a headdress element shaped like a small leopard previously came to light at the Almaty Kok-Kainar burial ground, which dates to the fourth century B.C. Also, the headdress of Kazakhstan's famous "Golden Man," a young Iron Age warrior buried in an extraordinarily lavish grave, also has a gold, sheep-shaped decorative element.

It's unclear which bear species the figurine depicts, but today Kazakhstan is home to two subspecies of brown bear: the Tien Shan or Himalayan brown bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus), which lives in the Tien Shan Mountains in the southeast, and the East Siberian brown bear (Ursus arctos collaris) in the Altai Mountains in the east, according to a study published earlier this year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Preliminary analyses date the recently excavated site to the fourth to third centuries B.C., according to the statement. Based on the number of bones they excavated, experts suspect that the mound, which is around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and roughly 85 feet (26 m) wide, may have been the final resting place for four adults and three children.

Archaeologists found a surprising number of human bones in the burial mound.

"Of particular interest is the unusually large number of human remains in a single burial mound, as such burials are atypical for Kazakhstan," Marat Mugalovich Nurpeisov, a senior research fellow at the Almaty Museums Association, said in the statement. "As a rule, burial mounds of a comparable size were intended for the burial of one or two people."

Archaeologists also found pieces of Saka pottery, most of which had been strewn about after the burial had been looted in ancient times, according to the statement. The thieves left behind a 10-foot (3 m) looting pit.

"Research into the Karagaily burial ground is ongoing," Nurpeisov said in the statement. "To clarify the circumstances of the burial and determine the exact number of individuals interred, further analyses are planned, including the involvement of anthropologists."

After all of the investigations are finished, some of the artifacts will be put on display at the Almaty Museum, according to the statement.

#6355. A Viking Couple’s Grave May Reveal Who Really Settled This Strategic Island 1,100 Years Ago

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man were surprised to find not one but two of the island’s most significant Viking finds.

Two metal detectorists searching the Isle of Man received double the surprise when they uncovered a 1,100-year-old double grave. It contained rare brooches typically worn by Scandinavian women and a sword that, according to one expert, would once have gleamed with a “bright silver” pommel. The site also produced intricately decorated trading weights, a Viking axe head, balance scales, and a ceremonial bronze ladle.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” Allison Fox said in a statement. Fox is curator for archaeology at Manx National Heritage, a museum and heritage trust on the Isle of Man, a self-governing British Crown dependency in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland. “What makes it particularly exciting is the combination of finds, which gives us a rare opportunity to explore the lives of some of the island’s earliest Scandinavian settlers.”

Experts believe the metal detectorists, Daniel Crowe and Rhett Britton, came upon the double grave of a man and a woman who were buried with some of their finest possessions: three brooches for her and a sword for him. Fox said the date of the brooches suggests the grave may be the “earliest known female Viking Age burial” on the island. Together with the other finds, she said, the objects “help us build a picture of the people who lived here more than a thousand years ago, how they traded, and the connections they maintained across the Viking world.”

The find dates to around 900 C.E. That places it at the early end of the Viking Age on the Isle of Man, just as Scandinavian communities were becoming established there. Some of the objects are also the first of their kind found on the island.

Museum experts believe the Vikings first arrived on the island during the ninth century. Recognizing the strategic importance of its location in the Irish Sea, they established trading links before settling there. A rich Viking heritage remains across the island, and burials found in the past show evidence of pagan traditions. Viking influence still runs through Manx culture today. Tynwald, the island’s parliament, was founded during the Viking Age and is known as one of the world’s oldest continuous parliaments.

After making their discovery, Crowe and Britton didn’t try to clean the objects. Fox says this has allowed experts to fully appreciate the objects’ intricate details. She added that the brooches still have soil inside them, and the team is carefully excavating it in hopes of finding traces of textile.

Two of the brooches are a matching pair of oval “tortoise” brooches, the kind Scandinavian women wore to fasten their dresses at the shoulders. Both are covered in intricate interlocking animals, a hallmark of Viking art. According to Manx National Heritage, only one other pair like them has ever been found on the Isle of Man, and that was found by Daniel Crowe’s own father, John Crowe, along with fellow metal detectorist Craig Evans. The new pair is likely about 50 years older, which is why experts think this grave may be the island’s earliest known female Viking burial. The third brooch, decorated with spirals and a glass center, is the first of its kind found on the island.

The sword is the type a man would have carried, and it’s the 13th Viking sword found on the Isle of Man. Although the blade is badly corroded and parts of it are missing entirely, Fox said in a video from the heritage group that the pommel still shows “signs of the really intricate decorating that would have been on the pommel when it was buried.” X-ray analysis revealed traces of silver and copper wire inlaid into the iron, which makes it one of only three swords found on the island with such decoration.

“When this sword was buried,” she said, “this top part of the sword would have been really bright silver, a really high-status object.” In addition, traces of wood show that the sword’s handle was covered in wood rather than thread or horn.

Although 1,100 years in the ground caused much of the sword’s damage, experts believe the Vikings broke it on purpose as part of a burial ritual.

Because the brooches were found alongside the sword (items linked to a woman and a man, respectively), a double burial seems likely. Experts said, however, that they can’t be sure whether the grave goods came from one grave or from two graves placed close together.

Beyond the burial itself, the decorated lead weights and bronze balance scales found at the site highlight the Isle of Man’s role in Irish Sea trade. The weights are the first of their kind found on the island. One of them has a decorative bronze fitting, with artwork typical of Britain and Ireland, that may have been taken from another object.

The bronze ladle, another first for the island, was likely used in ceremonies.

Despite all the experts have gleaned from the discovery, there’s still much to be learned. “Although the original burial site has been disturbed,” Fox said, “further research may reveal much more about these objects and the people who owned them.”

#6354. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

#6353. REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127

The smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years. Most of these scopes focus primarily on electronic imaging, though, and while amateur astronomers may marvel at the images, they also still enjoy the simple pleasure of looking directly through a telescope.

That’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach. Rather than replacing direct observing with a screen-based experience, the SP127 combines a traditional 5-inch (127 millimeters) f/15 Maksutov-Cassegrain telescope with a smart guidance and imaging system.

At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount. But looks can be deceiving.

The secret lies in that “finder.” On closer inspection, it is not a finder at all, but a 2.1-inch (53 mm) f/4 ED refractor outfitted with a digital camera. This second optical tube is the heart of the SP127’s electronically assisted system, serving as both guide scope and imager. The guide scope determines the telescope’s position through plate solving, slews to selected targets, maintains tracking, and captures images. Spectrum Optics also includes the same intelligent camera and 53 mm refractor in its separately sold SPi53 Smart Telescope system.

The camera is built around a Sony IMX662 CMOS color sensor with 2.9-micrometer pixels and a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels. It includes 64 gigabytes of onboard storage.

The MirroSky app, available for iOS and Android, is central to the SP127’s operation. It controls target selection, image capture, live stacking, and display, while the guide scope and camera work together to find objects and produce live-stacked images.

Meanwhile, the Maksutov is dedicated primarily to visual observing. The optical tube weighs approximately 6.5 pounds (2.95 kilograms) and measures 14.6 inches (370 mm) long. A Vixen-style dovetail makes it easy to remove the optical tube from the mount. Total weight for the assembled SP127 is about 26 pounds (11.8 kg).

In addition to the guide scope/imager, the SP127 comes with a 25 mm Plössl eyepiece, a 90° 1¼” star diagonal, a screw-on visual back, an adjustable tripod with steel legs 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) in diameter, cables, an AC adapter, and a Bahtinov focusing mask for the guide scope. The camera’s nosepiece is also internally threaded to accept standard 1¼” filters.

In its standard configuration, the included camera photographs through the 53 mm refractor rather than the Maksutov. Although the camera is removable, Spectrum Optics recommends a separate camera for imaging through the Maksutov because its long focal length and narrow field are not well-suited to the included camera’s plate-solving system. That doesn’t mean you have to invest in more equipment, though; I took some very nice shots of the Moon simply by holding my iPhone to the Mak’s 25 mm eyepiece.

The SP127’s hybrid arrangement works well in practice. After the user selects a target in the app, the guide scope directs the mount to the correct location, then tracks the sky. The observer can view the target visually through the Maksutov while the guide scope stacks and displays images via the app. A word of caution, however: Be careful not to shake the instrument when looking through the eyepiece. Even a slight motion will blur the image being photographed.

Like most Maksutov-Cassegrain systems, the SP127 excels at medium and high magnifications. Its 1,900 mm focal length is especially well-suited for observing the Moon, planets, planetary nebulae, and double stars.

Spectrum Optics MirroSky SkyPilot SP127 Primary Optical Tube: 5-inch 127mm Maksutov-Cassegrain Focal Length: 1900mm Length: 14.6 inches (370 mm) Focal Ratio: f/15 Guide Scope Optical Tube: 53mm ED refractor with Sony IMX662 CMOS camera Focal Length: 200mm Focal Ratio: f/4 Assembled Weight: 26 lbs. (11.8 kg) Mount Payload: 9 lbs. (4 kg) Connectivity: built-in Wi-Fi, 2.4 and 5 GHz Camera Storage: 64GB onboard storage Tripod: Full-size adjustable steel-leg tripod Eyepiece: 25mm Plössl Price: $999.99 Contact: Spectrum Optics 2175 S Grand Ave Santa Ana, CA 92705 1-888-879-5143 spectrumoi.com

For this review, I arranged to receive a sample SP127 directly from Spectrum Optics. It arrived securely packed and in perfect condition.

Setup was easy, thanks to the well-illustrated paper manual that came with the scope. After I aligned the guide scope with the Maksutov during the day, as the instructions suggested, the scope was ready to go. I had everything together in under half an hour.

Control is handled entirely through the MirroSky app. To initialize the scope to the sky, the system uses onboard sensors combined with date, time, and location information supplied by the connected smart device. The camera includes dual-band Wi‑Fi capability supporting both 2.4 and 5 gigahertz connections. During use, the app’s interface was straightforward and easy to navigate. Target acquisition was quick and accurate. Chosen objects were always centered in the field of view. The app also provides guided tours and a database containing more than 100,000 stars, solar system members, and deep-sky sights.

Tracking performance was accurate for visual observations and short-exposure imaging. Since the SP127 uses an alt-azimuth mount, field rotation may become evident around the edges with longer exposures.

The SP127 can be powered by eight user-supplied AA batteries in the mount, a suitable external 12-volt power source, or the included AC adapter.

I found that the Maksutov performed very well. Lunar views were well-defined, with crater walls, rilles, and other surface features standing out crisply. I was especially impressed when, in moments of steady seeing, the SP127 detected a few of the craterlets on the floor of Plato. It passed another tough test by resolving Schröter’s Valley, a sinuous rille near craters Aristarchus and Herodotus.

Planetary performance also proved impressive. Multiple cloud bands as well as the Great Red Spot were clearly visible on Jupiter, and shadows cast by Galilean moons could also be seen on the planet’s cloud tops.

Double stars were another strong point, thanks to the long focal length. The Trapezium in the Orion Nebula, for instance, was striking. The included eyepiece did well, but the view really sparkled when I swapped in my own eyepieces with shorter focal lengths.

Throughout it all, I was very impressed with the crispness of the images, showing the high quality of the Maksutov’s optics. Like most catadioptric telescopes, the SP127 focuses by moving the primary mirror. This takes tight manufacturing tolerances to maintain a precise focus without tilting the mirror. I found that alignment stayed spot-on after swapping eyepieces and refocusing the view.

I was equally impressed with the imaging results using the 53 mm guide scope. The app allows you to customize settings, including gain, exposure length, number of frames to capture, and dark frames. After I experimented with the settings, the Orion Nebula appeared in vivid color after only two minutes of exposure, even as it was setting in my light-polluted sky. The Pleiades also recorded beautifully, although not all members squeezed into the guide scope’s approximately 1.6° by 0.9° field. The Horsehead Nebula, the Whirlpool Galaxy, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, and more displayed details exceeding what you might expect from such a small aperture, especially after post-processing using apps like PixInsight, GIMP, and Photoshop.

The SkyPilot 127 is one of the most original entries in today’s smart telescope market. For observers who still enjoy looking through an eyepiece but appreciate the convenience of app-driven targeting and imaging, the SP127 offers something genuinely special. In a small but growing group of smart telescopes that combine traditional eyepiece observing with integrated electronic imaging, the SP127’s hybrid design makes it an appealing bridge between conventional astronomy and the smart telescope revolution.

#6352. How to watch Starship Flight 15

SpaceX is set to launch its 15th test flight of Starship on Friday, Nov. 13. For the first time, the company will try to catch both stages of the rocket — the Super Heavy booster and the upper stage, which SpaceX calls “Ship” — with the arms of its launch tower. If it works, Starship will become the first orbital rocket ever recovered in full.

SpaceX is targeting a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (4:45 p.m. CST) Friday from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas, pending regulatory approval. Starship launch dates often slip, so check the company’s Flight 15 mission page for the latest.

SpaceX’s live webcast begins about 30 minutes before liftoff — around 5:15 p.m. EST if the launch holds at the start of the window. You can stream it on the Flight 15 mission page or on SpaceX’s X account.

If you’re near the Texas-Mexico border, crowds typically gather on South Padre Island, across the bay from the launch site. On the Mexican side, the public beach at Playa Bagdad offers a head-on view of the launch tower.

About six and a half minutes after liftoff, Super Heavy should fly back to Starbase and be plucked from the air by the tower’s “chopstick” arms, a catch SpaceX has made three times before. Ship will continue to orbit and release 26 of SpaceX’s next-generation Starlink V3 satellites.

The real test comes the next day. Ship will circle Earth about 14 times at roughly 171 miles (275 kilometers) up before heading home. Until now, Ship’s test flights have ended with a practice landing at sea: it flips upright, and then fires its engines to set down gently on the water. This time, it will run that same maneuver over Starbase and hopefully settle into the tower’s arms instead. SpaceX’s flight timeline puts the catch about 22 and a half hours after launch — around 4:18 p.m. EST on Saturday, Nov. 14, if Starship lifts off on time.

SpaceX says Ship will head for the tower only if flight controllers confirm that every system it needs for reentry, the landing burn, and the final approach is healthy. If not, the company can bring Ship down at preplanned spots in the Pacific, with go/no-go checks built into the flight for splashdowns near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

Archaeologists have discovered the shoe of the first governor of the Danish West Indies, recovered from a 17th-century ship that was wrecked after one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark’s history.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Maritime archaeologists investigating a 17th-century shipwreck off the coast of Sweden have discovered a fancy shoe and two metal rings used as currency in the transatlantic slave trade. The items were lost during a mutiny on a slave ship in 1683, during which the governor of the Danish West Indies was thrown overboard.

The Danish frigate Havmanden (which translates to "Merman") was en route to St. Thomas, a Caribbean island that is now part of the U.S. Virgin Islands, with convicts and indentured servants aboard destined for work on the island with the Danish West India Company. The plan for the Havmanden, after dropping off the new colonists, was to sail to West Africa to buy enslaved Africans. But due to a shortage of food and water, several crewmembers and convicts aboard seized control of the ship near the Azores in the North Atlantic and began sailing it back to Copenhagen.

The mutineers shot the ship's captain and threw other officers ‪—‬ including Jørgen Iversen Dyppel, the first governor of the Danish West Indies ‪—‬ overboard in the English Channel. After the ship ran aground, the mutineers were tried for their crimes in Copenhagen and sentenced to death.

The story of the Havmanden is one of the most violent mutinies in Denmark's history, according to a Nov. 11 translated statement from the National Museum of Denmark. But now, underwater archaeologists are learning more about the fateful voyage from the wreck, which lies on the seabed just east of Gothenburg, Sweden.

Archaeological divers discovered the rear half of a man's "unusually fine" shoe in the wreckage, according to the statement.

"I see a great many shoes from shipwrecks, but I have never before seen a shoe of such high quality," Vivi Lena Andersen, director of the Rudersdal Museums in Denmark, said in the statement.

The sole has a high level of craftsmanship, Andersen said, which can be seen in the minuscule holes perforating the edge of the shoe. The regularity of the holes would have required tools and expertise that only the most skilled shoemakers had at the time. It was "undoubtedly an expensive and exclusive shoe that only the elite could afford to buy," Andersen said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Because the shoe was likely owned by an upper-class individual, experts think it could have belonged to Iversen, the Danish West Indies governor who was thrown overboard.

"The shoe testifies not only to Jørgen Iversen Dyppel's life and dramatic death, but also provides a personal point of entry into the larger story of the establishment of the Danish colonies in the West Indies and the widespread slave trade Denmark was a part of," Andreas Kallmeyer Bloch, a maritime archaeologist at the National Museum of Denmark's Center for Maritime and Underwater Cultural Heritage, said in the statement.

Additional clues to the Danish slave trade on board the Havmanden included two manillas, ring-shaped pieces of metal that were used as currency in West Africa. European merchants cast manillas from copper, brass or iron and traded them for enslaved people in West Africa, particularly along the coast of modern-day Nigeria. But manillas are rarely found in Scandinavia, according to the statement.

"The manillas add another layer to Havmanden's story and underscore the connection to the slave trade, which was a central part of Denmark's colonial activities in both the West Indies and on the west coast of Africa," Kallmeyer Bloch said.

Denmark continued to engage in the transatlantic slave trade for more than a century after the Havmanden sank. Although King Christian VII of Denmark-Norway banned the trade in 1792, slavery continued in the Danish West Indies until 1848, when hundreds of enslaved people revolted and were finally granted their freedom.
