#6349. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 14: Venus and Mercury in Virgo

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M.Sunset: 4:44 P.M.Moonrise: 11:33 A.M.Moonset: 8:56 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time on the 15th, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

#6348. A NASA Veteran Claims to Have Used Mind-Bending Physics to Conquer Gravity

Charles Buhler’s claim could change how spacecraft fly. But experiments show how much work it takes to establish that a mysterious push is real.

In April 2024, Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist who helped establish a laboratory at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, made a remarkable claim. His company, Exodus Propulsion Technologies, had built a device that could produce thrust without expelling propellant. He attributed the push to what he called a “New Force.”

As we reported in our earlier coverage, Buhler’s claim would have big consequences for spaceflight. That promise depends on whether researchers outside Exodus can reproduce the push and rule out an ordinary explanation.

One physicist has spent years investigating similar claims. Martin Tajmar, a professor and chair of space systems at Dresden University of Technology in Germany, has spent two decades measuring the forces produced by charged capacitors, including lopsided ones like the designs Buhler describes.

“It’s all negative,” he tells Popular Mechanics. Meaning, his tests found no evidence of that force within the limits of his equipment. He hasn’t tested Exodus’s hardware, but his experiments show what an independent test would need to account for.

A capacitor stores electric charge. Apply a high enough voltage to certain designs, and they can set the surrounding air moving, producing a push on the device itself. Tajmar calls this corona wind, “a discharge in air that drags air molecules with it.” In those cases, the device moves by pushing air backward, much as a fan does.

Tajmar’s team wanted to see whether a capacitor would still produce a push with almost all the air removed. For their 2024 study in Scientific Reports, they put the capacitor and its battery-powered electrical equipment together on a sensitive balance inside a vacuum chamber. At 10,000 volts, an asymmetric capacitor produced no clear sign of an unexplained force, even with instruments sensitive enough to detect a push measured in billionths of a newton.

Exodus hasn’t sent Tajmar a device, so he built his own capacitors for those experiments. He says his asymmetric design follows the principles in the company’s patent, though he doesn’t know the exact dimensions of its hardware.

“It’s Exodus who have to say why my asymmetric capacitor does not produce any thrust,” he says.

He believes his results challenge the company’s explanation, but he’d need its hardware to put its particular device through the same checks.

Keeping the battery and high-voltage equipment on the balance removes outside power cables that could interfere with the reading. Researchers also have to watch for electromagnetic forces or parts shifting as they heat up, either of which could look like thrust.

Tajmar also recommends swapping the device for an electrical dummy that draws power but should produce no thrust. If the balance still registers a push, something else in the setup is causing it. Researchers would need to track that down before treating the reading as evidence of a working drive.

Buhler has also said the devices can keep producing thrust after the power is switched off. Electrical charge can linger in insulating materials, leaving an electric field even after the supply is disconnected. Researchers would need to work out whether that leftover charge explains the reading and, if there really is a push, where it comes from.

In a short white paper, Exodus says other experimenters have reproduced the effect and argues that the device pushes against the vacuum itself, allowing momentum to be conserved. But it doesn’t include their laboratory reports. Without those details, readers can’t tell how the experiments were done or whether the researchers ruled out other causes of the push.

What leaving the propellant behind could change

Spacecraft have to bring along the propellant they’ll use to speed up, slow down or change course. That adds weight, which takes more propellant to move. The rocket equation puts numbers to that trade-off, showing how much a spacecraft can change its speed with the supply it carries.

If a drive could produce useful thrust without using up propellant, engineers could plan missions differently. A spacecraft could keep changing course as long as it had enough power and the drive kept working. Some of the weight now devoted to propellant tanks and their contents could go toward other equipment.

But the drive would bring its own baggage. It would need a power source and a way to get rid of waste heat, and all of that would have to travel with it. Engineers would need to find out whether the thrust was worth the weight of the complete system. Getting a reliable push in the lab would give them a reason to start working that out.

Light can give a spacecraft a push, too. When a laser sends light in one direction, the laser gets a tiny push in the other, because light carries momentum. Tajmar points out that this already offers a way to produce thrust without using up material propellant.

“If you just power a laser with the power that we use in our experiments, the thrust is also propellantless and actually already exists,” he says.

The catch is how much power it takes. To hold up a 1.2-ounce object, roughly the weight of the devices Buhler described, a laser would need to send about 100 million watts of light downward. A drive that produced a useful push with much less power would be worth engineers’ attention. Researchers would also have to explain what carries momentum in the opposite direction, as the light does for a laser.

“You have to test it in an independent laboratory. And then with a different method,” Tajmar says. He wants the results published so other experts can examine the work, including the equipment itself. Getting the same push on a different instrument would help show that the device deserves the credit.

Nobody needs to make the whole apparatus float. Even a small sideways push would warrant attention if it survived those checks and other researchers could reliably reproduce it. Then engineers could start asking whether it was strong enough to put to work aboard a spacecraft.

Buhler’s claim promises freedom from the propellant tank, which would change how we travel through space. The next move is closer to home. Put the drive in another lab, let someone else take the controls, and see whether the promise still has any push behind it.

#6347. Nov. 14, 2012: NASA announces an extended mission for Kepler

The Kepler Space Telescope, launched March 6, 2009, was designed to search the Milky Way for exoplanets. Using the transit method, Kepler ultimately observed over 500,00 stars and contributed to the discovery of almost 2,700 exoplanets.

Though Kepler was originally intended for a 3.5-year mission, NASA announced on Nov. 14, 2012, that the space telescope had successfully completed its primary mission and would be embarking on an extended mission. When a second gyroscope (also referred to as a reaction wheel) failed in May 2013 – the first having failed in July 2012 – that mission was in question, however, as it left the spacecraft with limited control for pointing. But engineers were able to craft a workaround using the momentum of the Sun’s light pressure to keep Kepler evenly and steadily directed, and the extended mission using this methodology, dubbed K2, was formally approved in May 2014. Kepler continued to function for a further four years, and was retired in October 2018 when it ran out of fuel. TESS (the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) has since inherited its planet-hunting mantle.

#6346. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#6344. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 15: Mars and Jupiter in conjunction

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

#6343. The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed their listed max output to see how well they could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts with 3,900-watt startup power and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

The Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

A new and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

The Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

This power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

What is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

The S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

With the Bluetti Apex 300, the name of the game is flexibility. Alone, it delivers up to 3,840 watts of continuous power and handles up to an impressive 7,680 watts of surge power. Capacity is a solid 2,764.8 watt-hours for decent runtime, though it depends on the amount of power you intend to draw from it. If you happen to have 240-volt appliances or circuits, this model has you covered, too.

But everything on this power station is scalable. It’s possible to add up to six additional batteries for a very high capacity of 19,353.6 watt-hours, and connect up to two other Apex 300 units and run them in parallel. This expandability makes it a great entry-level home power station that expands into a larger backup system that delivers whole-home power.

The Apex 300 features four 120-volt outlets across the front, plus a 120-volt 30-amp outlet and a 120/240-volt 50-amp outlet on the side for powering devices individually, plugging into an RV, or delivering home power through a transfer switch.

One downside for me was the lack of direct DC outputs, e.g., USB-C ports. For that, you have to purchase an optional hub. There are also power inputs for a standard AC plug, a 30-amp connection, and two solar connections. The Apex 300 uses two inverters as opposed to one, giving you two banks of 120-volt, 1,920-watt output (two outlets in each bank). We easily ran two high-powered appliances at the same time, including a space heater and a toaster, with no issues at all.

This station is serious about solar recharging, too. There are two ports for connecting solar panels up to 1,200 watts each. Having the option of 2,400 watts of solar input is uncommon in a station of this size and price point. Plus, you can reach even higher input by pairing with a Bluetti SolarX 4K voltage regulator, which is designed for connection to larger solar arrays.

Most of the control options are accessed with the Bluetti Mobile app, and it’s one of the best we’ve seen. It’s easy to finely tune settings in ways that other companies don’t offer, such as adjusting the recharging level from as little as one amp to 50 amps.

If you’ve been eyeing power stations but aren’t sure if you want one more for portable power or more for home backup power, this is the model for you. It delivers a great amount of power for portable use, but lays the groundwork for building a more dedicated system in the future.

This is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

The unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans, and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

We ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

The next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

During our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and new outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

As part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

The mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the important information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

All of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via Wi-Fi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel, via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge over a full 8 months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.

Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds that you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048 watt-hour capacity, and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

Keep in mind that the usable watt hours are not the same as the watt hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Mid-size models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

Often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

#6342. Nov. 15, 1988: The Buran orbiter launches

In 1976, the Soviet Union began development of the Buran orbiter. Concerned that the American space shuttle program might be used for military purposes, the Soviets responded with Buran and its Energia booster rocket, which were capable of carrying antisatellite and antimissile weapons and targeting locations on Earth’s surface. Though the nonmilitary objectives for Buran included ferrying crew and supplies to the Mir Space Station, Buran was also capable of flying unmanned and fully automated.

The Buran program marked several achievements – the development of 230 new technologies, a fully recoverable rocket capable of lifting 220,000 pounds (100,000 kilograms) to orbit, a shuttle that could carry up to 10 cosmonauts. However, it only made a single flight: On Nov. 15, 1988, Buran launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, performed two orbits, and returned to Earth. The 206-minute flight was seamless, and was performed fully under remote control, with no crew members aboard. Despite this success, the colossal expense of the program and the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union meant the end of Buran. In 2002, the roof of a hangar at Baikonur collapsed, killing eight people and destroying the orbiter and its rocket.

Mitochondria can become compromised in a number of medical conditions. What if they could be replaced like batteries?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newborn baby's heart is roughly the size of a walnut — which makes open-heart surgery challenging.

Each year, about 10,000 babies in the United States are born with critical heart defects that may require surgery to fix, often fairly soon after birth. In these infants, the two major arteries of the heart could have swapped positions or the left side of the heart may be far too small to pump properly.

Even if their surgeries go well, these babies face perilous recoveries. A complication can arise when blood flows back into the repaired heart, triggering what's known as an ischemia-reperfusion injury. This can stun the organ, triggering extensive damage that requires doctors to place the baby on a life-support machine that pumps and infuses oxygen into blood to sub in for the hampered heart and lungs. Only about 40% of newborns make it off the machine, because often, their tiny hearts don't recover.

Doctors and scientists at Boston Children's Hospital have been working to improve those odds using a creative idea: replacing the fuel source in damaged heart cells to help them bounce back from injury. That fuel source is mitochondria, the "batteries" found in most cells in the body. In this case, the mitochondria are isolated from an abdominal muscle and then injected directly into the heart.

As of April, 17 babies have undergone this procedure, and 80% made it off ECMO. It's too soon to say if the treatment improves overall survival rates, but the early data hints that it might. A clinical trial is currently underway.

James McCully (left) and his colleague Dr. Sitaram Emani of Boston Children's Hospital have developed a technique to transplant mitochondria into the hearts of children recovering from surgery.

"The first one or two for me were pretty nerve-wracking," said James McCully, a research associate at Boston Children's Hospital and associate professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School whose pioneering work paved the way for these procedures. His team isolates and purifies the mitochondria that a surgical team then transplants into patients.

"But you know, the heart comes back — you can actually almost see it coming back" in real time, he told Live Science. A heart deprived of energy looks pallid, while a freshly rejuvenated heart blushes a healthy pink.

Baby heart infusions are just one example of the promise of "mitochondrial transplantation." Following McCully's lead, other scientists have started investigating whether infusions of mitochondria could revitalize donated organs destined for transplantation, help stroke patients recover, and treat kids with devastating diseases. This work is still highly experimental, and its route to regulatory approval remains unclear.

But at its core is a straightforward idea: When a battery dies, you replace it.

The human body contains tens of trillions of cells, most of which contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria. Following some back-of-the-envelope math, that means the total potential energy in each person "is the equivalent of a lightning bolt," Douglas Wallace, director of the Center for Mitochondrial and Epigenomic Medicine at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told attendees last year at a symposium on mitochondrial medicine.

Mitochondria, in a word, are powerful. They produce most of the chemical energy used by complex cells by churning out a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The idea of transferring these fuel factories from one cell to another as a medical treatment emerged less than two decades ago — but cells have been doing such swaps on their own for eons.

A leading theory posits that mitochondria evolved from simple microbes. And today, they still retain distinctly microbial features.

Dr. Jon Brestoff, an associate professor of pathology and immunology and director of the Immunometabolism Initiative at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, describes this ability to move from cell to cell as a relic of mitochondria's bacterial past. "It is hypothesized that mitochondria transfer has likely been retained throughout evolution of eukaryotic life," the huge domain of life that includes all plants, fungi, protists and animals, Brestoff told Live Science.

Mitochondria are the powerhouses of nearly all complex cells on Earth, and there are a few theories as to how they adopted that ubiquitous role. A leading idea posits that, some 1.5 billion to 2 billion years ago, one simple cell engulfed another. The bacterial cell that got swallowed carried a circular loop of DNA inside its membrane, and that captured cell later became what we now know as the mitochondrion. The new organelle enabled cells to take advantage of the abundance of oxygen on our planet by converting it into usable fuel.

Mitochondria retained bacteria-like features, such as having their own DNA and membranes. But in 2006, researchers reported that mitochondria can also exit their "host" and survive the journey into a totally different cell — a phenomenon known as mitochondrial transfer.

"That was a complete revolution in thinking," said Dr. Lance Becker, professor and Chair of the Department of Emergency Medicine at Northwell Health and the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research. "With that notion that mitochondria might be mobile, that they might cross boundaries, that they might go from one cell to another cell, came the possibility that maybe that was something we could use to help people."

The 2006 study showed that cells that had been depleted of their own mitochondrial DNA could obtain healthy mitochondria from neighboring cells. After receiving other cells' powerhouses, the once-depleted cells were able to conduct energetically costly processes, such as cell division.

This research provided the first evidence that one cell can "donate" metabolic properties to its neighbor by sending over a fresh batch of mitochondria. Scientists once thought cells had to make all of their own mitochondria, but now, "I think cells have the ability to 'put their hand up' when they need mitochondria," Becker told Live Science.

Jon Brestoff is studying the use of mitochondrial transplantation for genetic diseases that impair the function of these cellular powerhouses.

Because those first experiments were done in lab dishes, initially, "it was unclear whether or not it was really biologically meaningful or relevant," Brestoff said. But within the past five to six years, improved tools and techniques have enabled scientists to watch mitochondrial transfer unfold within living organisms, he noted. It's been shown that cells of the same type can exchange mitochondria, as can cells of different types.

As scientists' fundamental understanding of mitochondrial transfer grew, the notion of doing the same thing therapeutically gained more traction.

"That procedure," Brestoff said, "is rooted in the biology of mitochondria transfer."

Just two years after the landmark 2006 paper, McCully's research group released data that hinted at the medicinal potential of mitochondrial transplantation.

Since then, these complementary lines of research — the foundational biology and the preclinical investigation — have continued in parallel. McCully's preclinical work helped to inspire other labs to explore the use of mitochondrial transplantation for a range of medical applications, including organ transplants and treatments for stroke and genetic disease.

McCully is "the pioneer — the guru of the field," said Dr. Giuseppe Orlando, a professor of surgery and regenerative medicine at Wake Forest University School of Medicine who is exploring mitochondrial transplantation as a way to maintain the integrity of transplant organs.

McCully's road to mitochondrial transplantation started in the 1980s. As a molecular biologist, he wanted to uncover mechanisms that protect the heart from damage, particularly when the organ's oxygen supply is compromised — such as during ischemia, or low blood flow. With an eye on older adults, he wanted to spare patients' heart tissue from the damage and cell death that can occur before and during heart surgery.

It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going.

McCully and his collaborators initially "didn't care about the mitochondria one iota," he said. They were more focused on the nucleus, the control center that houses most of a cell's DNA, and its influence on cellular pathways that might boost the heart's resilience to ischemia. But "what we found was that everything we did started coming back to the mitochondria," he said.

They found that ischemia triggers damage and dysfunction in mitochondria that persists even after the heart's oxygen supply is restored; this dysfunction ultimately kills cells. The damaged mitochondria swell up, leak their innards, and set off a chain reaction that causes a cell to self-destruct.

McCully and colleagues observed that biological pathways that seemed to reduce this cell death often centered on the mitochondria. "We were looking around at either pathways upstream of the mitochondria or downstream of the mitochondria," he said.

So, logically, they started looking directly at mitochondria, studying what the organelle looks like before, during and after ischemia. One day, while isolating mitochondria from a laboratory pig, the animal developed fibrillation, meaning its heart began beating very quickly, with an uncoordinated and rapid rhythm. The team tried to reset the heart's rhythm with electric shocks and medications, to no avail. But McCully had an idea.

"At that point in time, the heart's kind of [got a] gray pallor, and it looks dead," he said. "And I said, 'Go upstairs; grab some of those mitochondria that we've isolated from the non-ischemic type. Just bring them down.'" They'd previously gathered some healthy mitochondria from the same pig, in hopes of generating a "before-and-after" picture of ischemia. Instead, McCully suspended those healthy mitochondria in a solution and then injected them directly into the pig's fibrillating heart.

"And the heart came back — started beating normally. It changed color, went back to a pink hue, and just kept on going," he said.

Surgeons sample a small piece of muscle from the patient. That muscle will serve as the source of healthy mitochondria.

After mitochondria have been isolated from the muscle sample, they are prepared in a syringe and injected into the heart tissue.

That serendipitous experiment led to a formal test of the technique in rabbit hearts, the results of which were published in 2008. In the study, they introduced healthy mitochondria to the rabbits' hearts during ischemia, just before reperfusion — when blood is reintroduced into the oxygen-starved tissue. They found that the mitochondria improved the organs' recovery and reduced tissue death. Further research in animals suggested that mitochondria that originated from one type of tissue, like liver tissue or skeletal muscle, could be introduced to other tissue types, such as cardiac muscle.

After seeing McCully's results in various animal experiments, including more with pigs, Dr. Pedro del Nido, chair of cardiac surgery at Boston Children's and a professor of child surgery at Harvard Medical School, approached him about testing the technique in human patients — namely, in babies on a life-support machine known as ECMO.

"He saw it in the animals; he saw what was going on," McCully said. "And he deemed it as being a possible intervention to save these kids."

They sought permission from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to test the procedure and cleared the required regulatory hurdles. The process was made slightly easier because the mitochondria were coming from the patients' own bodies, not from a donor, McCully noted. Once given the go-ahead, they set forth with the help of Dr. Sitaram Emani, a heart surgeon at Boston Children's. The first procedure took place in 2014.

During each procedure, Emani and the surgical team collect a small sample of skeletal muscle from the patient, and McCully then isolates whole mitochondria from the tissue and prepares them in a syringe. He refined the isolation technique so the time from collecting the muscle sample to injecting mitochondria is only 30 minutes. Lately, the team has been developing a technique they can perform in the operating room, rather than in a lab, which could cut the time to 20 minutes. Emani uses various tests, including echocardiography, to see which areas of the heart tissue move the least, and injects mitochondria straight into those areas.

"It's great to be able to see something you've done and worked on for so many years actually provide a benefit," McCully said.

Dr. Giuseppe Orlando thinks that mitochondrial transplantation could serve as a potential method for fortifying donated organs that are intended for transplant patients.

While McCully is trying to protect infant hearts, other scientists want to do the same for other organs — including those destined for transplant surgeries.

To Orlando, mitochondria represent a potential way to make donated kidneys work better. "In transplant medicine, one of the major issues is making sure that the organs that are procured are well stored and kept viable until implantation," said Orlando, who is also president of the Cell Transplant and Regenerative Medicine Society.

Maintaining an organ's viability means preserving mitochondrial function as much as possible, but the transplantation process is tough on the organelles. "That energy plant is damaged. So it's pretty obvious that you should start thinking about a way to replace the damaged mitochondria," Orlando said.

Donated organs suffer some damage when they're unplugged from the donors' bloodstream, in part because this cuts off mitochondria's crucial oxygen supply. And then, paradoxically, the donor organs also get damaged when they're plugged into the recipient's bloodstream. That's because the fast flow of blood triggers the production of free radicals — unstable molecules that damage tissues.

While healthy organs normally produce some free radicals, reperfusion unleashes a flood. "It's more than the organ can bear and sustain," Orlando explained. This damage contributes to a phenomenon called delayed graft function, in which a transplanted kidney doesn't work right away so the patient ends up needing dialysis in the first week after surgery.

"You want to make sure that the kidney wakes up faster," Orlando said. That's where mitochondria come in.

Orlando was introduced to the idea of mitochondrial transplantation around 2019 through a collaboration with Dr. Benedetta Bussolati, a nephrologist and full professor of laboratory medicine at the University of Turin in Italy. Her lab had been studying mitochondrial transplantation in isolated kidney cells in lab experiments, and they reached out to Orlando about extending that work to lab animals.

In pigs, the researchers ran experiments in which the animals' kidneys were collected and stored in the same way human kidneys commonly would be prior to being transplanted. One set of kidneys received a placebo treatment, while another got an infusion of mitochondria from the donor pigs' muscle tissue. Upon being reperfused, the treated kidneys produced fewer free radicals and accrued less damage than the untreated kidneys did, the team reported in 2023.

They backed up this finding by analyzing RNA, a molecule that reflects which genes are active in cells. Compared with the untreated kidneys, the treated kidneys showed greater activity in genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and lower activity in genes involved in repairing injuries.

Orlando thinks that mitochondrial transplanations could help organs "wake up" faster after being transferred from an organ donor to a recipient.

Some groups are exploring mitochondrial transplantation in other donor organs, like the lungs — specifically, lungs treated with "ex vivo perfusion" (EVP), an emerging approach that helps retain the viability of transplant organs. Rather than placing a donor organ in a cooler of ice, as is generally standard, EVP flushes an organ with nutrient- and oxygen-rich fluid, helping to maintain its function until the transplant surgery. In lab experiments with pig and human lungs, scientists found that introducing fresh mitochondria during EVP further improved the organs' function while reducing inflammation and free radicals.

Across different organ transplants, Orlando sees mitochondria as a potential means to improve patient outcomes and expand the pool of available organs. There are scenarios in which would-be organ donors die unexpectedly of cardiac arrest and their organs are damaged in the process; mitochondrial transplants may help make such organs fit for patients, Orlando has said.

In the near term, Orlando and his colleagues are continuing to study the basic science of mitochondrial transplantation for this clinical purpose; they've also been cleared to run a clinical trial with donor kidneys but need more funds to proceed.

Looking to the more distant future, he and other experts in the field envision a world where transplant organs can be bioengineered and stored in banks, ready and waiting for the patients who need them, Orlando said. If that vision materializes, he suggested, mitochondrial transplants might be useful for preparing banked organs for transplantation "by giving them kind of an energy boost."

If infusions of fresh mitochondria could help the heart, kidney and lungs, what about the brain? That's the question Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues at the University of Washington School of Medicine (UW Medicine) want to answer.

Walker, a clinical professor of neurological surgery, treats patients who have had ischemic strokes, which are caused by blood clots blocking blood flow to the brain. The immediate aim of post-stroke treatment is to clear out the blocked "pipe" and restore circulation to the brain as quickly as possible, she said. But no matter how quickly this is done, some brain cells are damaged. And once the blood clot is removed, the brain may then suffer a reperfusion injury.

Standard treatments can dissolve the clot but don't protect the brain, Walker said. "What about all those cells that are maybe not quite dead — they're on the verge of maybe dying? What can we do to support those guys?" she asked.

The UW Medicine team had heard about McCully's work in Boston and wondered if something similar could be applied in stroke patients. But while heart surgery exposes the tissue in need of new mitochondria, accessing the brain is trickier. "You don't do a craniotomy to give an IV medicine," Walker told Live Science.

But Walker realized that a harmful downstream effect of stroke might provide an opportunity for treatment. Immediately after a stroke, the brain's protective shield — known as the blood-brain barrier — becomes more permeable than usual, allowing more substances to pass from the bloodstream into brain tissue. That might open a door for mitochondrial transplantation.

One method of treating ischemic strokes is to physically remove the clot using a procedure called a thrombectomy, which a surgeon is preparing for in the photo above. Dr. Melanie Walker and colleagues tried combining this approach with mitochondrial transplantation.

A 2023 mouse study spearheaded by University of Virginia researchers and co-authored by Walker backed this idea, finding that mitochondria entered the brain after stroke and integrated into brain cells. These mitochondria had been gathered from muscle tissue, as in McCully's studies, and introduced to the brain via an artery. The treatment increased ATP production while reducing cell death caused by the stroke, compared with untreated mice's brains.

This work paved the way to the first trial using mitochondrial transplant in the human brain. The small safety trial included adult patients who'd had ischemic strokes and underwent thrombectomies ‪—‬ surgeries to remove the clots from their blood vessels. Four received mitochondrial transplants during their procedures and 12 did not. Mitochondria were injected near the site of each patient's stroke, into the closest branch of one of the brain's major arteries.

No negative side effects were tied to the transplants, hinting that the procedure is safe in humans. "But the next question is, how do we understand if it helps? And those are harder trials to design," Walker said. That's partly because the transplants are tacked onto the clot-removal procedure, so it's difficult to separate their effects from those of the clot removal itself, she noted.

Future trials will also need to explore exactly where the transplanted mitochondria end up in the human brain, how well they function once inside brain cells, and how the dose and timing of the transplant affect patients' outcomes, the trial runners wrote in their report. For the moment, Walker said her team is focused on exploring the safety aspects of the approach and have no further trials planned at this time.

Beyond heart defects, transplant organs and stroke, researchers are looking to mitochondrial transplantation as a solution for genetic conditions that harm mitochondria directly. Brestoff and colleagues are investigating the therapy's potential for treating Leigh syndrome, a rare neurological condition caused by genetic mutations that disrupt the fuel-producing machinery in mitochondria.

"Those kids have a terrible prognosis," Brestoff said. Most children with the most common form of the syndrome, whose symptoms show up by age 2, die by age 3. There is no cure for the syndrome, and treatments to relieve its symptoms are limited. So if it works, mitochondrial transplantation could fill a big gap.

So far, the approach shows promise in lab mice with a severe form of Leigh syndrome, improving the rodents' function and extending their median lifespan by 19% to 24%, the researchers demonstrated in 2024. They're now studying the approach in cells derived from patients with the disease.

I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter.

Some companies, such as Israel-headquartered Minovia Therapeutics, are already running clinical trials with patients with other types of mitochondrial disease. Minovia is running one with children with Pearson syndrome, in which missing mitochondrial DNA hinders the function of bone marrow, which normally makes blood and immune cells.

While patients with a heart or brain problem may be able to pluck mitochondria from healthy muscles, people with mitochondrial disease don't necessarily have healthy mitochondria to spare. Especially for these patients, getting mitochondria from other people ‪—‬ known as heterologous transplantation ‪—‬ likely makes the most sense. What's more, for transplantation to be used widely for any purpose, there would need to be an "off-the-shelf" mitochondrial product available, Brestoff said.

Such a product could eliminate the step in Boston Children's heart procedure where mitochondria have to be isolated from a patient while they're waiting, open on an operating table. "Getting them from the recipient can sometimes be problematic, because the recipients are sick. All the organs, all the tissue is quite distressed," McCully noted. A standardized and safety-tested mitochondrial product would therefore be a boon for the field.

Brestoff is on the scientific advisory board of LUCA Science, a company developing mitochondria as therapeutic agents, and a consultant for Cellergy Therapeutics, which is making mitochondrial products to combat conditions from muscle degeneration and aging. These companies exemplify the effort to come up with ready-made products that could someday bring the therapy to more patients.

A shift to heterologous transplantation does raise concerns about immune reactions. "You have some variations in the proteins that are present in your mitochondria that I don't have," Brestoff noted. "So it is possible that our immune systems recognize heterologous mitochondria as non-self."

But McCully doesn't expect immune reactions to be a big problem, based on his research in animals. "I can get the mitochondria from you and put them into me, me into you — doesn't really matter," he said. Early trial results from Minovia and others suggest heterologous transplantations come with minimal side effects, at least at doses tested so far.

Another roadblock is that the FDA has not approved any organelles as therapies yet, so the standards and regulatory framework for the field are still being established, Brestoff said.

Despite that hurdle, the field has advanced significantly since its start as a niche, theoretical interest and then a highly experimental procedure for the sickest newborns. Scientists are now exploring the treatment as a solution to many common conditions, from rheumatoid arthritis to chronic pain.

Becker compared the state of the field to the early days of organ transplantation.

"It just turned out that it was revolutionary, when all of a sudden you could just give a person a kidney transplant," he said. "I think it's going to be kind of similar with mitochondria."

#6339. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

#6338. The Sky Today on Monday, November 16: Titan south, Rhea north

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 15: Mars and Jupiter in conjunction

It’s a great night to catch Saturn’s largest and brightest moon, Titan, as it skims south of the planet. Two hours after sunset, Saturn is roughly 40° high in the southeast, outshining all the other stars in this region of the sky. It lies to the lower left of the Circlet of Pisces and to the upper left of the bright star Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus.

Zoom in on Saturn with a telescope to first catch sight of its ring system, stretching 43” from end to end and tilted 8° to our line of sight. Currently we are seeing Saturn’s southern side, including the entirety of the planet’s southern hemisphere. The gas giant’s disk now measures 19” across.

Titan is difficult to miss, shining at mid-8th magnitude just south of the ringed planet. Don’t be fooled by a fainter 10th-magnitude field star, which lies just to Titan’s west. The three next-brightest moons, also 10th magnitude, are Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They lie closer to the planet. Tethys sits about 40” west of Saturn’s center shortly before 8 P.M. EST, while Dione is just west of the limb and Rhea just east of the planet. Dione and Rhea are moving westward, and Rhea will skim just north of Saturn’s pole along the way, standing due north of the planet around 10:40 P.M. EST. Tethys is moving east, and will disappear behind the planet’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 2:35 A.M. EST on the 16th (still late on the 15th along the Pacific Coast).

Sunrise: 6:46 A.M.Sunset: 4:43 P.M.Moonrise: 12:32 P.M.Moonset: 11:00 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (47%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.
