#6228. 10 Vacation Rentals Across North America For Your Next Family Reunion

Family reunions can be stressful. There’s much to consider, from dealing with a motley of personalities to making sure the kids are looked after. But things get much easier when you land on the perfect vacation rental, one in a crowd-pleasing location, with a spacious layout and plenty of amenities that will keep everyone happy. Whether you’re bringing the gang together for an outdoor adventure at Yosemite National Park, or seeking a laid-back sojourn in the Caribbean, the rentals on this list satisfy every kind of trip. Each featuring four bedrooms or more, these properties are sure to fit the entire clan with luxe amenities worth traveling for: think saltwater pools, golf simulators, and private beach access. What’s more, many are within the top 1% of guest reviews in their area, which means they’re loved by the people who have visited (and are often booked for return trips). Below, the best vacation rentals for family reunions across North America.

We've selected these listings based on ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 20Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 5.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private pool, proximity to beach, game room

Just steps away from Alys Beach, located on Scenic Highway 30A, this sunny and spacious six-bedroom home was designed for families: four king bedrooms with en suite bathrooms (one of which houses two extra twin beds); a bunk room with a double and four additional twin beds; and a queen with a trundle. There’s a game room, complete with ping-pong and Foosball tables, plus large-screen TVs. The little ones can enjoy amenities too, like mini cribs and pack-and-plays. If the family would rather swim at home, there’s a gorgeous heated pool for everyone to wade in, with sun loungers, an adjacent barbecue, and even a little tanning ledge for kids to take their first steps in the water.

Location: Inlet Beach, FloridaThings to do nearby: Seacrest Beach, Deer Lake State Park, Alys Beach

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Study area, in-unit washer/dryer, outdoor patio

Nantucket, with its pristine beaches and vibrant historic town, makes for an excellent family gathering. This classic, cedar-shingled home features an abundance of windows that bring in natural light, spotless interiors, and plainly chic furnishings. There are five bedrooms with high ceilings (some offer glimpses of the harbor), four full bathrooms, and a spacious kitchen. On the first floor, French doors open out to an outdoor entertainment area, with sectional seating, a dining table that seats 10, a gas grill, and an outdoor shower, all enclosed by a landscaped lawn—the perfect place for the group to kick back and relax.

Location: Nantucket, MassachusettsThings to do nearby: Nantucket Atheneum, Quaker Meeting House, Children's Beach

Number of guests: 20Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 6 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, proximity to ski resorts, golf simulator

This dreamy A-frame home in Pennsylvania’s Laurel Highlands offers adventurous family members proximity to the slopes at Hidden Valley and Seven Springs resorts. With seven bedrooms spread across three floors, there’s enough space for 20 guests to spread out, plus a fully equipped kitchen, dedicated theater area, game room, and even a golf simulator. After a long day of activities, there’s no better place to relax tired muscles than the hot tub outside, fit for six, or the firepit, surrounded by cozy loungers. Keep in mind the area does get icy over the winter, so 4WD is recommended.

Location: Somerset, PennsylvaniaThings to do nearby: Hidden Valley Resort, Seven Springs Mountain Resort, Ohiopyle State Park

Number of guests: 20+Bed and bath: 9 bedrooms, 8.5 bathsWhy we love it: Gazebo, valley views, fireplace

Located in the heart of Ohio’s Amish country, Hillside Villa is a bucolic escape for the extended family. While the entire villa can be booked (check for availability on the “Premier House” option), you can also opt for individual units, from a deluxe room for two with a jetted hot tub to a junior room that sleeps up to four. Each comes with scenic views of the hills, along with shared kitchen access (coffee and tea maker provided). There are 55-inch flat-screen TVs too, along with features like fireplaces and porches. In the backyard, you’ll find a gazebo with a firepit, perfect for watching the sunset descend over the farm-filled valley.

Location: Millersburg, OhioThings to do nearby: Country Acres Mini Golf, Pro Football Hall of Fame, Belden Village Mall

Number of guests: 14Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Contemporary interior design, private lake access, barbecue

Offering 200 feet of private lakefront in Austin, this modern four-bedroom is a rare retreat. Ideal for a multigenerational family, it’s composed of a main house with two king bedrooms and a guesthouse with a king bedroom, plus a large bunk room with eight twin beds. Spend your days gliding along the lake on a kayak or paddleboard, floating on the 16-foot lily pad, or taking a hike through the surrounding Balcones Canyonland Preserve. End the fun on the two-story party dock, where you can enjoy a meal outside, with s’mores for dessert around the firepit.

Location: Austin, TexasThings to do nearby: Lake Austin, Sixth Street, University of Texas at Austin

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hiking trail access, pool table, forest views

This Yosemite home, with its breathtaking cathedral windows and stone fireplace, will offer the family a stay they won’t forget. The perfect place to retreat to after a day spent at Yosemite National Park, this four-bedroom is wonderfully western, with its hanging deer antlers, wooden furniture, and tons of colorful textiles. Your group can spread out between two queen beds, two twin beds, and two bunk beds (one with a trundle). Prepare meals in the fully equipped kitchen, then enjoy some family time at the dining table, which seats up to 10. Up in the loft, you’ll find a mini arcade, a number of board games, and a pool table.

Location: Yosemite National Park, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Yosemite National Park, Yosemite Valley, Yosemite Arch Rock Gate Entrance

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Mountain views, gym, wildlife sightings

Cozy, inviting, and lived-in, this Jackson Hole property is the ultimate mountain escape. Located in Spring Creek Ranch, the home is in a 1,000-acre ranch community, perched atop East Gros Ventre Butte, 800 feet above the valley floor. The first thing you’ll notice upon walking in is a kitchen and dining area that flows into the living room, with large windows overlooking the mountains. There are four bedrooms (three kings and one with two twin beds), each with views of the Tetons. Poke around the woods, watch a movie around the fireplace, and look out for elk.

Location: Jackson, WyomingThings to do nearby: Jackson Hole Valley, Jackson Hole Wildlife Safaris, Jackson Town Square

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Scenic views, in-unit washer/dryer, beach access

In Quebec City, the Saguenay Fjord stretches over 62 miles and is surrounded by dramatic granite cliffs. This charming, four-bedroom home will place you right in front of the action. Settle back on the front porch with your loved ones and watch the tides roll in, or take sunset walks along the beach. The fully equipped kitchen has everything you need for meals at home, while the grand dining table looks out into the water. Outside, there’s a swing for little ones, plus a few Adirondack chairs for the adults to continue savoring the view.

Location: Saguenay, Quebec City, CanadaThings to do nearby: Saguenay River, Theatre du Palais Municipal, Okwari Le Fjord

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathroomsWhy we love it: In-unit washer/dryer, chef available upon request, beach access

Dreaming of a family reunion across the border? At this bungalow in Placencia, Belize, you’ll have the Caribbean Sea right at your doorstep. Ideal for two families, the four bedrooms (one king and three queens) are spread out in such a way that two of them have their own separate entrance. Spend your days soaking up the sun, swimming in the saltwater pool, gliding along the water on a stand-up paddleboard, or preparing a fresh lunch in the outdoor kitchen. And if you truly want to leave your worries at the door, in-house chef services are available upon request.

Location: Placencia, MexicoThings to do nearby: Placencia Beach, Placencia Pier, Maya Beach

Number of guests: 18Bed and bath: 8 bedrooms, 7 bathsWhy we love it: Panoramic windows, hot tub, in-unit washer/dryer

For extra-large families with great taste, this eight-bedroom beach house is a no-brainer, with jaw-dropping, panoramic views of Lake Michigan and plenty of luxe amenities, from a hot tub and game room to a heated pool. There are gorgeous design details throughout, like vaulted wooden ceilings and circular ship-style windows. Rooms are split between the main house and guest house, with two separate kitchens. Just an 11-minute walk from Saugatuck Dunes State Park, the house provides access to endless scenic trails. Bonus: It’s pet-friendly too.

Location: Saugatuck, MichiganThings to do nearby: Kalamazoo River, Saugatuck Dunes State Park, Oval Beach

#6227. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Not true (unless something changed) stayed here in May 2023 and got Globalist benefits

#6226. United Clears Halfway Mark on Starlink Rollout

Starlink satellite internet service is now available on more than half of United Airlines’ daily flights, the carrier announced Thursday.

The airline said it accelerated Starlink installations ahead of the Thanksgiving travel period. It expects to fly an average of 500,000 people per day between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1.

Customers can use United’s Starlink Wi-Fi tracker to check whether their upcoming flight is equipped with the service up to three days before their departure.

United selected Starlink as its onboard wireless internet provider in 2024. It first installed the technology on its regional jets and is now working on its long-haul widebody fleet.

Starlink Wi-Fi is free for MileagePlus members.

United expects to have Starlink on nearly 64% of daily flights by the end of the year. Installations should be complete by the end of 2027, officials said.

#6225. Rocket Failure Destroys 40 Amazon Leo Satellites And Complicates Delta Air Lines Wi-Fi Plans

Delta Air Lines made a calculated bet when it chose Amazon Leo over Starlink for its next-generation Wi-Fi. That bet became a little riskier on Sunday when a rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites failed before reaching orbit.

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on November 15, 2026, carrying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the low-Earth-orbit network Amazon is building to compete with Starlink.

About 10 minutes after launch, the rocket suffered what ULA called an “anomaly” and failed to deliver the satellites into orbit. The entire payload was lost. ULA, a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, issued the following statement:

“Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.

“Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.

“We will work closely with our customer and other appropriate organizations to find the cause, determine the appropriate corrective action, and return to flight as quickly as possible.”

This was the first complete mission failure in ULA’s approximately 20-year history and the first Amazon Leo launch aboard a Vulcan rocket.

The loss of 40 satellites is significant, but it certainly does not destroy the Amazon Leo project. Before Sunday’s failure, Amazon had already placed 398 satellites into orbit across 14 launches. The planned constellation calls for 3,236 satellites to provide global coverage, meaning Amazon had deployed about 12% of the initial network before this launch.

Amazon also has hundreds of satellites reportedly ready for launch and is not exclusively dependent on Vulcan. Its next mission, using an Ariane 6 rocket to carry 36 more satellites, is scheduled for November 23 from French Guiana.

So this is not necessarily a case of the entire Leo launch schedule stopping while ULA investigates. Amazon has contracts with several launch providers and can continue expanding its satellite network using other rockets. Still, Amazon planned to use Vulcan for dozens of missions. Any lengthy investigation or redesign could slow the deployment schedule and place more pressure on its other launch partners.

Delta has committed to installing Amazon Leo on an initial 500 aircraft beginning in 2028. The carrier promises download speeds of up to 1 Gbps and upload speeds of up to 400 Mbps through a purpose-built antenna, with service remaining free for SkyMiles members.

But unlike Starlink, which is already operating on hundreds of commercial aircraft, Amazon Leo remains a system under construction. Delta chose a product based on what it is expected to become rather than what passengers can use today.

That choice was defensible. Delta has a broad relationship with Amazon Web Services and wants to integrate connectivity with Delta Sync, its loyalty program, seatback entertainment, and broader customer data strategy. I have defended the logic behind that decision: Delta was choosing a technology and commercial partner that would allow it to retain more control over the passenger interface and potentially build a much broader digital ecosystem. I’d rather have Delta retain contorl over its system than Elon Musk do the same…

> Read More: Is Starlink A Trojan Horse For Airlines? New Musk Report Makes Delta’s Decision Look Smarter

But choosing an unfinished network carries execution risk, and we just received a vivid demonstration of it. One Mile At A Time puts it well: “One of the risks with picking a service that’s still in development is that the timeline is really quite fluid, and this is an example of that.”

United Airlines is already installing Starlink throughout its fleet and expects to complete the project by the end of 2027. Delta does not plan to begin installing Amazon Leo until 2028. In theory, United could finish bringing Starlink to its entire fleet before Delta installs Amazon Leo on its first aircraft.

Delta is not leaving passengers without internet in the interim. Free Delta Sync Wi-Fi is available across most of its fleet, and in my experience it generally works well on most flights. Delta also says it is adding Viasat capacity and deploying Hughes Fusion technology as it works toward full fleet connectivity.

The suggestion that Delta passengers are flying around without functioning Wi-Fi is simply not accurate. But Starlink is better than any inflight internet system I have used. It is fast, low latency, and remarkably consistent. I increasingly choose United flights where I know Starlink will be available because it allows me to work in the air almost as easily as I can on the ground.

Delta CEO Ed Bastian has defended passing on Starlink, citing disagreements over the business model and customer access rather than any personal dispute with Elon Musk.

Fair enough. But every delay to Amazon Leo gives United more time to widen its lead.

One failed rocket does not prove that Delta made the wrong choice. Amazon has the resources, technology, and launch contracts to build a serious Starlink competitor, and Leo may ultimately deliver an excellent onboard product. But Delta selected a network that does not yet exist at the necessary scale. Sunday’s launch failure is precisely the sort of development that can disrupt a carefully constructed timeline but is also hardly unique to getting new technology up and running.

Delta understood that risk when it passed on a proven product in favor of a deeper relationship with Amazon. Now it needs Amazon Leo to recover quickly and keep its 2028 installation promise. Ultimately, passengers will not be amused if faster Wi-Fi remains years away.

That’s in addition to Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket’s catastrophic explosion on May 28, 2026, during a static-fire test at Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. #6224. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6223. The Moment I Saw This Gorgeous Lake Como Airbnb, I Knew I Had to Plan a Trip to Perledo

Maybe it’s because I’m a dreamer, or maybe it's because I’m slightly impulsive, but whenever I'm planning a trip, I start by browsing Airbnb. I find it the easiest way to envision my time away, and I dropped the notion a long time ago that you don’t actually spend time in your accommodations. That's how I ended up finding myself in a teeny town called Perledo this past summer—my mom had always dreamed of visiting Lake Como for her birthday, so I decided to see what great accommodations I could find in the area for a visit in August, her birth month.

For a stay in Italy, if it’s sleek, minimalist, or modern, keep it away from me. I’m drawn to homes that feel like a reflection of the country I’m in—something uncommon with character and a story. So when I found this unbelievably charming rental in Perledo—a quiet village in the hills above Varenna, overlooking Lake Como—on the Airbnb platform, I booked it for my mom, sister, and I before we even had flights. I mean, look at it!

My family and I arrived in Lake Como on a scorching August day after spending seven days in Sardinia. After a flight, bus, train, and short taxi ride up and around the mountain, we were thrilled to land in our new home. A few days before our arrival, our host, Giulia (having the same name as her felt like a good omen to me!), helped us navigate getting to the apartment from the train, offering us multiple numbers for local taxis, as we hadn't wanted to rent a car. (I'm glad we went that route, because I wouldn't have wanted to deal with parking.)

Upon entering the home, after several trips up and down the stairs, we threw down our bags and immediately made our way onto the balcony. The sunlight beamed through the French doors with the mountains in the background, and the smell of crisp Alpine air made the three of us pause. Staring at the boats as they glided through the water, we all immediately forgot about the long journey it took to get there.

We discovered a bottle of red wine, taralli, and a bunch of Nespresso pods waiting for us on the kitchen table, and I was delighted to find the pantry filled with essentials—salt, pepper, olive oil, and vinegar. You know, those items you might need to complete a meal or a snack, but are annoying to buy on vacation.

The apartment felt warm from the sunlight, but also by design. The pearly walls, with green cabinets and warm wood accents, felt very grounding, like an extension of the atmosphere outside. The tile flooring in the living area reminded me of my cousin's house in Rome, and the pistachio-green-framed window in the bathroom opened wide for a clear picture of the mountains and lake.

After already spending a week with my mom and sister, I was ready for some space, so I opted for the sofa bed with a memory foam topper in the living room. The bed was already made, so it was easy to slip into the soft sheets for a nap after my shower. Throughout the stay, we were mindful not to let the hot water meter fall below a certain level, per Giulia's advice, but between the three of us, we rarely came close.

Giulia also gave us tons of information about the area, including ferry schedules, walking paths, and numbers for hairstylists (I'm always looking for a good blowout). Being able to communicate with her as a local resource felt like we had a personal tour guide with us at all times.

When we left the apartment on our first evening, we followed Giulia’s instructions to catch the complimentary Perledo Night Bus, a service provided by the town from 7 p.m. till midnight, to get to nearby Varenna, where we could grab the ferry to take us to other towns. Walking up and down the mountain, especially at night, would have been challenging and slightly dangerous, so we were happy to grab the shuttle, which was a 10-minute walk from our place.

Unlike Como town or Bellagio, Varenna is quieter, with restaurants that shut down around 9 p.m. Luckily, there are some places to eat and drink in Perledo too. For example, Bar Milano is where locals congregate for their morning espressos or evening nightcaps. For us, it was where we would grab our bus rides up and down the mountain, as well as breakfast (the apricot croissants are incredible).

The walk to Bar Milano was a deeply scenic experience for us—the sunlight glistening on the lake to our right; the lush green mountains dotted with homes to our left. We often noticed fountains and shrines to pray at on our journeys up and down, something consistent on most streets in the village. After arriving home with our breakfast every day, we would start our mornings slow, sitting on the balcony with our espressos and cornetti, taking in the postcard-perfect views of the lake. We often said hi to our neighbors just below us, families who were keen on enjoying the morning air too.

We made few plans for our days, except a reservation for my mom’s birthday lunch. We spent four hours indulging at Passalacqua, the boutique hotel in Moltrasio, and between the beauty of the space, the unhurried pace of the meal, and the kindness of the staff, it’s a memory we will all keep forever. Other afternoons were spent ferry hopping, exploring different towns. In Bellagio, it was imperative we walked down the most famous corridor—Salita Serbelloni. Filled with small artisanal shops and restaurants, it was here I bought a rosary necklace from a man named Filippo, the owner of Bellagio New Wave, a family business that has been in operation for over 100 years. He told me that he grew up above the building.

After days spent on our feet, ears buzzing from the large crowds, nothing was more serene than returning to the quiet of our apartment. Stepping off the shuttle and onto the street for our walk back to the Airbnb brought a sense of tranquility over our three days there, like we were truly going home. Being able to stare into the night sky, overlooking the stillness of the water while being hit with a slight breeze, offered a respite from the adventures of the day.

When I think of Lake Como, I think of two things: romance and luxury. Away from the noise but still close enough to the action, this Airbnb gave us a slice of that fantasy. I now recommend Perdolo to everyone. Safe to say, I’ll continue building my trips around great Airbnbs. The rest always figures itself out later.

#6222. Introduction: I Crossed The Atlantic Six Times So My Kids Could Spend A Month In Germany

Taking my kids to Germany for a month should have required one flight across the Atlantic and another flight home. Instead, getting them there, returning to the United States, flying back to pick them up, and inserting one especially circuitous journey along the way meant I crossed the Atlantic six times…including a memorable detour through Greenland.

I realize I will certainly not win any accolades for my environmental stewardship, but my wife and I are trying to create a comfort with Germany for our kids which includes both the culture and the language. They are German citizens too after all.  And so what I did this summer, as I did last summer and as I will do next summer, was take them over to Germany in mid-July and pick them up in mid-August.

That was a lot of travel for me, but I’m not going to lie: I loved (just about) all of it.

I booked a round-trip economy class ticket in spring to get us home from our ski trip and then back in the summer, which included SWISS economy class ticket from Zurich – Chicago and Austrian economy class from Los Angeles – Zurich via Vienna and was even able to squeeze in an overnight in Vienna at the Park Hyatt, which I booked for 25,000 Hyatt points.

The week I booked (the last week in February) was the week the conflict in Iran broke out and I was very happy I booked when I did because I got the tickets for $764 r/t. I also booked before United cut off awarding mileage on basic economy tickets. Since I booked on United ticketing stock, I received PQPs (status points) and RDMs (redeemable miles) for these flights. I also figured the lack of advance seat assignments would not matter because I was traveling with two young children.  That gamble paid off well and we were seated together at check-in on each flight.

That got us to Germany, but I had to find a way back to the USA and then back to Europe the following month to pick them up, plus a ticket home for all three of us.

Flying Blue came through with a perfectly-timed last minute 60K redemption on Air France from Basel – Paris – New York, plus €453 in taxes. It was such a pleasure to fly on Air France and I look forward to sharing all the details from my A350-900 business class flight.

Recall I landed in JFK around 10:00 pm and drove overnight to Pittsburgh, which itself was a journey. Then from there I flew home via Lisbon, Frankfurt, and Washington, DC…as one does.

But then I had to get from Southern California back to Basel and decided to fly via San Francisco, Denver, Newark, Nuuk (Greenland), and Copenhagen. That was three tickets, including:

I found SAS Business Class saver award space to get the three of us back to the USA, which has to be one of the best deals out there at 60K EuroBonus miles for me and only 30K miles for the kids, which included business class from ZRH-CPH as well. Taxes were €214.59 total for the three of us.

The flight availability forced an overnight in Copenhagen, but a late arrival so we used 36,000 Marriott Bonvoy points to stay at the AC Hotel Bella Sky Copenhagen near the airport, a towering property that was perfect for the overnight layover.

I won’t review the JetBlue A220 flight to Burbank since we all fell asleep right away after too much Taco Bell in Times Square…

These are the segments for this trip report:

I look forward to sharing this report with you!

#6221. American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at this elite status, and talk about what it is, how you can earn it, what the benefits are, etc. The truth is that very little is officially published about this, so we mostly have to go off of data points.

The reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines. That’s because a not-insignificant portion of the frequent flyer community finds this status to be rather “sexy,” and will go out of their way to earn it. Since the qualification requirements aren’t published, it keeps people on the hamster wheel, booking as many expensive tickets as possible.

On the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level. There’s no published criteria to earn it, and it has to be renewed every program year, so you can earn it one year and lose it the next.

Going back many years, Concierge Key was completely separate from the AAdvantage program, but that’s no longer the case. Nowadays Concierge Key is a formal part of the AAdvantage program, and it’s a tier above Executive Platinum status (American’s highest elite tier with published qualification criteria).

I think it’s also worth mentioning that Concierge Key is perhaps the most well-known invitation-only elite status in the industry, as it was a major theme of the popular 2009 movie “Up In The Air,” starring George Clooney. Ugh, I can’t believe that was over 15 years ago.

The criteria to earn Concierge Key is not published, but generally there are a few ways to earn it.

One way is to spend a ton on American Airlines travel. We’re talking $50,000+ of spending per year. That’s not to say that spending $50,001 will get you Concierge Key status, but rather that if you spend less than that, don’t assume you have any real chance of being invited. As a matter of fact, nowadays you might need to spend significantly more than that. So you absolutely can earn Concierge Key purely through your own travel, and that’s probably the most common way it’s earned.

We don’t fully know what American looks for in this regard, though. Does the airline care purely about the dollar amount you spend, the typical fare classes you fly in (consistently full fare first class, for example), or something else? There are also some indications that the qualification criteria vary based on markets, so you have a better chance of earning it if you’re not living in a major hub city of American.

In other words, on some level it’s competitive, and you’re ranked against other travelers in similar markets. Expect that it takes more effort to earn Concierge Key if you primarily fly out of Charlotte (CLT), Dallas (DFW), or Miami (MIA), rather than out of Atlanta (ATL), Seattle (SEA), or Tampa (TPA).

Keep in mind that nowadays American Airlines elite status is based on the Loyalty Points program, so you can even earn elite status through credit card spending. So, does non-flying activity similarly count toward Concierge Key status? The reports I’ve seen suggest that it does, but you need to engage with the program a lot. For example, I’ve heard of people earning Concierge Key through credit card spending, but we’re talking about many hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending, if not over a million dollars.

You can also earn Concierge Key through the influence you have over others’ travel. Sometimes American Airlines will give Concierge Key nominations as part of a big corporate contract, or to key travel planners who have influence over a lot of others’ travel.

American Airlines is even known to comp Concierge Key to some “influencers.” For example, going back several years, YouTuber Casey Neistat was comped Concierge Key status and was really unhappy when it was taken away.

For avoidance of doubt, I’ve never been offered Concierge Key status, and I’m totally fine with that. 😉

Just for context on how these requirements compare to Executive Platinum, that requires 200,000 Loyalty Points per year. All AAdvantage members earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on credit cards, and Executive Platinum members earn 11x Loyalty Points per dollar spent on flights. So Executive Platinum requires $200,000 in credit card spending or around $18,200 in spending on flights.

American Concierge Key has quite a few published benefits, but some would argue the biggest benefit of the status is better “soft” treatment in the event of irregular operations.

The first thing worth understanding is that Concierge Key automatically comes with all Executive Platinum benefits. This includes everything from oneworld Emerald status, to space available first class upgrades, to complimentary Main Cabin Extra seating, to 120% bonus miles on flights, to three free checked bags, to a free drink & snack in economy, to priority services, to same day flight changes & standby.

This also includes access to the Loyalty Point Rewards program, allowing members to select additional perks, ranging from systemwide upgrades to bonus miles. Beyond that, benefits of American Concierge Key include the following:

Assistance during irregular operations is probably both potentially the most valuable perk, and also the most inconsistent one. On a good day, Concierge Key members may get proactive rebookings when flights are canceled and delayed.

American even has a fleet of cars at hubs for Concierge Key tarmac transfers, so during a short connection you may be picked up planeside and driven to your connecting flight. At the same time, there are also instances where you’ll likely be disappointed, because Concierge Key agents aren’t going to deliver 100% of the time.

If you’re looking to at least get Concierge Key levels of airport support with a particular trip, keep in mind that American offers Five Star Service, which is a paid program for more attentive service at the airport.

In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention some perks that Concierge Key used to offer, but no longer does:

American Airlines understandably hasn’t revealed how many Concierge Key members there are, so the best we can do is speculate. If I had to guess, I’d say there are somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 Concierge Key members. To be more exact, my assumption is that the number is roughly in the middle of that range.

In 2019 there was a clue — American worked with a company to send out chocolate to Concierge Key members, and the company posted that 11,300 packages had been prepared. Now, not all Concierge Key members received this chocolate, suggesting to me that there are more members than that.

If you’re curious how other elite ranks compare, I’d guess the number of Executive Platinum members is maybe 4-5x as high as the number of Concierge Key members. Again, that’s purely speculation on my part, and with the Loyalty Points system nowadays, the number may be even higher than that.

It’s hard to say whether something like Concierge Key is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Concierge Key varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Flagship Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal — you’ll get to board first, but there’s not necessarily all that much more to it.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including Delta 360 and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, though, I’d say that Concierge Key is probably the strongest of the tiers, in terms of the number of perks, including additional lounge access to the carrier’s most premium lounges. A couple of thoughts, though:

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. It gives you priority over Executive Platinum members for just about everything, lounge access, and also (hopefully) proactive help in the event of irregular operations. However, don’t expect it to earn it if you don’t spend at least $50,000 per year on American Airlines flights, and even then it’s not a sure bet.

Is the status life changing? While I’ve never had it, I’m inclined to say “no.” But others certainly may disagree…

If you’re a Concierge Key member (or have been one in the past), what has been your experience with the status? How does it compare to Executive Platinum status?

This is a funny thing to read. Living in Miami, I know three people that CK and they all say the same thing- "its so much traveling, and its not great to live like this".

The staff at the FL in MIA seems to take great pride on their CK customers, a couple of times I overheard conversations between them telling how valuable their CKs are. @Lucky, isn't Flagship First Check-In also available at ORD? enjoyed it many times until 2025 with my non US OWE status

I was a CK for 10 years thanks to my former employer (we did a lot of long haul international travel in business class). The automatic domestic upgrades were nice, the Flagship Lounge access impressed friends and family (said one experienced traveler when we were handed champagne at the FL in ORD, "Wow, I heard stories about this but assumed it was an urban legend"), the expediters at certain international airports were helpful, and getting to the front of the lines during storms and chaotic days like today was reassuring. The most important benefit, though, was the elimination of hassles -- the tight connection, the missed flight and, in one memorable case, helping my daughter get out of Paris in the midst of a nationwide transportation strike when she wasn't even flying AA. My colleagues and I referred to the CK team as "the angels" because they could perform miracles. We often joked (sort of) that our employer could cancel our health insurance, seize our retirement benefits, but that they would have to pry our CK card out of our cold, dead hands. When I left for a new position at a much smaller company, I was able to keep my CK status for the remainder of the program year (about six months). Watching it flip to "Executive Platinum" at 12:01 am on March 1 -- yes, I stayed up to mourn -- was unnerving, but somehow I survived...

#6220. 9 Chefs on the Meals They're Traveling For in 2027—From Korean Soups to Peruvian Ceviche

Any professional chef can confirm that while menu development, staffing, interior design, and operations are all part of running a restaurant or kitchen, finding the time to travel in search of different flavors often feels like a rare luxury. But spending time in a different city or region is key to staying inspired. Even a quick weekend getaway can lead to incorporating new ingredients in familiar dishes, serve as an opportunity to learn a new culinary technique, help forge a connection with one’s own heritage, or connect with peers who are pushing the industry forward.

As the end of the calendar year draws near, we spoke with some of our favorite women chefs about where they’re most excited to visit in 2027—from a sushi counter in Tokyo to the oldest restaurant in Beirut—and what they’re hoping to eat and learn from those travels.

A table at ARREA!, Almuerzo Otoño's restaurant in Álava, Spain

“I went [to the Basque Country] for the first time in 2013, but it was such a quick, rushed trip that I left feeling like I’d barely scratched the surface. I’ve been wanting to go back and really do it right ever since. At the top of my list of spots is Arrea!, Edorta Lamo’s restaurant in Kanpezu, a small village in the mountains of Álava. I’ve heard such wonderful things about it. What excites me is that it’s not the Basque Country most people think of first—as in, San Sebastián with its coastline and all of its pintxo bars. It’s inland cooking, built on what’s hunted, foraged, and grown right there in the mountains. And I'll be eating my way through plenty of pintxo bars too, of course. — Katie Button, chef/co-founder of Cúrate Bar de Tapas in Asheville, and author of Spanish Accent cookbook

“I’m in love with Erin French’s new cookbook [Seize the Supper], and wildly enough, Maine is one of the few states I've never been to. So, I'm plotting something for next summer. I love that it's a mostly female crew, a standout (unfortunately) in our industry. Erin’s focus on local produce and connecting to the earth speaks to my own regenerative cooking and inspires me constantly to dig deeper and deeper. I also admire her ethos of humble simplicity, distilling dishes to their core, filled with soul and properly honoring ingredients, with a nod to her family's heritage. I dream of her play on sweet and savory—like the soft polenta with honey and ricotta.” — Camilla Marcus, chef and founder of Westbourne

The seafood platter at the new Casa Juani in Boulder

Casa Juani's Spain-inspired sea urchin dish

“I am most looking forward to traveling to Boulder to visit my friends Kelly Jeun and Eduardo Vallelobo at their restaurant Casa Juani. Both are accomplished chefs who are experts in Italian and Spanish cuisines, and they recently made Bon Appétit's Best New Restaurants list. I am most excited to try everything on their menu, which is entirely Spanish. Eduardo is very proud of—and from!—Madrid, and the menu celebrates Spanish cuisine and culture.” —Melissa Rodriguez, Chef & Partner at Crane Club & Bar CC in New York City

For cookbook author Rebekah Peppler, edomae-style sushi is a must-eat in 2027.

“[Sushi Meino], a six-seat counter in Tokyo’s Azabujuban neighborhood by Chef Mei Kougo, one of only a few female sushi masters in Japan, has been high on my list since it opened in 2023 and I haven’t yet had the luck of securing a very-difficult-to-get reservation. I'm heading back to Tokyo in the spring and hoping 2027 will be my year! If I don’t get in, I’ll still be heading to Makimaki, her takeout-only hosomaki shop that opened nearby earlier this year.” — Rebekah Peppler, recipe developer and author

Baekyangsa Temple, where Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan hosts meals

Freshly foraged ingredients, including mushrooms, herbs, and greens, used by chef Jeong Kwan

“Eating at venerable Jeong Kwan’s table has been high on my list for years, and I was devastated to be out of town when she and Chef Esu Lee were cooking together at his excellent restaurant Orson in Paris recently. It lit a fire in me to finally prioritize booking a trip to Baekyangsa Temple [where she cooks] to attend one of her demonstrations in 2027.” — R.P.

Street bread Ka'ak is the reason chef Mary Attea will be headed to Lebanon in 2027.

“I'm dying to try manakish and shawarma straight from the source. Plus ka'ak, the ring-shaped street bread with sesame, along with all the spreads from the market. And [I want to pay a] visit to El Soussi, one of Beirut's oldest restaurants, famous for its Lebanese breakfast, especially msabbaha, the warm mashed chickpeas with lemon and tahini. I'd be sure to get an order of beid ghanam as well, which is lambs testicles cooked in lemon and olive oil, served with fattet hummus. Growing up in the US with Lebanese heritage, we often ate many Lebanese meals as a family. But the dishes we prepared and enjoyed were such a small sliver of everything Lebanon has to offer. I've been wanting to go for such a long time so I could experience the vastness of this incredible cuisine and the country's beauty. I was meant to travel there this past March, which was postponed, so it's top of my list for 2027!” —Chef Mary Attea, executive chef of Musket Room and Raf’s in New York City

A ceviche dish at Lima restaurant Al Toke Pez

“I’m especially excited to explore Nikkei cuisine and experience Peruvian ceviche firsthand. In Mexico, we make wonderful ceviches, but I believe Peruvians have truly mastered the art of preparing this dish. I want to experience their approach to seafood, acidity, and flavor in its place of origin, while exploring the broader culinary traditions of Peru. I believe there are many shared histories and points of connection between Latin American cultures that we don’t always recognize, and I want to explore those connections through food. I’m also drawn to the opportunity to experience traditional Mesoamérican markets that are still operating throughout Peru, not only in Lima but in other regions as well. Markets reveal so much about a place: its ingredients, its people, its traditions, and the ways food connects communities. I’d also love to experience Inca culture firsthand and better understand the country’s rich cultural and culinary heritage.” —Norma Listman, chef and co-founder, Masala y Maíz in Mexico City

Traditional Assamese food items on sale at the annual Bhogali Bihu Festival in Assam

“I’m particularly interested in Assam’s distinctive use of black sesame and wild greens. During a trip to Mumbai, I had the opportunity to taste Assamese food prepared by two sisters who cook and preserve traditional Assamese foodways. Their food completely blew my mind. I would love to travel to Assam to learn more about the region’s culinary traditions and experience its food culture firsthand. As a chef who cooks both Indian and Mexican cuisine, I feel a responsibility to keep learning and exploring the vastness and richness of India’s food traditions. India is incredibly diverse, and there is still so much for me to discover. Now, as the mother of a mixed child with Indian heritage, I feel an even greater responsibility to expose him to his culture. Traveling to Assam would be an opportunity to continue learning for myself while creating a meaningful connection between my son and his cultural roots.” — N.L.

“I hosted a pop-up at ADI last year, and was able to witness firsthand the ways in which chef Kanchan [Adhikari] is doing the most incredibly inventive things with food within the South Asian diaspora while also marrying it with a Japanese omakase-style sentiment. One of my favorite restaurants of the past year and I am counting down the days until I can eat a meal in that gorgeous dining room again!"” —Samah Dada, chef and creator of recipe platform DADA Eats

A bowl of pollock soup, a dish local to Inje in South Korea

“Inje is the smallest county in South Korea and is most famous for hwangtae guk (dried pollock) soup. You can find many restaurants clustered together there that serve this regional specialty, but my absolute favorite is a place called Song-yi Sikdang. The brief menu basically comes down to the hwangtae jungsik—a set that includes pollock soup, a whole grilled pollock, an assortment of 12 perfectly seasoned namul banchans, and a warm bowl of rice. Inje is located in the Taebaek mountains alongside rivers and basins, so when you get there, you’re surrounded by stunning landscape and flora, which is absolutely gorgeous year round—ranging from verdant mountains, to golden and crimson foliage, to snowy tree tops. Inje is a short and tranquil two-hour drive from Seoul and feels similar to that of driving upstate on the Taconic from Manhattan. The geography and climate makes it the perfect environment for preparing dried pollock and also foraging for diverse wild greens and herbs (namuls), rare ones that you can only find there and are seasonally available at local farmers markets. —Clara Lee, co-author of Korean Soups and co-founder of food company Queens

I have been wanting to travel to Italy for many years, and Puglia has been top of mind. It feels like a place where food is still very much connected to the culture and deeply rooted in the abundance of the land. Since the provenance of things is our ethos, this feels particularly aligned for me. Anytime I travel (but specifically Europe). “I am really drawn to the simplicity of the cuisine. A beautiful local grilled fish with olive oil, handmade pasta, regional cheeses—these are all things that truly excite me as a chef because their beauty is in how uncomplicated they are. Local, fresh bounty, cooked well: to me this is what makes food memorable.” —Abigail Dahan-Kramer, pastry chef at Provenance in Philadelphia

#6219. Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there. Understandably a lot of people get cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) to maximize the rewards they’re earning for their spending, and that’s a great idea. These cards offer valuable bonus categories, no foreign transaction fees, great travel coverage, and more.

But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense. That’s because hotel credit cards largely offer some incredible perks that more than justify the annual fee, including free hotel elite status, and even some free night certificates. So even if you’re not loyal to a hotel group, it’s easy to get outsized value.

In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.

There are hotel credit cards issued by Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, and World of Hyatt, which offer the opportunity to earn free night awards. To be clear, I’m not talking about the ability to earn points, but instead, the ability to earn free night awards that can be redeemed at a set of properties.

These free nights come in different forms — some free night awards are offered for spending a certain amount on a card, and some free night awards are offered as an annual benefit just for having a card, with no spending required.

So let’s take a look at the details of how these free night awards work, and then we’ll talk about whether they’re worth it. Note that I’m focusing specifically on cards that offer free night awards on an ongoing basis (rather than as part of a welcome offer), and am also limiting this to cards that are open to new applicants.

Hilton Honors has two credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Hilton Honors free night awards are my single favorite hotel free night awards out there, given that they have no category caps, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Hilton points at 0.5 cents each.

Hilton free night awards can be redeemed for standard rooms at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, and there’s only a small list of excluded properties. They’re even valid at Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties that are part of the Hilton Honors partnership. It’s easy to redeem these at properties costing $1,000+ per night.

IHG One Rewards has three credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

IHG One Rewards free night awards are also potentially quite valuable, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value IHG points at 0.5 cents each.

While IHG free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, what I really like is how you can top them off with an unlimited number of points. So if a hotel requires 100,000 points, you could use a 60,000 point free night certificate, and then top it off with 40,000 points.

Marriott Bonvoy has four credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Marriott Bonvoy free night awards are also extremely lucrative, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Marriott points at 0.7 cents each.

While Marriott free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, you can top them each off with up to 25,000 points, to redeem at more expensive properties. So you could book a hotel costing 60,000 points per night by redeeming a 35,000 point free night award, and then redeeming 25,000 additional points.

World of Hyatt Honors has one credit card that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

World of Hyatt free night awards are valuable, but definitely the most restrictive of the bunch. Free night awards issued with the card expire 12 months after they’re issued. I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

Category 1-4 covers a lot of Hyatt properties (these can cost up to 25,000 points per night), but the catch is that you can’t use these certificates to redeem at more expensive properties by topping them off. Still, it should be very easy to get outsized value.

I’ll let my credit card portfolio speak for itself — I have quite the selection of hotel credit cards. They’re not necessarily cards that I spend a ton on, but instead, they’re cards I largely have because of the very strong perks that they offer, which to me, more than justify the annual fee. Let me just give a few direct examples…

I have the Hilton Honors Aspire Card, and it’s my single favorite hotel credit card. The card offers a massive number of perks, but in particular, the free night alone more than justifies the annual fee for me. I try to use this at properties that would retail for $1,000+ per night, so it’s pretty awesome to get that, along with all kinds of other perks, just for having the card.

I also think there’s merit to spending $60,000 per year on the card, if you can swing it. That spending would earn you a minimum of 180,000 points (since you earn at least 3x points per dollar spent with the card), plus two additional free night awards, potentially worth up to 500,000 points. So this is a great card to consider if you’re making a big purchase.

In the case of Marriott Bonvoy, I have both the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card and Marriott Bonvoy Business Card, which get me free night awards worth 85,000 and 35,000 points, respectively. These also in and of themselves more than justify the annual fees on the cards. I generally redeem the larger free night award for a luxury hotel stay, while I redeem the lesser free night award for a stay at a mid-range property.

Lastly, I also have the World of Hyatt Credit Card, and that free night award also more than justifies the annual fee in and of itself. Admittedly I wish the free night award cap would be increased to reflect inflation, but even so, I get a ton of value out of this. At an absolute minimum, I use it when I have an overnight near JFK to stay at the Hyatt Regency JFK, which typically costs $300+ if paying cash.

There are potentially lots of great benefits to hotel credit cards, including big welcome bonuses, easy opportunities to earn hotel status, generous rewards structures for spending, and more.

The best part is that most issuers let you have multiple credit cards, meaning you can potentially earn more than one free night certificate per year. In the case of just about all of the above cards, I’d say the free night certificates more than justify the annual fees.

What’s your favorite hotel credit card free night certificate?

#6218. US Flights Have Been Grounded Nationwide

The United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, with all outbound flights from the US being directed to halt ground operations. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated in a press conference that there was “no indication as of yet” that anything “nefarious” caused the ground stop, and suggested that it was due to a broad was a telecommunications outage.

“There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted,” the FAA said in a statement on X. “Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.”

Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement that the ground stop was due to a "communication issue" and that “FAA technicians are investigating.”

The halt on take offs and landing is in place for both domestic and international flights operating within the US. United Airlines, one of the four largest airlines in the nation, said that the order did not apply to in-transit aircraft: “United Airlines is responding to a nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. United flights that are already airborne will continue. New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place,” United Airlines said in a press release. “United will work with our customers to get them to their destinations once this issue is resolved.”

The last time a nationwide ground stop occurred in the US was in January 2023 following a computer outage in the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) pilot notification system (NOTAM).

CNBC reported that the widespread server outages affecting telecommunications over the past 24 hours were to blame, citing internal information from Alaska Airlines.

According to Cirium, an aviation analytics company, there are 26,284 flights scheduled to depart on November 13 from the US. As of 5:50 p.m., 600 flights have been diverted so far, with 496 of those 600 flights (82.7%) returning to their origin airport and the other 104 diverting to a different airport. At this time 481 have been canceled or no fly nationally, representing 1.83%. This will grow today,” a company spokesperson said. “After 4 p.m. Eastern time today, there were still some 11,000 flight scheduled to depart from US airports today.”

#6217. What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges. When I rank the lounges that I like the most, some readers understandably have very different takes.

I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.

Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.

Broadly speaking, what I’m looking for in a lounge is a (relatively) quiet place to sit, connect to Wi-Fi, recharge electronics, use a clean bathroom, and maybe have some water or coffee. Other things are good to have, but not something I necessarily expect.

There are also some deal killers for me when it comes to airport lounges. Personally, if a lounge is packed, I have no interest in being there, and that largely reflects that over the years, terminals have become much better places to spend time:

I figured I’d share my expectations for lounges, and I’ll break it up into three tiers of lounges (admittedly some of the lines are blurred here):

I think it’s also important to note that everyone is looking for different things in lounges:

I think the two below videos from Cathay Pacific from several years ago oh-so-beautifully sum up what makes lounges great. The commentary in the videos is almost poetic.

With that out of the way, let me share my basic expectations of various types of lounges, and admittedly these reflect my preferences and biases.

My expectations for Priority Pass lounges, airport contract lounges, airline membership lounges, and credit card lounges, are pretty simple. I’m happy if I can actually consistently get in and have a quiet place to sit. Sadly that’s not as straightforward as it may sound, with so many stories of lounges denying entry to club members, Priority Pass members, etc.

What sets a “basic” lounge apart? I’d say showers, bathrooms that are significantly nicer than in the terminals, workstations, a good food selection (ideally with hot food), good coffee, and employees who actually make you feel welcome.

Just to give some examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be exceptional:

My expectations are a bit higher for purpose-built international business class lounges. In addition to what I expect from the more “standard” lounges above, I hope that international business class lounges will have hot food, a more premium drink selection, showers, and workstations.

What sets an international business class lounge apart? I’d say a la carte dining, nap rooms, barista-made coffee drinks, and generally elevated decor.

Just to give a few examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be quite good (we’re actually pretty lucky in North America):

International first class lounges are as premium as they get, so expectations should be high. In international first class lounges I expect a la carte dining, barista-made coffee, some sort of an area to rest, a truly tranquil environment, and staff who make you feel welcome.

What sets an international first class lounge apart? Dining that’s (high-end) restaurant quality, an amazing drink selection, individual nap rooms, spa treatments, and a ground experience that extends beyond the lounge. That’s to say either tarmac transfers or an escort to the gate, and that’s no doubt an area where many airlines fall short.

I’ve reviewed the world’s top first class lounges in detail, so it’s no secret what my favorite options are the Air France La Premiere Lounge Paris and Lufthansa First Class Terminal Frankfurt.

We’re all looking for different things from airport lounges, and I think that’s totally fair. Standards should differ based on what kind of a flight you’re taking, how you access the lounge, what you’re trying to accomplish by visiting a lounge, etc.

Everyone will have a different take on which lounges are great vs. just okay, and that’s fine. While I care about tranquility and good coffee, others care about great food and drinks.

I’m curious to hear from OMAAT readers — what makes a lounge great, in your book?

#6216. American Adds New Routes, Drops Others in Reshuffle at LAX

American Airlines will add new connections and cut others as it works to optimize its network at Los Angeles.

The carrier confirmed Friday that it will launch year-round service from LAX to Reno, Nevada, and seasonal service to Bozeman, Montana, and Grand Junction, Colorado.

LA-Reno will operate three times weekly, starting May 27, 2027, using Embraer E175 aircraft.

The routes to Bozeman and Grand Junction will operate from May 27 to Aug. 9, with Bozeman service using an E175 and Grand Junction flights using a Bombardier CRJ700.

An American official said Grand Junction is a “seasonal market addition” while service to Aspen/Pitkin County, Colorado, is temporarily suspended due to construction work there.

American will also add frequencies on some existing routes out of LAX next summer:

The carrier also confirmed that it will drop service from Los Angeles to Cleveland and Des Moines, Iowa, on February 11.

One of the easiest ways to score a discount is by signing up for REI’s email newsletter. Upon sign-up, you’ll score 15% off one full-priced item, which you can redeem on anything eligible on the site, from backpacks to hiking boots. After signing up, you’ll receive a unique coupon code sent directly to your email; keep in mind you have to use it within 30 days of receipt, or you’ll forfeit your discount. A newsletter subscription means more than just a one-time discount—once you sign up, you’ll be one of the first people to receive updates on all the latest gear arrivals, any upcoming sales, and exclusive coupons in the future, all delivered directly to your inbox.

For the greatest bang for your buck, head to REI’s deals section, which features all of last season’s gear for up to 77% off. Looking for a rain jacket or parka to protect you from the elements? Score savings of up to $200. In need of some hiking boots for your next excursion? They’ve got you covered with up to 70% off your desired footwear, including savings on favorites like 19% off men’s Bondi 9 Road-Running shoes and 50% off Merrell men’s Moab 2 Decon SE hiking shoes. You can also expect savings on backpacks (up to 30% off top brands like Osprey, The North Face, Patagonia, and more), as well as socks (10% off bundle deals when you buy three or more full-priced socks).

Thinking of starting another hobby? There’s never been a better time to exercise your free will (and just plain exercise) by scooping up a new bike or tent to start your next outdoor adventure. Customers can expect savings of up to 30% off bikes and a whopping 50% off camping gear on REI’s deals page. Score big on electric and mountain bikes, like 20% off the Co-op Cycles CTY 1.1 bike, so you’ll be able to traverse any terrain in style.

For those interested in dipping their toe into the camping lifestyle, expect savings on plenty of the gear you’ll need to get started, including tents, sleeping bags, and camping essentials, like a whopping 50% off the REI Co-op Campwell 6 tent. Head out on your next big trip through Yellowstone National Park or Glacier in style, and without the worry that you’ll be underprepared once you arrive. From camping chairs to keep you comfortable around the firepit to video cameras that always capture that perfect shot for your Instagram (or your memories), there are plenty of ways to save on all your necessities—and a few extras just in case.

No longer do you need to head to a store in person and battle it out for the last jacket on the rack: REI’s online outlet has tons of great gear to save on, all shoppable from the comfort of your own home. From shoes and socks to helmets, boots, and bags, expect huge savings on something for everyone. One of my favorites includes 27% off Smartwool Active Fleece Wind pants. There’s also plenty of other deals on travel gear worth calling out, like 30% off the CamelBak All Around travel tumbler and 41% off the Osprey Arcane small crossbody bag. On REI’s outlet page, shop top brands like Arc’teryx, Hoka, Keen, Osprey, Patagonia, Salomon, and Columbia, all in one spot.

For something a bit more consistent, sign up for an REI lifetime membership to score an estimated 10% off every year on all eligible purchases. Memberships are a one-time payment of $30, and last the rest of your life, so you’ll be able to score benefits for years to come. To get your rewards, simply shop as you usually would, and earn back an estimated 10% Co-op Member Reward annually on eligible full-price co-op purchases. Your reward will automatically be uploaded to your account in the following month.

Members get more benefits, like free standard shipping on every order (5–7 business days)—a convenience that non-members can only reap the reward of when they hit the $60 minimum spend. Members also save 20% off on bike and snow shop services, have extended return windows of up to a year rather than the usual 90 days, get free ski and board wax and a flat tire tube with repair, and up to 33% off gear rentals. All of these benefits more than make up for the $30 fee.

As an added bonus, those who sign up by November 12, 2026, will also receive a $30 gift card, which they can use on whatever they please for 30 days after they sign up. To be eligible to receive this gift card, all you have to do is make a $50 purchase at REI and buy your membership in the same order. This means your $30 one-time membership fee is basically free once you take advantage of the gift card.

Give your gear and clothing a second life when you trade in gently used products to REI’s Re/Supply platform—and receive a gift card for eligible items. Simply fill out the trade-in form to get an estimate on your product’s eligibility and credit value. Then drop your products off at your nearest REI store. Once your trade-in is complete and your product has been evaluated, you’ll receive an email with an REI e-gift card that you’ll be able to use to purchase more of your favorite gear.

Your used products will head to REI’s Re/Supply shop. Not only is this a great way to keep textiles and other items out of landfills, but you’ll get money back to spend on something else. These gently used secondhand products are shoppable as well, and at great discounts, so if you’re open to taking home a pre-loved item rather than springing for a new piece, expect to find some excellent savings. The brand is closing its online version of the shop, but customers can still purchase gently used items in its brick-and-mortar stores.

One final way to keep to your budget and still get some great deals is by signing up for the REI credit card. Customers who open an REI Co-op Mastercard get a total of 15% in REI rewards (5% card rewards on all REI purchases and 10% Co-op member rewards). Cardholders also earn 1.5% in rewards on all other purchases when not shopping at REI. As a bonus, there is no annual fee, and the rewards no longer expire.

REI credit cards are only available to members, so you’ll have to complete the one-time sign-up and $30 membership fee, but once you do so, you’ll be able to sign in online and validate your Co-op membership to join and start racking up rewards. All rewards are ready to be redeemed online and in stores at REI as soon as they pop up in your account. As a bonus, customers can expect a $100 REI gift card after their very first purchase outside of REI, but use it quickly, as the gift card expires 60 days after your account is opened.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6213. Hilton Honors Amex Card Bonus: Points + Free Night Award Welcome Offers

For applications through January 13, 2027, American Express and Hilton are offering increased welcome offers on their four co-branded credit cards, and these are among the best deals we’ve seen on the cards. With these lucrative welcome offers, you can earn both points and an uncapped free night award (valid at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, which is Hilton’s highest award cost for standard room redemptions).

Not only are these great welcome offers, but these cards offer valuable benefits for those who stay at Hiltons with any frequency, so if you travel often, it’s worth having (at least) one of these cards in your wallet. In particular, I love the free night awards, given that they can even be redeemed at top Waldorf Astoria or Conrad hotels, or even Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties.

Link: Learn more about the Hilton Honors American Express Card, Hilton Honors American Express Surpass® Card, Hilton Honors American Express Business Card, and Hilton Honors American Express Aspire Card

For applications through January 13, 2027, Hilton Honors’ co-branded credit cards are offering limited time welcome offers, which are among the best that we’ve ever seen on these cards.

In addition to offering bonus points, three of the cards also include a free night award as part of the bonus (and the fourth card offers a free night award as an annual benefit, including the first year). For the purposes of framing the value of the points, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Hilton Honors points to be worth 0.5 cents each.

These are standard Hilton Honors free night awards, which can be redeemed at a vast majority of Hilton Honors properties around the world for a standard room, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I’d consider this to be the single most valuable hotel credit card free night award out there, given that it can be redeemed at a property costing up to 250,000 points per night.

Let’s go over the details of the Hilton card bonuses, from least premium to most premium.
