#6212. Inside 'Grand Theft Auto VI'—and the Real-Life Florida Locations That Inspired It

Set to be released on November 19, 2026, Grand Theft Auto VI is expected to be the most profitable piece of media ever created. Pre-sale estimates suggest the game has made a staggering $476 million in revenue already.

Dreamt up by Scottish developers Rockstar Games, the GTA series has been big business for some time now. The previous instalment, Grand Theft Auto V has reportedly made a whopping $11 billion since its release in 2013. Not bad for a game in which you essentially steal cars and shoot guns.

If you haven’t played the games, you should know that they take place in a sort of shadow version of the US, with each game taking place in a new city inspired by a real-world counterpart. For me, they’ve been a fascinating companion to my travels in America. When I’m in New York, walking among towering skyscrapers, I can’t help but be reminded of Liberty City, the location of 2001’s dark and atmospheric Grand Theft Auto III. On holiday in Los Angeles, driving along the Pacific Coast Highway, the long, ocean-view roads of GTA V’s Los Santos were front of mind.

It works both ways. Red Dead Redemption 2, an open-world cowboy game released by Rockstar between GTAs V and VI, is perhaps the most immersive video game to date. In it, you can wander everywhere from dry, open deserts to lush forests where you can kick back with your horse, camp, and look for rare herbs and flowers. For me, it’s inspired trips to the deserts of the American Southwest and served as an interesting entry point into learning about US history. Now when I’m abroad, I’m thinking of these games, but also learning more about the real-world events and cultures that inspired them. It’s a full-circle moment that only enriches my travels.

These gaming vacations, or ‘gami-vacations’, are becoming increasingly popular. Fans are traveling to Tokyo to visit real-life locations from the Yakuza series and role-playing classic Persona 5, to Paris to see locations featured in the Assassin’s Creed series, to the Pacific Northwest to soak up the vibes of zombie classic Day Gone, and to Iceland to walk dramatic black sand beaches like those in the Hellblade series.

“Santa Monica, the Sunset Strip, and Griffith Observatory from GTA V,” one Reddit user replied to a post asking about video game locations fans wanted to visit in real life. “Old town Tallinn feels like a very fairytale environment to me. If you went in winter, it would feel like a set from Assassin's Creed,” suggests another Redditor.

Far from being confined to their rooms, crouched over consoles, gamers are increasingly inspired to get out into the world. It’s a beautiful tradition, and one that GTA 6 looks set to continue. Set in the fictional state of Leonida, GTA 6 is set to be the franchise’s largest map to date. With six key locations, there promises to be something for every type of traveller. Here’s what you need to know, along with the real-world inspirations for each game location.

“We’re a long way from the ‘80s, but Vice City is still the sun and fun capital of America,” reads Rockstar’s official guide to GTA VI’s base of operations, Vice City.

As fans are aware, the new game returns to the setting of the 2002 release, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. Set in the 1980s, that game borrowed pretty heavily from the story of Brian De Palma’s brace of crime films Scarface and Carlito’s Way, giving players the ability to control one Tommy Vercetti as he rises from the streets to build a narcotics empire. As expected, disco, perms, neon signs and flared trousers were the order of the day.

Updated for 2026, GTA VI’s Vice City is a modern cityscape full of high-rises, trendy rooftop bars, nightclubs. and more. It sounds pretty idyllic, but this being GTA, there’s a shadier side, too. “When the sun fades and the neon glows, everyone has something to gain—and more to lose,” the official longline reads.

The recent Netflix preview of the upcoming game gave us a bit more insight into the locale, including shots of BASE jumping from city bridges, a jewelry store robbery and subsequent high-speed escape, and a shootout through a drug den in a down-on-its-luck neighbourhood. In other words, as the main large city in the game, it looks like there’s plenty to keep Vice City residents occupied—on both sides of the law.

Inspiration: While Rockstar doesn’t explicitly explain that ‘game location X equals real world location Y’, it’s pretty obvious that Vice City is based on South Florida’s party capital, Miami. Despite the criminal element of Vice City, the real-world city has been keen to play on the connection. A New York Times story suggests the city is keen to embrace its fictional twin due to a drastic drop in real-world crime recently. Which is, of course, great news for tourists. For the full GTA experience, you can enjoy Miami’s beaches, bars, and car culture, alongside iconic EDM nightspots like Club Space and E11EVEN Miami.

In Leonida Keys, the dress code is casual and the bars are loaded. “Life in this tropical archipelago isn’t flashy, but it’s easy,” runs the official description. In game, the Keys look like an ideal place to hit pristine tropical waters for a dive, jet ski, or scuba trip. Naturally, there seems to be a strong party boat presence too, with a Spring Break vibe. While we’re sure some absolute in-game carnage will take place there, at present, it actually looks like quite a nice place to unwind and escape the more criminal elements of the game’s plot.

Inspiration: The obvious IRL comp here is Key West, nestled at the very southern tip of Florida. In fact, here you can see the southernmost point in the continental US, just 90 miles from Cuba as the crow flies. As well as a plethora of luxury hotels, casual bars, and seafood spots, you can kick back on white beaches, or enjoy a glass-bottomed boat tour.

For a break from all of this, you can visit the Hemingway Home, where Ernest Hemingway finished books including A Farewell to Arms and To Have and Have Not—that is, when he wasn’t out big-game fishing. The house is home to the first-ever swimming pool built in the Keys, as well as descendants of Hemingway’s famous six-toed cats.

Fans don’t know much about GTA 6’s Grassrivers yet, although the official synopsis does suggest some intrigue: “You never know what lies beneath the surface of this primordial expanse. The gators may be the most famous attraction, but there are far deadlier predators and weirder discoveries among the mangroves.” So far, all we’ve seen is an airboat tour and a birdwatching tower, suggesting a heavy emphasis on encounters with the natural world. Watch this space.

Inspiration: Clearly inspired by the Florida Everglades, Grassrivers will surely have a feel and flavor all of its own. The real Everglades has a rich cultural history. Yes, there are airboat tours catered to tourists during which you can spot ‘gators and learn all about the invasive pythons that are terrorising the ecosystem. And yes, you will be able to try deep-fried gator afterwards. But the real treasure is traditional foods like thick and chewy fry bread, swamp cabbage, or sofkee, a thin porridge made from corn.

And, at the Ah-Tah-Thi-Ki Museum near Fort Lauderdale in the north of the Everglades, you can learn about the Seminole nation, a group made up of Native Americans moving south to escape the British, mixed with escaped formerly enslaved peoples from the area’s plantations.

If GTA 6 were represented on an old-timey naval map, Port Gellhorn a “failed resort on the edge of the map" might be marked “here be monsters.”

We know very little about the area yet, except for the fact that it’s rooted in poverty, with locals pushed to extremes to make ends meet. According to Rockstar, “Cheap motels, shut-down attractions and empty strip malls won’t bring the tourists back, but there’s a new economy in this once-popular vacation spot. It’s fuelled by malt liquor, painkillers and truck-stop energy drinks. Jump on a dirt bike and hold onto your wallet.” In other words, it sounds like a great place for a video game, less so for a holiday.

Inspiration: Again, Rockstar hasn’t been open about which area of Florida Port Gellhorn is based on, but fans and Florida locals think it takes inspiration from Panama City and the surrounding areas in the Florida Panhandle. Off the beaten track of most holidays, Panama City nevertheless has a strong reputation for seafood and water sports. Given its deepwater port, there’s also a strong maritime history. St Andrews State Park might be your best bet for snorkelling, swimming, kayaking and a calm and safe designated tidal pool.

Ambrosia sounds, possibly, like the least appealing locale in GTA 6. It’s reportedly a factory town, overseen by vicious biker gangs. “In the heart of Leonida, American industry and old-school values still reign supreme – whatever the cost. The Allied Crystal sugar refinery provides the jobs, while the local biker gang provides almost everything else,” runs Rockstar’s official primer on the place. The Netflix preview didn’t help. We saw a shootout in a dilapidated house, backyard wrestling, and possibly some mud-wrestling too. Mark this one as the biggest unknown of the game.

Inspiration: Florida locals think Ambrosia is based on Clewiston, Florida and the surrounding agricultural area around Lake Okeechobee. The main crop here is sugar, with Clewiston known as "America's Sweetest Town.” The irony in the in-game depiction is pretty obvious here, but the IRL location is well worth a visit if you’re a fan of fishing, with the local largemouth bass on Lake Okeechobee a particularly sought-after prize.

Mount Kalaga National Park looks like a truly beautiful in-game location, teeming with wildlife and activities from bicycle riding to kayaking. What’s not to love? Well, this bucolic utopia may actually prove to be too good to be true. In the Netflix preview, a televised advert for the ‘Prairie Sandwich’ seemed to take place in the park, suggesting that rather than enjoying the park’s animals in their natural habitat, your main goal might actually be to shoot them. If so, hunting will be an interesting addition to the game, and one that worked well in Red Dead Redemption 2. Of course, players will probably be able to opt out of the bloodshed and just enjoy a nice stroll among the trees instead. Here’s hoping.

Inspiration: While there’s no one-for-one comp for Mount Kalaga National Park, the Southern US States in particular are well known for their stunning national parks. Fans think this one takes inspiration from North Carolina’s Table Rock Mountain, Georgia’s Providence Canyon State Park, and the Suwannee River, which runs through Georgia and Florida. Whatever the real inspiration, if you are visiting Florida, it’s a reminder to get off the beaten path and out of the cities into lovingly preserved wild areas.

#6210. How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt. What are the best ways to redeem World of Hyatt points, how many points do you need for a free night redemption, how does the award chart work, etc.?

Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. There’s no science to that, but rather I think that’s a fair, conservative valuation for what the points are worth. In other words, I won’t redeem points for a hotel stay with Hyatt unless I’m getting well over 1.4 cents of value per point (and that has to factor in the points I’m forgoing by redeeming rather than paying cash, etc.).

It’s important to come up with a points valuation for yourself (it can be different than mine), so that you can decide whether to pay cash or redeem points for a hotel stay.

I have lowered this valuation a little recently, in light of the World of Hyatt award chart devaluation we’ve seen, where Hyatt has gone from three tiers of pricing within each category to five.

World of Hyatt has no blackout dates, which is to say that if a standard room is available for sale with cash, it can also be booked with points.

Now, the important thing to keep in mind is that some hotels have a very small pool of “standard” rooms, and a vast majority of rooms at a hotel may be considered “premium.” If a hotel has 150 rooms, it’s possible that only 10 rooms are considered “standard,” so that’s the major issue you’ll run into when redeeming points at some properties.

Unfortunately in the hotel industry overall, we’ve seen a reduction in the number of standard rooms at many properties that are popular for redemptions, which is essentially a way for hotels to create indirect capacity controls.

Keep in mind that Hyatt has a great points availability calendar, which at least makes it easy to find the nights that are available with points, for those properties that are challenging.

Hopefully this isn’t an issue anyone runs into, but just keep in mind the World of Hyatt points expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. Any points earning or redemption activity resets the expiration of your points by a further 24 months.

Unlike Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt continues to publish award charts for award redemptions (the exception is Mr & Mrs Smith properties, which I’ll talk more about in a bit).

The catch is that at this point, World of Hyatt has five tiers of award pricing for standard room redemptions — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper, and Top — and the variance within each category is huge. So while I appreciate that there’s not technically dynamic pricing, when a Category 1 hotel can cost 3,000 or 9,000 points, and a Category 8 hotel can cost 35,000 or 75,000 points, you’re not exactly getting a lot of assurance.

The standard award chart applies at a vast majority of properties globally, including most Hyatt branded properties. There are eight categories of hotels, and 40 different pricing tiers, given the five pricing bands within each tier. Pricing ranges from 3,000 points for a Category 1 property during the “Lowest” period, and 75,000 points for a Category 8 property during the “Top” period.

Next, World of Hyatt has an all-inclusive award chart, which applies to an ever-growing number of properties across Hyatt’s all-inclusive brands. Hotels fall into one of six categories, with the similar five bands of pricing, all based on double occupancy. Pricing ranges from 12,000 points for a Category A property during the “Lowest” period, to 85,000 points for a Category F property during the “Top” period.

Lastly, World of Hyatt has an award chart for Miraval properties, which are Hyatt’s super-luxurious wellness resorts. Pricing varies based on single or double occupancy, and then there’s also the five bands of pricing.

Note that unlike Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt doesn’t offer a fifth night free on award redemptions. So you’ll pay the points that correspond to the number of nights you’re staying.

World of Hyatt is the only major hotel loyalty program that lets you efficiently redeem your points for suites. This can come in the form of free night redemptions, or in the form of an upgrade award. Unlike with standard room availability, there are capacity controls on suite redemptions, so these won’t always be available just because a suite is for sale.

You can find the standard suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, the premium for a standard suite can range from around 20% to 100%, so there’s quite a bit of variance here. In many situations this could represent a good deal. Of course the ways that hotels choose to designate suites differs by property, so in some cases this can represent a huge upgrade, while in other cases it doesn’t.

You can find the premium suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, there’s also quite a bit of variance here in terms of how much of a premium you’re paying.

World of Hyatt also lets you upgrade to club rooms, suites, and premium suites, using points. You can find the chart for that below, though note that this is only possible when booking a fully paid stay at the flexible rate directly with Hyatt. This requires a rate code, so it’s not even combinable with Hyatt Privé rates.

There are also more capacity controls here than you’d have if redeeming Hyatt suite upgrade awards, which are issued through the Milestone Rewards program.

World of Hyatt offers Points + Cash awards, whereby you can book a stay at a hotel using a combination of points and cash. This might sound appealing to those who want to reduce the cash cost of a stay using points, or those who don’t have quite enough points for a stay.

Points + Cash redemptions follow an award chart. The way this works, you can redeem 50% of the standard points required, plus you’ll receive around 50% off the cash component of a stay, in comparison to the flexible rate.

It’s always worth taking a look at this, though more often than not I don’t find this to be as good of a deal as just outright redeeming points. Also note that Points + Cash redemptions have capacity controls, unlike free night redemptions.

Hyatt acquired luxury travel company Mr & Mrs Smith, and you’ll find that many Mr & Mrs Smith properties are bookable through Hyatt channels. This is an opportunity to earn and redeem Hyatt points for stays at all kinds of independent luxury properties that you’d not otherwise have access to with a major loyalty program.

While the opportunity to earn points is potentially exciting, the catch is that points redemptions largely represent a bad value. Award pricing is fully dynamic, and you’ll find that in many cases, points only get you around a cent each toward a stay. That’s significantly less than I value them, so I wouldn’t recommend redeeming that way.

While I wouldn’t say it’s my favorite use of points, World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, whereby you can redeem points toward a folio credit that can be applied to on-property dining and spa awards. With this, you’ll get anywhere from 1.0 to 1.54 cents of value per point.

While there are some restrictions to be aware of, this is still something that has the potential to be useful for those with lots of points, who are looking to splurge on incidentals during a stay.

With the Milestone Rewards program, World of Hyatt members can earn Guest of Honor certificates. This extends World of Hyatt Globalist status benefits over the course of a stay, for up to seven nights. These can be applied to any eligible revenue stay or points stay, and offer lots of value.

Those booked with a Guest of Honor certificate receive the standard Globalist perks, including complimentary breakfast, suite upgrades subject to availability, and much more. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there.

World of Hyatt has a generous policy when it comes to letting members transfer or combine points between accounts. World of Hyatt members can transfer points between accounts at a 1:1 ratio.

Members can transfer a minimum of 1,000 points, and can transfer in increments of 500 points above that. Members can transfer up to 525,000 points per transaction, and may transfer or receive up to that many points across accounts per calendar year. World of Hyatt accounts must be at least 60 days old in order to send or receive points.

World of Hyatt members are also limited to making one free points transfer every calendar month, and six free points transfers every calendar year. Transfers generally happen within 24 hours, but in rare cases could require additional review, and could take up to 10 business days.

This can be a great way to combine points in order to have enough for a particular redemption, or even to transfer points in order to make a booking out of an elite member’s account, or using a Guest of Honor award.

Nowadays many properties charge resort fees or destination fees, which are essentially a money-grab. All World of Hyatt members don’t have to pay these when redeeming points, which can add significant value. Furthermore, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay these even on revenue stays.

As a further perk, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay for parking on award stays (however, non-Globalist members do have to pay for parking).

World of Hyatt has three elite tiers — Discoverist (10 elite nights), Explorist (30 elite nights), and Globalist (60 elite nights). While status isn’t quite as easy to earn as with some other hotel groups, there are still some opportunities to earn status with credit cards. World of Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards include the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more). You can earn elite qualifying nights and status with these cards:

Even if you’re not a Hyatt loyalist, the great news is that earning World of Hyatt points is pretty easy. However, the ratios aren’t as consistently good as in the past.

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

On top of that, World of Hyatt frequently has promotions for purchasing points. The reason this matters is because there are lots of situations where you could get outsized value simply by buying points from Hyatt and then immediately redeeming them for a hotel stay.

With the above basics out of the way about redeeming World of Hyatt points, how do you get the most value with your points? Let me share my approach to redeeming Hyatt points.

As a Hyatt Globalist member, I exclusively redeem my points for free night award redemptions in standard rooms. While I think there can be value in redeeming points for standard or premium suites, my general strategy is to redeem for standard rooms, and then use suite upgrade awards to confirm suites.

The reality is that I get huge value with my World of Hyatt points throughout the award chart, and not just at aspirational properties. Generally I decide to redeem points if I’m getting at least two cents of value per World of Hyatt point. There are several things I factor into that, though. When deciding whether to redeem points:

With World of Hyatt charging such vastly different amounts across the five bands of pricing, in some cases you’ll get the most value per point when redeeming during an off-peak period, while in other cases you’ll get the most value when redeeming during a peak period. You of course always want to compare the cash rates to the points redemption rates.

With a little bit of effort, I have no issues redeeming a vast majority of my Hyatt points for well over two cents each, in comparison to the cash cost.

Ultimately the reason I collect airline miles and hotel points is for aspirational redemptions. I try to redeem for things that I typically wouldn’t pay for in cash, where I’m getting outsized value.

So just as airline miles are best redeemed for first & business class travel, hotel points are often best redeemed for five-star properties that would cost a lot in cash. So the main reason I earn Hyatt points is to be able to redeem at properties belonging to brands like Alila and Park Hyatt. From Alila Napa Valley, to Alila Ventana Big Sur, to Alila Jabal Akhdar, to Park Hyatt Kyoto, to Park Hyatt Milan, to Park Hyatt Paris, I’ve had some amazing award redemptions over the years.

World of Hyatt is my all-around favorite hotel loyalty program. I greatly value the elite perks I receive as a Globalist member, and I also consistently get great value with my points, especially for aspirational properties. I also love how World of Hyatt points can efficiently be transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, providing an easy pathway to racking up this currency.

Personally my favorite use of World of Hyatt points is for stays at Hyatt’s top luxury hotels, where you’ll almost consistently get the best value, assuming you can find award availability. However, I’ve gotten great value at lower end properties as well.

Now, in fairness, the value of Hyatt points is definitely decreasing a bit at the moment, and on top of that, the reduced transfer ratio from other currencies is frustrating, and definitely eats into the value a bit. That being said, that’s true of the industry at large, as we’ve also seen endless devaluations with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy. I do still get the most value with Hyatt.

What has your experience been with redeeming World of Hyatt points?

When it comes to most frequent flyer and hotel loyalty programs, my philosophy is simple, If it gets too complicated, just walk away. People need to put a value on their time. If you're spending hours trying to figure out how to maximize a benefit, at some point it simply isn't worth it. The complexity often works in favor of the programs, not the customer. #6209. A TikToker Went Viral for Kayaking 500 Miles of Congolese River—and Started an Even Bigger Conversation

Last month the Welsh adventurer and self-described extreme athlete Ash Dykes was paddling along the placid waters of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River flowing through Cameroon, Central African Republic, and Republic of the Congo, when something stirred underneath his vessel, kicking up bubbles. Dykes, with the local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire and cameraman Will Perez, had just pushed off on a kayaking trip through the Congo Basin, the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike. The team knew they might encounter lowland gorillas, or perhaps forest elephants, as they made their way nearly 500 miles down the river. Perez then brought up another possible cause for the sudden ripples: a hippo. If the travelers had happened upon a hippopotamus, as many locals had warned them about, they were in immediate peril.

In October, adventurer Ash Dykes, local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire, and cameraman Will Perez embarked on a 500-mile kayaking trip in Republic of the Congo.

When Dykes posted the minute-and-a-half-long video of this “encounter” in the Sangha—cause still unknown—the post racked up over 8 million views on TikTok. The thousands-deep comments section, full of viewers hooked as to what might happen next, burst with theories: Some swore that Mami Wata, a water spirit said to frequent the riverbanks, had caused the sudden movement. One user mused that the three men were in “a real game of Hungry Hungry Hippos,” while others zoomed in on Perez’s visibly tense expression. Another user quipped: “I quit my job to focus on this expedition.”

Though intended as a joke, the latter reaction succinctly illustrates the attention this trip has garnered on social media. For weeks millions of viewers were glued to the team’s frequent TikTok dispatches—which they later fleshed out into a longer YouTube series of deep dives. The videos documented the logistical hurdles in reaching the Sangha; their trudging amid the heat and threat of parasites and disease; their day spent with the Ba’Aka people, a seminomadic Indigenous tribe in Dzanga-Sangha Protected Area, where they foraged for wild coconut and joined a traditional hunt; and extended stretches of the three bobbing through calm waters. Those following online celebrated alongside the men when they spotted forest elephants, and their pulses quickened when they outran a swarm of bees chasing their kayaks. When the team went abruptly silent for a prolonged stretch, following a power bank failure, viewers worried that something catastrophic had happened.

The Congo Basin is the world’s second-largest rainforest and a critical ecosystem for humans and wildlife alike.

The Sangha expedition—or “mission,” as Dykes has dubbed it—was the first leg in an ambitious undertaking called Project 6. The venture involves the Welshman—who’s made a career of adventure travel and breaking world records (such as becoming the first person to walk the length of the 4,000-mile-long Yangtze River, which took him nearly a year)—traverse “extreme” parts of the globe by performing intensive feats of athleticism. He will soon cross Kyrgyzstan on horseback in subzero temperatures for the second installment of the project; he is revealing ensuing stops one by one.

“I'm fascinated with corners of the world that I am unfamiliar with and learning from the people there that call it home,” Dykes says. “Then [it’s] mixed in with the challenge of: Can I do what is deemed impossible, or can I do what people have tried to do before but failed to complete?”

Aside from accomplishing the athletic challenge of constantly paddling down the Sangha every day for weeks, Dykes says he aimed to showcase the beauty of the Congo Basin, and its inhabitants, in a responsible way—stressing to viewers that “you can go to places like this as long as you put the right preparation in,” he says.

Video on TikTok and Youtube showed the trio of Tuyumvire, Perez, and Dykes on their river adventure.

Dykes is quick to credit those who made the Congo Basin excursion possible—especially Tuyumvire, who works in conservation advocacy and ecotourism through his Kigali-based company, Kumbukumbu Tours. Born in a forest village near Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of Congo, he fled the region following the civil war and lived in a refugee camp for over a decade before founding his tour company in 2015; he says those experiences shaped his belief that responsible tourism can be a means of helping make a local impact, particularly for young people. Tuyumvire agreed to join Dykes’s excursion because he saw an opportunity to tell meaningful stories about the Congo Basin for a larger audience.

“Because we have been surviving these out-of-context stories or even more exaggerated stories,” says Tuyumvire. “I myself feel the responsibility to always say yes to someone who has the microphone, and I tell the right context.”

Ahead of the excursion Tuyumvire worked with Dykes to pick the specific location for the journey and scouted out the upper headwaters of the Sangha. Tuyumvire offered context and commentary in videos throughout the trip, speaking about the critical endangerment of forest elephants, the deforestation threatening the Congo Basin, and noting that women were on the front lines of hunting when they met the Ba’Aka people.

Yet straddling the line between education and entertainment for a predominantly TikTok viewership resulted in unexpected tensions. Internet connectivity posed a challenge due to the forest canopy; still, Dykes insisted the journey be “as live as possible” online. “I can’t be claiming that this is a lifetime expedition and then we use either recycled content or we go dark,” he says.

Forest elephants are among the wildlife that inhabits the Congo Basin through which the team traveled.

While a plurality of viewers seemed genuinely fascinated by the three-week-long trip, even during less-exciting moments, Dykes noticed that some expressed a morbid glee for destructive content. Dykes says that some online commenters even started to bet money on how the trio might die in the Congo Basin, perhaps at the hands of a hippopotamus or a crocodile. “I think people are lost or confused as to what is a video game and what is a movie, and then what is reality,” he says. “So it's almost like this disconnect where people just wanted to be entertained: ‘If I'm going to the Congo, I want to see you escaping wildlife, wrestling.’” Tuyumvire saw the conflicting responses from viewers as “another kind of challenge for me to…create a story that will continuously be fed to the audience, but that will not also be overcrowded by too much exaggeration.”

Others have criticized Dykes, drawing parallels between him and other foreigners entering so-called forbidding places and, intentionally or not, reinforcing outdated tropes. Guy Dieudonne Moukandi N'Kaya, a lecturer and researcher at Marien Ngouabi University in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, says that Dykes’s trip through the Sangha felt honest in that it showed the “tense coexistence” between humans and wildlife in the region. Yet the way Dykes framed the expedition gave N’Kaya pause: Leading up to the trip, Dykes noted in a TikTok teaser that he would be “dropping into the heart of darkness,” a phrase culled from Joseph Conrad’s controversial, turn-of-the-20th-century novella about a Belgian trading company siphoning resources from the Congo River. N’Kaya says that descriptors such as “heart of darkness” and “unexplored,” which Dykes has also used in some of his posts, erase the presence of those who have long lived within the region: “The Sangha is not empty,” N’Kaya writes over email. “For centuries it has been traversed by people in dug-out canoes—fisherfolk, traders, and families.”

The water of the Sangha River, a tributary of the Congo River, is tranquil—but the threat of disease-carrying bugs, dangerous wildlife, and the physical challenge of traveling 500 miles on human power made this one of Dykes' six missions.

While Dykes emphasizes that he wanted to raise awareness of the Congo Basin, which is under dire threat of deforestation, some viewers have questioned whether the adventure has truly benefited the region—or whether it’s more of a boon to his Project 6 venture. The Congo Basin has long grappled with interlacing issues including extreme poverty, corruption, and illegal mineral mining, which Tuyumvire says stem from the legacy of colonialism and slavery. “People are poor in the sense that they are ready to sell anything they are able to, to be able to just survive,” Tuyumvire says. “People seeing a white person in this region, it brings memories of the past: ‘This guy’s coming for timber. This guy’s coming for minerals.’ Things that really don't give them any kind of hope to develop the area. And that itself, the mindset, is a threat to the forest.”

After returning from the trip in late October, Tuyumvire has been resting and resuming his routine following the physical demands of kayaking. He’d never kayaked at length before a few weeks ago; he says his real motivation was to “share the stories and to try to transform the adventure into something impactful.” The widespread interest in the videos hasn't translated to bookings of his tours, but that was never the goal: “The audience we had is not an audience of travelers, to be honest,” he says. He has been reflecting on how, in hindsight, he wishes he had created a stronger call to action so that TikTok viewers’ curiosity could have a direct impact on the region. (Alongside his tours Tuyumvire helps run the Congo Rainforest Fund, a local NGO that works with local communities to understand threats to the forest and create solutions, such as shoring up educational efforts and job opportunities.)

But he believes that broadcasting the journey did help viewers further understand a place that they may not have been familiar with. “[The] Congo Basin has been represented as a difficult place to access, a difficult, complex place to understand,” Tuyumvire says. “So people were saying, ‘Finally, someone is going to give us the real information’…we want to see them in the reality."

My husband and I have always dreamed of visiting London, but we knew we wanted to do it the right way: comfortable flights and a chic hotel stay, with room left in our budget for things like afternoon tea, souvenirs and even a day trip.

All of that can sometimes require some pretty deep pockets, which is why we spent the past year allocating our spending strategically, using my to earn points toward both our flights and our hotel stay.

But like anyone on a budget, we wanted to get the most bang for our “point.” So when American Express last offered a 30% transfer bonus to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers, I knew I had to jump on the opportunity and book our trip asap. The good news? Amex is offering this same transfer bonus to Virgin again, now through Nov. 30, 2026.

Here’s how I made the most of the transfer bonus, including the redemptions I made and how you can do the same with the current offer.

First, let’s break down how the bonus works:

The American Express Membership Rewards® program is offering a 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers until Nov. 30, 2026. That means every 1,000 Membership Rewards points you transfer becomes 1,300 Virgin Points®. Terms apply. Note that Amex points must be transferred in multiples of 1,000, with a minimum of 1,000 points.

Now I’m no math whiz, but I do know that means 100,000 Membership Rewards points would convert to 130,000 Virgin Points, instead of the standard 1:1 ratio. That's one of the best transfer rates Amex offers.

Several Amex cards earn transferable Membership Rewards points, including:

Editor tip: If you’re new to transferring Membership Rewards, like I was, I highly recommend checking out our beginner-friendly guide that breaks down how to transfer Membership Rewards points to partners like Virgin step by step, along with any restrictions you need to be aware of.

The best part about Virgin as a transfer partner is its surprising breadth. You can redeem your points for flights on Virgin Atlantic, as well as stays at Virgin Hotels and cruise sailings with Virgin Voyages.

I had built up a solid balance of Membership Rewards points through a combination of the Gold Card's welcome offer and my everyday spending, but the limited-time window of that bonus meant I couldn't afford to think about it for too long.

I live in Central Florida, and luckily for me, Virgin Atlantic offers nonstop flights from Orlando

International Airport (MCO) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR). However, Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop to LHR from airports across the U.S., including:

Personally, I’ve always been curious about Virgin’s premium economy cabin after hearing so many great things about it from my fellow TPG colleagues. So for our outbound flight, we booked premium economy, which comes with perks like extra legroom and an elevated meal service.

It cost me 35,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. With the 30% bonus, I only needed to transfer 54,000 Amex points for the two of us, which means I saved 16,000 Amex points on the outbound leg alone.

Note that taxes, fees and charges apply in addition to the points price for reward flights in all classes. These vary depending on factors such as your destination and travel dates, and the applicable amount is shown at the time of booking.

From check-in to landing, the premium economy cabin proved to be the perfect balance of value and comfort. Extra touches like a dedicated check-in desk, a glass of bubbly after boarding, upgraded dining and amenity kits made the experience feel so special. The wide leather seats with extra legroom meant we arrived in London well-rested and ready to explore. I could see why so many people rave about it; it was the perfect middle ground between budget-friendly and comfortable.

The real splurge was our return flight, which turned out to hardly be a splurge at all because I found a nonstop Upper Class flight home from LHR to MCO for just 29,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. Thanks to the bonus, I only needed to transfer 46,000 Amex points total for two people. That's 12,000 Membership Reward points saved on an already incredible redemption. Needless to say, I felt like I’d won the lottery.

I’ll be the first to tell you that it doesn’t get any better than Virgin’s Upper Class for R&R on a nine-hour flight across the Atlantic. The direct-aisle-access seats converted into lie-flat beds, and the amenity kits were well curated. Not to mention that the dining and inflight service made me feel like, well, royalty.

By the time we touched down in Orlando, I had slept through most of the flight, which is a rarity for me as a nervous flyer. We arrived home feeling restored rather than depleted.

Combined, our flights cost us 128,000 Virgin Points plus taxes and fees, which took 100,000 Amex points to cover. The transfer bonus saved my husband and me 28,000 Membership Rewards points across both flights, and we used them to redeem on Virgin Red for a rewards stay at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch.

Once I had committed to the Virgin Atlantic booking, staying at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch was a no-brainer with that 30% transfer bonus. And yes, when you transfer Membership Rewards points to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you can use them toward a stay at a Virgin Hotels property.

On our dates, the stay came out to about 60,000 Virgin Points per night. For our four-night stay, I was looking at 240,000 points in total, which felt like a lot to give up. With the 30% transfer bonus, though, I only needed to transfer 185,000 Membership Rewards points, which was much easier to wrap my head around.

When I booked the hotel, I had a feeling using my points would be well worth it, and from the moment we arrived at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch, my suspicions were confirmed. The hotel sits in trendy East London, far enough from the crowds and tourist traps, but close to the Old Street Tube station for easy access to activities and dining across the city. It’s also a convenient 10-minute walk from Liverpool Street Station, which has direct access to LHR.

The hotel has quintessential Virgin design, with red accents everywhere, from the lobby carpets to the Smeg fridges in the guest rooms. Beyond the rooms, the property has a rooftop pool for the warmer months and a retro hi-fi listening bar called Hidden Grooves, which serves creative cocktails that are perfect after a long day exploring London.

As for how it compares to cash pricing, a comparable room size runs around $450-$550 per night. Our four-night stay on Virgin Points was equivalent to saving roughly $2,000 in cash, which suddenly made the Amex transfer bonus feel like money in the bank.

With our flights and hotels covered by points, we had cash to spend on our most anticipated experiences in London. Here are a few of my favorite trip highlights:

My Membership Rewards transfer to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club covered nearly every big-ticket item on our London trip: flights in both directions, including a lie-flat Upper Class seat home, and four nights at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch. With the 30% transfer bonus stretching every point further, we were able to spend our cash on experiences, dining and souvenirs.

If you've been sitting on a stash of Membership Rewards points, this is one of the best ways to use them right now, and you don’t need to go to London. Your points aren't limited to flights, either. You can put them toward a stay at Virgin Hotels or even a Virgin Voyages cruise. #6207. FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop, Shuts Down The Skies: What’s Going On?

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented. Admittedly we’ve had our fair share of air traffic control issues in the United States over the years. But this is really on a different level, unlike anything we’ve seen since 9/11, in terms of operational disruptions. I guess it’s fitting that this is happening on Friday the 13th.

At 3:54PM ET today (Friday, November 13, 2026), the FAA issued a ground stop for flights across the country, as pilots received the following message:

DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

As of now, the ground stop is through 11:30PM ET, though it’s possible that it’s lifted before then. That timeline clearly reflects the extent to which the current situation is a complete mess, and this won’t be an easy fix.

As usual, JonNYC was among the first to break the news, and he even reported on this before the official ground stop was issued, when airports in the Northeast started having issues, prior to this going nationwide.

Kind of major, started at approx 3:15pmBoston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center, New York Approach have all lost numerous frequencies. All facilities are in ATC Alert. Some sectors in New York Center are unable any traffic currently. Numerous— I mean NUMEROUS frequencies…

“All airspace is currently being sterilized and centers are preparing for ATC Zero operations. Airborne’s should NOT be majorly effected— i.e, at least for now, this is not a “9/11 type of event” where airbornes are being forced to land at the closest airport available. All…

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed this development a while later, sharing that there were “communication issues impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” and he stated that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

As of now, there’s no timeline for this ground stop ending. To my knowledge, I believe this is now the most significant ground stop we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years (since 9/11).

If you’re flying this weekend, expect that things will be a mess. To those flying right now, good luck. Ford is on a flight that was supposed to depart at 3:59PM, so suffice it to say that he had some pretty bad luck here, as they pushed back, and then this happened. I hope not too many others are in the same situation.

There’s a major issue when you have flights landing but flights can’t depart, since you have way more planes than gates. So get ready to be patient if you’re onboard a flight, given the complicated logistics.

What could explain an air traffic outage of this scale? As of now, all we can do is speculate, though there are a few interesting things to point out.

First, it remains to be seen if this is related, but the FAA reportedly began its rollout of the new AI-powered air traffic management tool this week, known as SMART (which stands for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories”).

Timing-wise, it seems like there’s a possibility this could be related. At the same time, you wouldn’t assume this leads to communication issues, which is what seems to be going on here. So it’s worth pointing out the timing, but we have no reason to believe the two things are related.

Yes the FAA began its nationwide rollout of the SMART AI for ARTCCs to use this week. It’s not clear at this time if the rollout is related to this outage, but if it’s a rolling communications issue, it’s much more likely it’s within already established equipment pilots-ATC use https://t.co/PXqSFdOA1q

One can’t help but wonder if a cyber attack might be to blame. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin insists that there are no indications of this being a cyber attack. However, if they’re still investigating the cause, it seems hard to rule anything out.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the agency had no indications of outages being tied to a cyberattack or potential terror threat, adding that the nationwide ground stop was “just a telecommunications outage." https://t.co/cb8xON9Xrz

If this is truly “just a telecommunications outage,” then that represents a major failure. How can air traffic control nationwide have that issue, rather than it just being isolated to one region? Are there no redundancies?

I don’t want to be a conspiracy theorist, but it sure feels to me like some very unusual things are going on. We just saw a huge Microsoft outage, and it has been a very strange week in general. Those two things can of course be completely unrelated, but you can’t help but point it out.

The FAA has grounded flights nationwide, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” For nearly two hours now, no flights have taken off in the United States, making this the largest outage since 9/11, to my knowledge.

It remains to be seen what the cause of this was, and whether this is a tech glitch, a cyber attack, or what. To those flying now (or this weekend), good luck… you’re going to need it!

What do you make of this strange ATC outage?

Total chaos at AA. My MIA/PHX flight first gets delayed according to the alert due to maintenance. I get down to the gate 10 minutes before boarding and a plane is coming into the gate from ORD. Not sure if I misheard, but they let slip in the press conference exactly what the issue is. They connected new equipment to the old legacy and overwhelmed it. This was clearly an IT screw up whilst trying to incrementally upgrade the infrastructure. No more complex than that..... Or somebody plugged a laptop into the network and tried to pre-load GTA6 :-)

#6206. The Real Reason Why The GE9X's 134-Inch Fan Beats Out The Diameter On Every Other Jet Engine Ever Made

Standing at an astonishing 134 inches (340 cm) in diameter, the General Electric GE9X is so massive that its front fan casing matches the entire fuselage width of a Boeing 737. It is an engineering milestone that instantly dwarfs every commercial turbofan built before it. Even so, the true marvel of this colossal design is not simply that it is the largest jet engine in aviation history, but why GE pushed the envelope to such unprecedented extremes in the first place.

For many years now, conventional wisdom in aerospace engineering linked massive size directly to chasing raw, record-breaking takeoff thrust. However, the 134-inch fan tells a fundamentally different story, one rooted in thermodynamic efficiency, bypass physics, and fuel burn reduction. This article explores how expanding fan diameter became the definitive master key to unleashing the true potential of long-haul operating economy, looking closely at the iterative evolution of the widebody power plant.

Moving a larger mass of air at a lower exhaust velocity needs significantly less energy than expelling a smaller mass at extreme speed, and this principle is at the very heart of widebody engine design, as detailed in publications from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. In large turbofan designs, the front fan functions as the main thrust-producing element, generating the vast majority of the total propulsive force while the core primarily provides power to drive that fan. The basic division of labor explains why widebody propulsion relies so heavily on volumetric airflow rather than raw jet exhaust velocity.

Expanding the fan diameter, reaching a massive 134 inches (340 cm), is the single most direct geometric lever available to engineers to scale this mass airflow. Through the widening of the intake area, the engine captures and accelerates a vastly greater volume of ambient air around the hot engine core. The deliberate scaling drives the bypass ratio up to approximately 10:1, maximizing propulsive efficiency and greatly changing the thermodynamic performance of long-haul flight.

The direct operational payoff of these high-bypass mechanics is a decisive reduction in Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC). Because the enlarged fan handles a greater volume of air at lower rotational speeds, it minimizes the kinetic energy wasted in high-velocity exhaust plumes while delivering the smooth thrust required for transoceanic routes. The aerodynamic foundation then removes excessive fuel burn, giving way to that volumetric expansion that is the absolute master key to unlocking long-range operating economy.

Reaching the milestone 134-inch (340 cm) diameter was not an overnight conceptual leap, but the result of an aggressive, multi-year iterative design trajectory during the evolution of the Boeing 777X family. When General Electric initially laid out the propulsion design to succeed the legendary GE90 family, early studies contemplated retaining the proven 128-inch (325 cm) fan casing of the GE90-115B. However, as Boeing refined the aerodynamic profiles, maximum takeoff weights, and ultra-long-range operational targets for the incoming 777-9, engineers realized that minor tweaks would fall short of the radical efficiency leaps demanded by modern airline economics.

Through successive design iterations, GE incrementally pushed the outer fan containment casing outward. The development path saw the diameter step up to 132 inches (335 cm), before briefly testing configurations at 133.5 inches (339 cm), and ultimately locking in the record-breaking 134-inch envelope. Each fractional expansion of the fan face resulted in measurable gains in bypass ratio and mass airflow, which helped to show that in the specialized world of widebody turbofan design, every additional inch of intake diameter can make exponential dividends in overall fuel burn reduction.

The GE9X's step-by-step upscaling necessitated a total rethinking of fan dynamics, as a larger diameter compounds both centrifugal stress and aerodynamic drag if not meticulously managed. So, through carefully tailoring the fan tip velocities and expanding the casing boundaries through advanced computational fluid dynamics, GE made a brand new geometric baseline. This careful stretching of the fan envelope paved the way for unprecedented bypass efficiency that did not lead to a destabilization of the core mechanics of the engine.

Unravel the secrets of the massive GE9X, a jet engine that redefines scale and efficiency in the skies.

Building an engine fan wider than a 737 fuselage is a huge problem for runaway rotational weight. Scaling a conventional metal fan to a massive 134 inches (340 cm) using traditional titanium or heavy alloys would create massive centrifugal loads, needing exponentially stronger containment rings and heavier shafts. It would instantly cancel out any thermodynamic or fuel-burn gains achieved by high-bypass geometry. GE solved this profound engineering problem through advanced material science, with the help of fourth-generation carbon-fiber composite fan blades.

The breakthrough came in the aerodynamic efficiency and material properties of these advanced composite structures. Each fourth-generation blade is stiffer and capable of managing a vastly greater aerodynamic workload, so engineers were able to slash the total blade count from 22 on the legacy GE90 down to just 16 on the GE9X. Furthermore, these blades incorporate specialized steel leading edges and impact-absorbing fiberglass trailing edges to handle foreign object damage, all while maintaining an ultra-thin profile that keeps aerodynamic drag to its very minimum.

Such a radical reduction in blade count, paired with a lightweight carbon-fiber composite fan case that saves roughly 350 pounds (158.8 kg) per engine relative to traditional metal casings, strips away massive amounts of dead weight. By shedding structural mass despite the record-breaking physical envelope, the low-pressure spool can rotate with optimal efficiency. The GE9X is just the latest example of how crucial advanced composites are to the modern widebody power plant design ethos.

The relentless pursuit of fuel efficiency naturally tempts propulsion designers to dream of even larger fan diameters, but the GE9X’s 134-inch (340 cm) envelope is seen as a strict, practical ceiling for direct-drive commercial turbofans. Pushing fan dimensions significantly beyond this threshold triggers immediate, almost uncontrollable structural and geometric penalties that threaten to offset any thermodynamic gains. Chief among these barriers is aircraft ground clearance; when fitted to the 777X, the massive nacelle leaves a tight static clearance above the tarmac, as noted by Jalopnik. Scaling the fan any further would result in substantially taller and heavier landing gear legs, bringing further structural weight penalties that would instantly prevent high-bypass fuel savings.

Furthermore, swelling the fan casing beyond 134 inches leads to crippling aerodynamic drag and frontal cross-section penalties during high-speed cruise. As aerodynamic studies consistently demonstrate, the external drag penalty of an oversized cowl eventually eclipses the internal thermodynamic efficiency gained from a larger bypass ratio. For direct-drive turbofan designs, 134 inches hits the absolute mathematical sweet spot, balancing maximum propulsive mass flow against the rigid constraints of modern airframe integration.

It is quite clear that the GE9X’s monumental fan diameter stands as a definitive milestone in conventional engine design, though even the most impressive engines have caveats. It extracts every available fraction of efficiency from a direct-drive layout, creating the absolute outer boundary of what is physically and operationally feasible for widebody propulsion before radical new architectures, such as open-rotor or geared systems, must take the stage.

A closer look at the GE9X's troubled development.

One of the most counterintuitive realities of the GE9X program is that despite possessing the largest fan diameter in commercial aviation history, it is not engineered to deliver the highest raw takeoff thrust. While its predecessor, the GE90-115B, is rated at up to 115,000 pounds (511.5 kN) of max thrust, the GE9X is calibrated to a nominal 105,000 to 110,000 pounds (467.0 to 489.3 kN), as per Simple Flying analysis. Ultimately, the deliberate reduction in maximum rated thrust highlights a key shift in how modern widebody propulsion is conceptualized and optimized.

The justification for this lower thrust rating rests in the aerodynamic brilliance of the 777X airframe itself. Featuring a high-aspect-ratio composite wing, the 777-9 and 777-8 generate exceptional lift and cruise efficiency compared to the 777-300ER. Due to the airframe being inherently more efficient during climb and high-altitude transit, it does not need that raw, brute-force runway thrust to hoist heavy loads across intercontinental routes that was seen on the GE90-powered predecessor.

Rather than chasing higher poundage ratings, GE engineers channeled every ounce of headroom into slashing Specific Fuel Consumption and mitigating thermal stress across the core. The goal was to tailor engine output precisely to the aerodynamic profile of the 777X, and therefore, the propulsion system achieves elite fuel economy without needing to match the maximum raw output of older, heavier power plants.

The GE9X’s 134-inch (340.4 cm) fan is far more than a showroom spectacle; it is the definition of what thermodynamic optimization should look like. Prioritizing bypass ratio and mass airflow over raw, unneeded pounds of thrust, GE successfully resolved the conflicting demands of modern long-haul aviation, and did so without falling into the trap of brute-force escalation.

Now, with the Boeing 777X family moving closer to full commercial entry, this monumental fan has made the definitive benchmark for widebody efficiency. It proves that the future of jet propulsion lies not in burning more fuel to create raw power, but in mastering the physics of air on an unprecedented scale. Delays have pushed its entry to service way out of initial projections, but when it does finally take to the skies in customer colors, the world will finally be able to see the full power of GE Aerospace's most radical creation yet.

#6205. Livery of the Week: Etihad Partners with McLaren

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

While traditional marketing theories advise airlines to avoid sponsoring events such as motor racing because of perceived associations with “danger” and “uncertainty” — concepts that could reflect negatively on air transport operators — the past couple of decades have seen several airlines establish partnerships with Formula One teams and events.

Today, some carriers are title sponsors of their home Grands Prix. Gulf Air, for example, has been the title sponsor of the Bahrain Grand Prix since its inception in 2004. Singapore Airlines, which has held the same role at the Singapore Grand Prix since 2014, has extended its commitment through 2028.

Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways has been the title sponsor of the UAE Grand Prix since the race’s debut in 2009. This year, it also entered into a partnership with McLaren Racing, bringing together “two organizations with a shared commitment to innovation, ambition, and delivering exceptional experiences for fans and customers around the world”.

To mark the partnership, Etihad has painted one of its Boeing 787-10 aircraft in a special livery, taking McLaren Racing’s distinctive color to the skies.

The livery features McLaren’s signature papaya orange across most of the fuselage — the same color used on its racing cars and team uniforms. The “Etihad” and “McLaren” names appear side by side above the cabin windows, while the McLaren logo is displayed toward the rear of the aircraft against a black background. The tail fin retains Etihad’s signature mosaic pattern, with its colors adjusted to complement the fuselage’s black-and-orange scheme.

Papaya has taken flight 🧡✈️Keep your eyes on the skies and let us know if you spot us 👀#McLarenF1 | #BeyondBorders | @etihad pic.twitter.com/NCHxsdAMTi

The aircraft chosen to showcase the special livery is a Boeing 787-10, registered A6-BMI. It was delivered to Etihad directly from the manufacturer on Oct. 14, 2020.

The aircraft features one of Etihad’s older cabin designs, introduced in 2018. It has 327 seats in a two-class configuration: 32 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout and 295 economy class seats in a 3-3-3 layout. The first 10 rows of the economy cabin are designated “Economy Space,” offering a seat pitch of 35 inches rather than the standard 31 inches.

Not your usual livery 👀 ✈️ See the making of our special edition @etihad x McLaren Racing livery 🧡 #McLarenF1 #BeyondBorders pic.twitter.com/I2SaS0hyR7

Looking for a new airplane model? Head over to our friends at the Midwest Model Store for a wide selection of airlines and liveries.

#6204. What’s My Lebensphilosophie? I Went to the Austrian Alps to Find Out

When I was told the general rule of thumb at Hotel Nesslerhof, an alpine wellness resort nestled in Austria’s Großarl Valley, was that it’s weird if you’re not naked, I listened.

In Austria, being naked isn’t just a physical state. It’s an emotional state, too. Austrians strip themselves down, both figuratively and literally, to achieve a mindset they call “Lebensgefühl,” a deep mind-body awareness and lifestyle that is difficult to define, let alone translate.

Großarl Valley, also known as the “Valley of Alpine Pastures" in the Salzburger Land region of Austria.

Originally a German concept, the idea stems from “Lebensphilosophie,” a 19th-century intellectual movement popularized by big name thinkers like Friedrich Nietzsche, Georg Simmel, and Wilhelm Dilthey. Translating to “philosophy of life,” the framework is centered around the idea that life can only be understood from within oneself, as opposed to through applying external dogmas like logic and science. Life, according to this framework, is a joyful, vibrant, and embodied experience—a philosophy now widely integrated and cherished by Germany’s neighbor, Austria.

Language, of course, falls short when attempting to describe what Lebensgefühl means in practice; this complete awareness of being is a physicality, an emotion, a lifestyle, and a philosophy all rolled into one. It can’t be described, only felt (ah!). It’s the pleasure of simply existing. Leben (life), Gefühl (feeling). It’s an experience I wanted to understand firsthand. So when I found myself in Munich, less than a two-hour train ride from Hotel Nesslerhof, with a lifelong friend oblivious to my schemes, I decided it was time to get to the bottom of it.

The root of Lebensgefühl is being entirely present in a moment: a conscious effort to slow down, gauge your own energy in the here and now, and choose the way you want to live your life accordingly. While the Austrian National Tourist Board uses the concept of Lebensgefühl as a marketing language, the feeling itself is real–and you can cultivate it anywhere. Admittedly, though—hand of accountability raised—it’s a whole lot easier when you’re surrounded by the postcard-perfect Austrian Alps.

Reaching this state of awareness requires an analog attention span and total presence. This is exactly what is demanded of you at Hotel Nesslerhof, which has dubbed itself the “natural happiness hotel.” The sprawling, sun-warmed property is an emerald-colored garden punctured by buttery blonde oak 1643 Austrian longhouse architecture. Here, the world is calm. Quiet.

I arrive burned out, my attention scattered across screens and obligations. Stepping into a place fully immersed in nature with nothing expected of me, is jarring. It's been a while since I've consumed life this way. We’re conditioned to scroll, desire, save, project, and imagine, rather than to simply be—even to just be for a little bit.

Finding the answer started with carving out time and space, and letting go of everything I thought presence was supposed to look like. Next thing, I was naked in Austria with 40 strangers wondering the same thing.

Natural swimming pond for post-sauna plunges in the Zwanzigsechzehn sauna area for guests aged 16 and older.

The hotel’s dedicated wellness area features five co-ed clothing-optional saunas (plus an additional private sauna in select suites), a salt steam bath, infrared loungers, and expansive natural swimming pools. To practice, or fully embody, Lebensgefühl successfully, you must be aware of your environment. At Nesslerhof, the alpine nature allows your body to break away from any externally imposed schedules and return back to your natural circadian rhythm, where an omniscient digital third person doesn't determine your flow; you do.

A Swiss pine sauna in the Zwanzigsechzehn sauna area for guests aged 16 and older.

As a lifelong advocate for a good time, I mustered some gumption to join one of the daily themed sauna “infusions.” During these sessions, a sauna master leads thematic experiences using natural, regional botanicals like thyme, sage, Swiss stone pine, and eucalyptus. It’s held in the adults-only sauna event room, a space large enough to accommodate nearly 50 people.

I walk in—towel on—and it occurs to me I’m the one making it weird here. There’s a lot I can swallow in life, but one thing I certainly will not do is be the person making things weird in a room. So, I lose the towel, join the crowd, and, in a state of mild panic, take a seat on the floor. Now, retrospectively speaking, I couldn’t grasp how all my choices in life had led me to this single, very conscious state of nudity in front of 40 Austrian strangers. There I was—sitting on the floor, completely floored. Which actually made things weirder, because I was later told you aren’t supposed to sit on the floor.

Enter the sauna master. Also nude. A sauna master is like a spiritual guide to a proper schvitz, and the infusions at Nesslerhof are next level material. At pivotal moments, I’m watching him execute rainbow ice acrobatics, teasing large, colorful chunks of ice around the room in a giant spoon before launching them onto the glowing-hot stones. Steam is sizzling everywhere as thick aromatics sweep across the room.

Hotel Nesslerhof's outdoor saltwater pool (with indoor access) surrounded by the Großarl Valley.

And it’s hot. To make matters worse for myself—still on the floor—we’re given a natural body scrub to apply. So, whatever, sure: I start scrubbing amidst the rainbow ice, dense botanical air, and naked strangers unabashedly sprawled across the room in their entirety. I begin to gain consciousness of the palpable sense of self-assurance emanating from everyone as they laughed and chatted heart-to-heart. They were all having…fun. Slowly, decidedly, I reach a state of compos mentis: the only thing mortifying about this experience is my belief that this is a mortifying experience. This is not an intimidating reality. In fact, it’s pretty funny—and wildly inclusive, despite the fact that no one here speaks English but me. For the first time since arriving here, I feel entirely in the moment, free from any pressure to make it something else. I’m there, existing. I watch as my friend walks by the glass door and we lock eyes—him sending a distress call, and me, now a part of the sauna hijinks, completely in on the bit. Yeah, we’re all naked. So what?

Over the next three days, I continue this conversation with myself about the humility of physical form, alternating between stone pine saunas and crystal-clear mountain ponds. One amber afternoon, as I float between lily pads dotted by flowers and busy dragonflies, I stare at the burgeoning purple-pink Austrian Alps blanketing me, and I remember what it’s like to feel small again. Perception, both of ourselves and from others, has never really been that serious, has it? This is the body that’s given me life, the body that makes everything I do possible. Suddenly, I’m aware of every inch, from my fingertips to my toes. And I’m aware of my awareness. Lebensgefühl, for sure.

Mid-mind-body connection, a group of Austrian regulars hand-signals for me to come over for a beer. “For the electrolytes” is their roundabout scientific mojo after two to three courses of saunas and plunges. I catch what feels like an illegal glimpse of myself in the reflection of a sauna door and laugh. Gratitude emerges.

Hotel Nesslerhof's 800 m² natural swimming pond surrounded by a sunbathing lawn.

Gratitude for your body means food is more than just fuel, it’s an offering. The art of a meal has been a ritualistic practice since we were homo erectus: slowing down to practicing eating as an experience, not a function. And an eating environment can communicate a lot: savor this, stay with me, I’m here.

At Nesslerhof, eating was a slow and meditative practice, always beginning with a dedicated space: a seat at their table that was mine for my entire visit, an altar of sorts. Libations aplenty. In Austria, the Vorspeisensuppe—the traditional first-course soup—is served before almost every meal as a ceremonial anchor of hospitality and warmth. It’s often a non-negotiable, and acts as a symbolic moment to ground yourself before eating, or, as I’m practicing as an honorary Austrian here, to ground myself in a state of Lebensgefühl. For breakfast, lunch, dinner, and even the occasional snack, the soup is served first, and my brain instantly locks into being entirely in the moment. How could I not—I’m sipping on fresh ginger, carrot, and seasonal herb soups pulled directly from the mountains of Großarl—the lush valley an hour outside of Salzburg where the property sits.

Daily breakfast spread by the “Gästeflüsterer” team, including a wide selection of regional specialties.

Austrian Zwiebelrostbraten (pan-seared beef roast with crispy fried onions) served with seasonal Alpine accompaniments from the Großarl Valley.

When you are sick, what do you feed yourself to get better? How do people care for you using food? A lot of roads lead back to soup. It’s nourishing, easy for a strained body to digest, and a slow, intentional practice. It’s an antidote to hurriedness, a gateway to culinary Lebensgefühl.

Outside of the soup, a daily breakfast and lunch menu of fresh regional dishes, served on a strict schedule in the main parlor, makes indecision obsolete. In the evening, a five-course dinner at Atelier N, the hotel’s dedicated dining space, feels like stepping into an Austrian grandmother’s kitchen and hitting all the classics: Perftillbauer lamb, roast venison, fried veal Butterschnitzel, and pan-fried fish fillets. Everything is local, organic, and rooted in a genuine "nose-to-tail" principle—completely free of pretentious trends. And everyone here is known by their first name. The baker, Toni, brings fresh bread and pastries every morning. Elisabeth crafts the butter, curd cheese, yogurt, and whey—a real lactose lady. Anni and Sepp Inhög’s bees live on the sunniest side of the valley, which means their honey is something else entirely. Fresh local salmon trout, rainbow trout, brook trout, Arctic char, and local game are sourced directly from the nearby Hohe Tauern National Park. It’s a literal "alp-to-table" dining experience.

Kreuzkogel mountain in the Großarl Valley, accessed by the Kieserlbahn cable car.

The writer stopping for wild blueberries on a hike in the Austrian Alps.

Hotel Nesslerhof's hospitality was the last dance to Lebensgefühl. Longing for an escape–more often than not–coincides with a longing to feel in touch with yourself again. A weltanschauung, or worldview, can easily become skewed by the monotony of everyday life, which is why it takes displacement to course-correct. Human connection—which in this case took the form of the warm hospitality of Nesslerhof's staff—can serve as the intermediary. An agent [what do you that can create safe third spaces, and abstractly direct you to where your values lie.

On a hike just outside Nesslerhof’s front door in Hohe Tauern National Park, I meet one of Hotel Nesslerhof’s owners, Tina Neudegger. She built the property from the ground up with her husband, Hermann, and their three daughters. That’s over 40 years of family tradition and expertise coursing through this space. Tina is a consumingly luminous person, a natural caregiver. What she fosters at the property extends beyond hospitality–it’s a sense of security. It’s a maternal, comforting awareness that I am entirely taken care of, that my environment is safe, and that I don’t need to be on the defense. At Nesslerhof, I receive the same attention she gives her daughters and her husband, who treat the hotel like their home because, well, it is their home.

Employing my primate purpose, step by step with Tina as I teeter along an intimidating alpine cliffside, and attempting to eat a handful of fresh berries I covertly hoarded from a wily bush because I couldn't stop myself, I tune into her flow. We talk about how life can be a comedy of errors, and how we as humans cling to a gravitas that seems funny from a higher perspective. “Life’s simple. You can do anything once, right? So do it,” is Tina’s cheeky motto, something that makes all the seriousness in the world abruptly fade. I’m arrested by the smell of cows and am drawn back to the present. Weirdly, I like it.

The writer above Großarl Valley with Austrian libation.

The August 2026 total solar eclipse dips behind the Austrian Alps.

Later, Tina drives me up the mountain to watch the solar eclipse from Wolke7, her family’s ski lodge, which is normally reached by the Kieserlbahn cable car adjacent to the hotel. We’re on a 40-minute, long, winding road up the Austrian Alps that feels alarmingly close to vertical. I’m bearing intense witness to the fact that there’s no guardrail, but I'm at ease knowing I can free my gaze because of Tina's confidence. We continue on a path that’s already there, a path that's always been there, a path that will always be there. Something about that feels nice. At the summit, I meet the family she’s created in Großarl: her eclectic collection of friends who uphold this alpine town's legacy. They look at her with complete adoration as they pass me homemade Kaiserschmarrn and a Radler. We watch the eclipse slowly fade behind the Austrian Alps—the totality of it lasting just over two minutes.

But as I stand there, witnessing the world in its most sublime form, surrounded by Tina’s friends, who are vivid, complex, and completely magnanimous, the awe I feel expands from my chest, and those two minutes feel endless. I dub Tina the Mayor of Großarl, and as I overlook her valley, 6,500 meters above sea level, I see the whole picture again. At its deepest level, Lebensgefühl–your Lebensphilosophie–is painfully simple. What made you feel alive today? Build the environment for it. Pause and marvel. Continue forward.
